articles.title: Portuguese police with dogs and batons dismantle housing protest camps
articles.summary:
More than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in Porto

Police in Portugal have dismantled housing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto,…

blocks.text: Police in Portugal have dismantled housing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto, baton-charging campaigners in the early hours of Sunday and arresting more than 30 people.

The raids were the latest incident in days of clashes between police and campaigners who – inspired by similar camps in Spain – had sought to pitch tents in central squares to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis.

Dozens of officers, some with dogs, moved shortly after 2am on Sunday to clear out the more than 100 tents that had sprung up in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Police said they had also taken down a smaller camp of about 50 tents in Porto’s Dom João I Square.

The camp in the heart of Lisbon had been set up after thousands of people marched along one of the Portuguese capital’s main thoroughfares to rail against housing prices that have soared past average incomes in the country.

Police described their actions on Sunday as proportionate and said they had earlier urged people to leave the camps of their own accord. The operations in the two cities led to the arrests of 31 people for disobedience and 171 structures were removed, police said on social media. Eleven people were injured, including three police officers.

blocks.caption: Riot police arrest a woman in Lisbon.  Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPA

blocks.text: Reuters reported that 25 people detained in Lisbon had been released with orders to appear in court on Monday.
The group Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) contested the police figures, saying the raids had left more than 20 people injured as police moved into the camps with batons, dogs and rubber bullets.

“Choosing the early morning to deploy police dogs and fire rubber bullets at people who were sleeping or peacefully protesting is a political decision,” the group said in a statement as it called for further protests on Wednesday. “It shows that this government would rather crack down on those who speak out against the housing crisis than solve the crisis itself.”

Fabian Figueiredo, an MP with the Left Bloc, described the police action as a “wound that had been inflicted” on the country’s democracy. “Fighting for a home is a right. So is peaceful protest. The constitution guarantees both,” he said on social media. “Let’s keep going – for the sake of our future.”

The housing protest camps in Portugal trace back to early October when campaigners began pitching tents in Porto, prompting police to clear them out. Similar actions soon began sprouting up in Lisbon, leading to dozens of arrests and reports of injuries as police repeatedly clashed with campaigners.
As European cities grapple with a wave of discontent, much of the focus in Spain and Portugal has been on housing costs that have priced many local people out of the market.
after newsletter promotion

House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while those seeking to rent have struggled with prices that have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises.

Residents have long told of bearing the brunt of a market that has surged as a result of liberalisation, the issuing of so-called golden visas, digital nomad schemes and the proliferation of short-term rentals.

Campaigners have called on the centre-right government to scrap proposed legislation that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The legislation recently passed a first parliamentary reading.

In Spain, the sprawling housing camp in the centre of Madrid marked its fourth week on Saturday, becoming one of the most tangible symbols of a widespread protest movement that has led to early general elections on 29 November.
With contributions from Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections
articles.summary: Serbia is heading to the polls as a student movement attempts to oust longtime populist leader Aleksandar Vučić.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
People queue outside a polling station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city
ByNick Thorpe
Reporting fromBelgrade
Early reports suggest Serbian voters have turned out in large numbers for the country's election, as a student protest movement attempts to end the rule of its right-wing populist leader.

Preliminary reports from the parliamentary election suggest a record high turnout, with 46% having cast their vote by 14:00 local time (13:00 GMT), nearly a million more than the comparable figure for the previous election in December 2023.
The apparent high turnout is fuelling the hopes of opposition party Student List that they can oust Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), who have been in power since 2012.

The snap elections called by Vučić follow two years of student protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.

Anti-corruption movement Student List are running on a manifesto including purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists heading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.
Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
Most commentators suggest that a high final turnout, 65% or above, would favour the students.
Voting ends at 20:00, with first indications of results expected two hours later.

Long queues formed outside polling stations in larger cities and smaller towns alike in Serbia, and at polling stations abroad - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Munich, Los Angeles and Chicago. In Paris, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain.
Tensions are high across Serbia. In Belgrade, police have closed streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK).

In the street nearby, cars at the traffic lights lowered their windows to blast one of the students' anthems from loudspeakers, 'I want three kisses' - a folk song favoured because the Students' List is number three on the ballot paper. Young people on the pavement nearby started dancing.

blocks.caption: Image caption, People wait in line to cast their votes in capital Belgrade

blocks.text: People wait in line to cast their votes in capital Belgrade

Vučić and his SNS party are number one on the ballot paper. He has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.

Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.
SNS posters plastered around cities show two hands clasped together in solidarity: the hands of doctors and nurses, farmers, construction workers, teachers and parents.
"These are the hands that hold Serbia in their palms," says Vučić in his campaign video. "And with these hands, calmly and with dignity, we shall finish what we started."
That is question of this election, continuity or change.

blocks.caption: Image caption, SNS candidate Aleksandar Vučić waits in line at a polling station

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
SNS candidate Aleksandar Vučić waits in line at a polling station
Amid fears of electoral fraud by the SNS, the students have delegated at least two observers to each of Serbia's 8,210 voting stations.

Videos circulating on social media on Sunday morning show a cafe in the southern city of Nis, where ballot papers were allegedly filled out in advance in a practice known as 'chain voting'. Signs in the window read "private party". When they realise that they are being filmed, the papers are quickly hidden.
There have also been reports of attacks on election monitors and journalists at several polling stations.

"We are witnessing a unique experiment in European contemporary history," Žarko Korać, a former deputy prime minister and long-term opponent of nationalist parties in Serbia including the SNS, told the BBC.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ilija Srdanović tops the Student List's 250 candidates, but would not necessarily lead Serbia if they won

blocks.text: Image source, Guy Delauney/BBC
Ilija Srdanović tops the Student List's 250 candidates, but would not necessarily lead Serbia if they won

Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Ilija Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.
The Student List of candidates for parliament also includes doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities

"These are people that don't know each other, you have no idea what their political beliefs are, and we now expect them to create a functioning government. So it's anybody's guess what happens after they win," Korać says.
"On the other hand, if Vučić declares victory this evening, probably late in the evening, I don't think the students will accept that."

Korać suggests that many former Vučić loyalists in high office could change sides at the last moment, if the students win. A close result, however, with both sides claiming victory, could result in weeks or months of political instability.

The electorate is 6.45 million in a population of 6.53 million, raising concerns about the reliability of the electoral register. Serbs from Kosovo, and dual Serbian citizens from neighbouring Bosnia also have the right to vote.
Additional reporting by André Rhoden-Paul

articles.title: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
articles.summary: The authorities had justified the ban by saying online content was fuelling conflict, while the opposition had condemned it as an abuse of power.

blocks.text: Gabon says it has lifted a ban on social media imposed eight months ago - a move that triggered widespread criticism at the time.
The High Communication Authority (HAC) announced the U-turn on Saturday in a televised statement. The BBC has approached the country's media regulator for comment.
The ban had been introduced on 17 February, with the HAC saying that online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions in the country.

The move came as a shock to the central African nation of about 2.5 million people, where social media platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram have been particularly popular with younger people who use it for business as well as pleasure.
Many turned to VPNs in order to continue accessing social media sites following the ban.
The ban had been imposed at a time when the Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema was facing a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election.
Teachers and civil servants had staged strikes over what they said were low pay and poor working conditions.
The opposition said the suspension was an abuse of power.
Nguema won last year's elections with more than 90% of the vote, two years after his coup had ended more than five decades of rule by the Bongo family.
At the time he pledged to reform Gabon, a small, oil- and timber-rich country, where digital blackouts were used by the previous governments to control information.

articles.title: Carlos Yulo dethroned in world vault final, finishes 7th
articles.summary: Carlos Yulo goes home empty-handed this time from the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships after missing out on the podium in his pet events

blocks.text: STRENGTH. Carlos Edriel Yulo of the Philippines in action during the vault final of the 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam.
Piroschka Van De Wouw/REUTERS
Carlos Yulo goes home empty-handed this time from the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships after missing out on the podium in his pet events
MANILA, Philippines – It appears fatigue may have caught up with the Philippines’ gymnastics golden boy Carlos Yulo.

For the second straight final, Carlos Yulo finished off the podium, placing seventh and falling short in his bid to defend his vault crown at the 54th Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in Rotterdam, Netherlands, on Sunday, October 25.
A day earlier, Yulo finished eighth and last in the floor exercise final.
Armenia’s Artur Davtyan claimed vault gold with 14.850 points, dethroning Yulo, who ruled the apparatus in 2021 and 2025.
Yulo scored 13.833 points, with 8.033 in execution and 5.600 in difficulty, while incurring a 0.30 penalty.
However, competing in two international events in just one month proved too much for Yulo.
His World Championships campaign came after Yulo captured gold in both men’s floor exercise and vault at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan.
Joining Davtyan on the podium were Great Britain’s Jake Jarman, who took silver with 14.650 points. Norway’s Sebastian Sponevik secured bronze with 14.366 in the eight-man final.
On Saturday, October 24, Yulo finished eighth in the floor exercise final with 13.233 points, recording 7.633 in execution and 5.800 in difficulty, along with a 0.10 stick bonus and a 0.30 penalty.
Floor exercise and vault are among Yulo’s pet events, having won gold in both apparatus at the 2024 Paris Olympics. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Suspect in shooting death of teen on Missouri highway charged in second road incident
articles.summary:
Man accused of shooting teen, who was driving to a party, has also been linked to shooting of a vehicle days earlier

A man accused in the shooting death of a Missouri teen has been charged…

blocks.text: A man accused in the shooting death of a Missouri teen has been charged in a second shooting incident – both of which involve firing into cars on the highway.

Alyssa Wilson, 17, was shot and killed as she drove down Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri, on 14 October. The teen was on her way to a Halloween party at St Louis Zoo, called Boo at the Zoo, when a suspect fired a single shot into the back of Wilson’s Buick Encore.
The shot struck Wilson in the back, incapacitated her, and sent her crashing into a concrete highway median, according to prosecutors. She was pronounced dead at Barnes-Jewish Hospital.
The suspected shooter, Willie James Herndon, 43, of Texas, had no known relationship to the teen.

“Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” her father Robert Hickman said, as state charges were announced. “She had 60 days until she turned 18, and we were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana, and unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that any more. This was a senseless act.”
Now, federal court documents show that Herndon has been charged in a second shooting incident, this one just a few days earlier.

On 11 October, St Louis metropolitan police received a report that a vehicle was shot just after exiting Interstate 55 in Missouri. Surveillance footage captured a white SUV fleeing the scene – a vehicle that matched the appearance of Herndon’s Buick Enclave.
A shell casing was also recovered from the scene. Prosecutors said they were conducting ballistics tests to determine if it was fired from the same weapon that killed Wilson.

In a federal criminal complaint, prosecutors lay out how they tracked what appeared to be Herndon’s Buick Enclave from the first shooting incident on 11 October, then the scene of Wilson’s death on 14 October, to a Days Inn in Caseyville, Illinois 16 October.

There, prosecutors approached Herndon’s wife Taiya Herndon, 45, and were speaking to her when Herndon “emerged” from the hotel room and began to flee. As he was arrested, he was “screaming words about a shooting”, prosecutors said.

Inside the Days Inn hotel room, prosecutors said they found a ABC-15 rifle “in plain view”, ammunition that matched the kind used in Wilson’s shooting, a receipt from a gas station near the scene of Wilson’s death on Interstate 170, two license plates and handwritten notes describing police vehicles Herndon believed were tracking him.

Federal prosecutors in Illinois have charged Herndon with being a felon in possession of a firearm. He has separately been charged with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in St Louis county, Missouri. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Almost two-thirds of Australians bulk-billed for all GP care amid extra incentives for doctors
articles.summary:
Exclusive: RACGP survey reflects Medicare investments, but experts caution quality of care and outcomes also matter

  • Get our

blocks.text: The proportion of general practitioners bulk-billing all of their patients has more than doubled in a year, a report has found, after the government introduced financial incentives for doctors and practices.

And almost two-thirds (63%) of Australians are now bulk-billed for all their GP care, up from 56% in both 2024 and 2025, which the report says is “likely a reflection of the federal government’s recent investment in Medicare bulk billing incentives”.
The findings come from the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) annual health of the nation report, to be published on Wednesday, which includes a survey of 2,766 GPs.
Of the respondents, 26% of GPs reported bulk-billing all of their patients, up from 12% in 2025.

In November, extra financial bonuses were introduced to practices that bulk-bill all eligible services for all Medicare patients, with those clinics receiving an additional 12.5% top-up payment split between the practice and the doctor.
But the proportion of people bulk-billed for all GP care remains short of 2019 figures, when the report found it to be 70% of patients.
The report, which also draws on Australian Bureau of Statistics data, found the proportion of Australians delaying GP care due to cost fell from 8.8% in 2023-24 to 7.7% in 2024–25.
The RACGP president, Dr Michael Wright, said the findings indicate “greater affordability across the healthcare system”.

“For those patients who have a preferred GP, more than two-in-three were always able to see them when needed,” he said. “These are positive outcomes and show that when governments invest in general practice, patients benefit. Funding gets results.”

Dr Luke Slawomirski, a health economist with the Australia Institute, said while the bulk-billing findings were “certainly good news”, it was important to remember the survey represents about 7% of the GP workforce.
“We should be mindful of possible selection bias and distinguish GPs’ reported experiences from administrative data and measures of patient outcomes,” he said.
Slawomirski said a strong health system depends on more than just affordability and bulk-billing rates, with access, quality of care and patient outcomes also important.

“We should judge the investment by whether people are healthier and receiving better care, rather than how many consultations are bulk-billed,” he said, adding there was still “a sizeable access problem” when one-third of patients were unable to see a GP when they needed to.
Wright agreed, saying “we can’t measure success solely by bulk-billing rates”.
“There is a risk that inequities could emerge between communities if some patients continue facing higher out-of-pocket costs or reduced access to care,” Wright said.
“This means improving affordability by ensuring Medicare patient rebates reflect the real costs of providing care for complex and chronic conditions.”
after newsletter promotion

While Medicare administrative data shows 81% of GP consultations were bulk-billed in 2025–26, up from 78% the previous year, Slawomirski said these figures differed to those of the RACGP in that Medicare measures the proportion of services bulk-billed, rather than the proportion of patients.

The RACGP is calling for increases to patient Medicare rebates for longer consultations, and for the government to establish an independent primary care pricing authority to ensure Medicare funding reflects the true cost of delivering care.
Slawomirski said reforms needed to “go further” than this.

“As the Strengthening Medicare Taskforce recommended, we need to move away from our heavy reliance on fee-for-service payments towards blended funding models, particularly for people with chronic and complex conditions,” he said.

“We also need to support multidisciplinary teams, which the current payment system discourages. An independent pricing authority could help, but the aim should be to pay for the value of care rather than simply reimburse the cost of providing it.”
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare estimated that potentially preventable hospitalisations cost the economy $7.7bn in 2023–24.
“Better primary care could help reduce that burden,” Slawomirski said.
One solution could be to pay GPs more relative to other medical specialists, he said.
“We need more people working in primary care, and a payment system that rewards them for keeping people healthy.”

articles.title: All aboard the TrainTok trend: spotters and staff boost rail content online
articles.summary:
Number of videos about British trains doubles in three months as creators find audiences interested in workings of railways

They are not just gathered at the end of your local train station…

blocks.text: They are not just gathered at the end of your local train station platform any more. Now they are on your social media platforms too.

Trainspotters have played a part in more than doubling the number of videos about British trains on TikTok in the last three months. According to the platform, the rise in rail content is also down to more people seeking information on cheap tickets, facts about the London Underground and tales from train staff.

Posts tagged with #UKTrains have increased by 247% over recent months. The trend has even led to train staff moonlighting as content creators. Shamal Cain, who goes by the handle Tube Bellingham, is a Transport for London employee who shares advice for commuters across the capital.

According to Cain, scrollers are keen to learn more about topics they know little about but that affect their daily lives. “I realised how many people use London transport but don’t actually know a lot of information about it,” he said.

Cain said many commuters were not fully aware of the TfL journey planner or how to avoid penalty fares from not tapping in and out. After noticing the gap, he thought: “Why don’t I just record giving information on what I do?”
He said: “A majority of people commute through TfL. I think because a lot of people are doing that on a daily basis, they’re very engaged with information.”
When Cain joined TikTok, direct messages came in fast, with followers asking him about alternative routes when services were down or for advice on getting a job with TfL.
The popularity of train content has also risen thanks to enthusiast rail influencers such as Nathan Pinnock-James, who makes educational transport videos.

“Since I started posting on TikTok, there’s been a lot of people that have the context of what a train is, how to use a train, but may not have noticed certain aspects of it,” said Pinnock-James, AKA Network Nathan. “They’re like: ‘Oh, wow! That’s quite shocking!’”

He said obscure hobbies thrived on the app. “TikTok has really opened the door to really niche, specific topics coming on to your ‘for you’ page. It’s allowed people to find things that they didn’t know were interesting to them.”

The 24-year-old said he found an audience online by creating videos about the best trainspotting locations, station openings, and explainers on how the shape of train wheels make DLR carriages wobble.

Yazmin How, the head of emerging communities at TikTok UK, said: “It’s inspiring to see such a wide variety of creators, whether it’s professional train drivers, tube historians, young enthusiasts or comedy creators, using short-form video to make transport content entertaining and accessible to everyone.

“The growth we’re seeing in #traintok reflects a real appetite among our UK community for authentic, educational storytelling that connects people, turning everyday travel into a shared community interest.”

blocks.caption: Francis Bourgeois found popularity on TikTok in 2021. Photograph: Alex Lake/The Observer

blocks.text: Short video content about trains, sometimes called TrainTok, has been a growing part of the social media app for years. The media personality Francis Bourgeois found popularity on TikTok in 2021 after his videos of him reacting to British locomotives went viral.

While human creators are jumping onboard, AI-generated videos – including clips that show high-speed trains and passengers falling out of tube carriages – are also contributing to the growth. In late 2025, TikTok revealed that more than 1bn videos that included AI were hosted on its application.
The company said its content operations team “works closely with creators and publishers to support the flow of high-quality content in the TikTok ecosystem”.
TikTok, which announced the increase in train content during an annual trend report at its UK headquarters, said there was a growing interest in niche topics across its platform.
It said searches about history in the UK had gone up by 50% in the last six months, and posts about the National Trust had doubled during the same period.
How said: “The rise of train content on TikTok shows that even a niche passion can build highly engaged communities.”

articles.title: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home
articles.summary:
VW investment creates 4,500 jobs in Georgia comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs

Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its…

blocks.text: Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company Volkswagen struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.

The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.

Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.

Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.
It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.

Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.

The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.
Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.
after newsletter promotion

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
Volkswagen chief executive Oliver Blume told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.

However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.

articles.title: Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases, but infections in Kenya and Nigeria are prompting fresh scrutiny
articles.summary: Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria crossed paths at Uganda's main airport as conflicting accounts cloud the source of one infection.

image.caption: Both patients are known to have traveled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3Image: Sumy Sadurni/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The first confirmed Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria may have crossed paths at Uganda's Entebbe International Airport, according to African health officials, as new information from Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account of the Nigerian patient's travel history.
Uganda, a country reporting no active Ebola infections, has become a focus of investigations into cases thousands of kilometers apart.

Uganda insists that it has no confirmed active cases of the deadly virus. Yet health authorities in Kenya and Nigeria are investigating Ebola infections involving people whose travel histories or contacts are connected to the East African nation.

Both patients passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, according to Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
Health officials say the two may have crossed paths, although it has not been established whether they encountered each other or whether any transmission occurred at the airport.

The differing accounts have raised questions about whether Uganda was simply a transit point for infected travelers. Or could infections be going undetected along some of Africa's busiest cross-border routes?
The latest developments come after Switzerland disputed claims that the Nigerian patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where an Ebola outbreak is underway.
Did the two Ebola patients cross paths in Uganda?
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate confirmed an Ebola case in the capital, Abuja, involving a woman who had recently traveled to East Africa, including Uganda.
"Today we are confirming that there has been one imported case of Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory," Pate said.
The woman developed symptoms on October 7 and visited a private health facility on October 11. Further laboratory testing confirmed Ebola, and she was subsequently isolated for treatment.
Pate said the patient was stable and health officials had identified 44 contacts, including health care workers, caregivers, patients and people who may have encountered her during her travels.
But the woman's journey has become central to the investigation.

Speaking on Thursday, Mankoula said the first confirmed patients in Kenya and Nigeria were both known to have traveled through Entebbe International Airport on October 3. Investigators are examining whether the two patients were at the airport at the same time and whether their movements overlapped.
Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account
Uganda's Health Ministry says preliminary findings indicate that the Nigerian patient traveled to eastern DRCfor business before passing through Uganda without symptoms and returning to Nigeria.
"Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in an October 20 statement.
But, on Friday, Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs directly disputed the account.
"She and her husband did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the department said in a statement to Reuters news agency.
The woman, identified by Swiss authorities as a Swiss national of Ugandan origin, is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja.

blocks.caption: Ebola cases have now been detected in multiple African countriesImage: Afolabi Sotunde/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Thursday, the Swiss government told Reuters that she was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling with her husband in Uganda, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC also said Thursday that they had not received confirmed information establishing that the woman had traveled to the DRC.

The conflicting accounts raise fresh questions about where the woman was exposed to the virus and how accurately her movements were initially reconstructed. They do not, however, establish that she contracted Ebola in Uganda.
Uganda maintains that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says it is awaiting more detailed information from Nigeria about the woman's movements.
Kenya's missing contact complicates investigation

In Kenya, Uganda has emerged in a separate investigation involving the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, who died in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 5. The patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before reaching Kenya.

Health officials have now established that the patient passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, the same day as the woman subsequently diagnosed in Nigeria. Kenyan authorities have since reported additional infections linked to the initial case.
But one aspect of the investigation remains unresolved.
According to Kenya's Daily Nation, health officials are searching for a Ugandan national identified as a contact of the deceased patient.
"We know him (the Ugandan) by name and passport number and from his phone but we are not able to reach him," Kenya's director-general for health, Patrick Amoth, told the newspaper.
The Daily Nation reported that the man was using a South Sudanese telephone number, complicating efforts to establish his whereabouts.
Being an untraced contact does not mean that he is infected. However, locating potentially exposed individuals is essential to preventing further transmission.
Can border screening stop Ebola?
Uganda shares a lengthy border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Ebola outbreaks have repeatedly challenged health authorities.
Cross-border trade, population movements and international travel make it difficult to establish where someone was exposed to the virus.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak
Ebola symptoms typically develop two to 21 days after infection. According to the WHO, people infected with Ebola are not considered infectious until symptoms appear.
Even well-functioning border surveillance systems cannot identify every infected traveler.

The discovery that both patients traveled through the same international airport on the same day illustrates the complexity of tracing potential exposures across multiple countries. It also highlights the importance of reconstructing travel histories and identifying close contacts.
Uganda says it is strengthening screening and public health controls at points of entry. Nigeria has intensified contact tracing and infection prevention measures.
The challenge is ensuring that authorities across different countries can exchange accurate information quickly enough to identify potential exposures.
Anxiety grows in Nigeria

In Abuja, the confirmed infection has revived memories of previous Ebola outbreaks. Resident Peace Kolawole expressed concern about the consequences of another outbreak. "So here is my hand sanitizer, so I'm actually very concerned about it," she told DW.

Others fear that Nigeria's health care system may struggle to respond while many citizens face economic hardship. "Because now people are not even worried about sickness anymore, people are worried about surviving," Abuja resident Jonathan Steven told DW.
Nigeria's health authorities say the patient is receiving medical care and contact tracing is continuing.
What remains unanswered?
Uganda's position between the DRC and other regional destinations offers one explanation for its appearance in both investigations.

But the latest findings have added two significant questions: Did the patients from Kenya and Nigeria come into contact at Entebbe International Airport on October 3? And where did the Nigerian woman contract the virus if, as Switzerland insists, she never traveled to DR Congo?
Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew?

The conflicting accounts from Uganda and Switzerland have made establishing the Nigerian patient's travel history an urgent part of the investigation. The WHO and Africa CDC have yet to confirm the disputed DR Congo travel history.
Uganda's declaration of zero confirmed active cases does not establish that all infections have been ruled out. Equally, the travel histories do not prove an undetected outbreak.

For Kenya and Nigeria, the immediate priority is containing confirmed infections. For Uganda, the challenge is demonstrating that its surveillance systems are effective and reassuring both its citizens and neighboring countries.
The Africa CDC will convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials on October 28 as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.

articles.title: Burnham call for debate on free movement with EU draws mixed Labour response
articles.summary:
Angela Rayner backs PM’s plea for ‘honest discussion’ but MPs in heavily pro-Brexit seats may be more cautious

Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers including Angela Rayner but risks causing concern among fellow red wall MPs.

The prime minister made his plea for an “honest discussion” about free movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.

Burnham said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].

“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

His remarks were supported by Rayner, the housing secretary, who told Sky News that it was “just pragmatism”. She said: “It’s about what is the best deal for Britain and that’s what we are asking the public to look at. The prime minister is clear that you can’t take anything off the table when you’re having a conversation.”

Stella Creasy, a Labour MP and the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means to our supply chains and for jobs for British citizens”.

blocks.caption: Stella Creasy said the UK was ‘long overdue for a grown-up conversation about what EU freedom of movement means’. Photograph: Milo Chandler/Alamy

blocks.text: A number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result. Those in favour of reopening the discussion include Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary.

However, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is among those who have been more cautious about the arguments. Mahmood told a New Statesman event at the Labour party conference that rejoining the EU would not be a “simple, straightforward thing” and there were “quite hard trade-offs”, such as eliminating trade friction without “some of the burdens that also brings”.

A number of Labour MPs with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the so-called red wall in the north and Midlands are also wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU. Those include Jonathan Hinder, the MP for Pendle, who recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement.

Concerns were raised on Sunday by Richard Walker, the Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, who told Times Radio that restarting the debate would be a “dangerous precedent” and that opening the borders would not help the “one million young people that are out of work”.

Burnham’s comments drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”.

blocks.caption: Kemi Badenoch said Burnham ‘hasn’t thought this through or the implications’. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

blocks.text: She posted on social media: “He hasn’t thought this through or the implications. Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn’t want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities.

“We have had more than enough experience of what happens when politicians, including previous Conservative governments, promise control but fail to deliver it. The answer is to learn from those mistakes, not reopen free movement.”

Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called it a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch”. “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty,” he added.

Polling suggests voters in the UK are increasingly open to rejoining the EU or a single market arrangement involving free movement. The concept of free movement was that British and EU citizens could move freely within the bloc, which also shared a single market for goods and services.

During the Brexit referendum, the topic was hotly debated, with the leave campaign arguing that the UK would be able to take control of its borders if it voted to exit the EU. However, in the years that followed, net migration rose to a peak of about 900,000 in January 2020 under a new points-based system, up from 330,000 before the Brexit vote.

articles.title: Ethnic minorities in England less likely to get breast cancer diagnosis from routine screening
articles.summary:
Exclusive: People from marginalised groups more likely to be diagnosed via urgent referral or in emergency setting, research finds

People from minority ethnic backgrounds in England…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: People from minority ethnic backgrounds in England are up to a third less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via routine screening, and are more likely to be diagnosed in an emergency setting, analysis has found.

The research, carried out by academics at the University of Surrey and funded by the charity Breast Cancer Now, involved analysis of 86,564 adults diagnosed with the disease between 2009 and 2019, from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink and the Cancer Registration Tumour and Treatment datasets.

The analysis found that people from Black, Asian and mixed backgrounds, alongside people from deprived backgrounds, were up to 33% less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via screening, while these groups were also up to 31% more likely to be diagnosed via urgent suspected cancer referral, and up to 37% more likely to be diagnosed via emergency presentation.

Manveet Basra, the associate director of public health, inclusion and awareness at Breast Cancer Now, said the analysis revealed that people from marginalised groups “face inequalities at every stage of their breast cancer experience, and tragically this impacts their survival rates”.

Basra added: “This research helps us understand who is less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via screening, [who] might wait longer to get diagnosed or experience delays in treatment, and knowing what barriers they face enables us to work towards eliminating them.

“Determined to improve breast cancer care and survival rates outcomes, we’re funding world-class research that actively identifies and addresses inequities, working with policymakers to improve equal access to screening, and ensuring our information, campaigns and life-changing support services reflect the diverse needs of everyone affected by this devastating disease.”

Breast cancer is the most common cancer worldwide among women. It accounts for about one in four cases of cancer and is one of the leading causes of death in women under 50. Identifying women at higher risk early can pave the way for additional screening or preventive treatment.

The research also revealed that people living with a learning disability faced poorer cancer outcomes: their time to diagnosis was 18% longer than people without a learning disability, and they faced a 10% longer wait time for treatment.
This research adds to existing evidence of the unequal outcomes people from marginalised backgrounds face in regards to cancer.

A previous study showed that ethnic minorities required more visits to GPs than other people before being diagnosed with cancer. On average, one in five people across England require three or more GP interactions before being diagnosed with cancer. But for people from ethnic minority backgrounds, the figure rises to one in three, according to analysis of the NHS cancer patient experience 2022 survey by QualityWatch, a joint programme from the Nuffield Trust and the Health Foundation.

Research from the UK Health Security Agency has also suggested that young black women are more likely to have aggressive breast cancer tumours, experience poorer care and have higher mortality rates, but are significantly under-represented in clinical research.

Dr Rob Kerrison, an associate professor of cancer care and co-lead of the cancer care expert group at the University of Surrey and the lead investigator of this study, said: “We know that some groups of women in the UK have poorer breast cancer survival than others, but until now we have had only a limited understanding of why. Our findings suggest that inequalities in access to screening and timely treatment may be part of the explanation.

“Women from a range of disadvantaged and under-served groups were less likely to have their cancer detected through screening and often waited longer to start treatment. If we are serious about improving breast cancer outcomes, we need to ensure that everyone can access screening and receive prompt treatment, regardless of their background or circumstances.”

articles.title: Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker?
articles.summary: Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is the clear front-runner for football's most prestigious individual prize, which will be awarded on Monday. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an…

image.caption: Harry Kane is already Bayern Munich's seventh top Bundesliga scorerImage: Carina Johansen/NTB/REUTERS

blocks.text: To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. Fans with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, recall Rummenigge as one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or — in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer, in 1996.
That long drought looks set to end on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, the favorite to pick up the trophy at a ceremony held, as a one-off, in his native London.

"It's obviously special for me that the ceremony is taking place in London. "I come from London and lived there for a long time — maybe that's a good omen," Kane told club magazine Säbener51. "The Ballon d'Or would be a massive success for me."

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16 looks to be the main competitor. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain, as well as the La Liga title.
Kane's career not just measured in numbers

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season make for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 158 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," Vincent Kompany said of Kane last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now — it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

Kane continues to improve at 33, a point when many footballers start to regress. Though he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions League against Arsenal on Wednesday. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all-round game. "The pass was one of my best ones," Kane said after the match. "I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals."
Kane's 'greatest strength'

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach, Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after he joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care — he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone, and that is his mindset, and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills, Tuchel said in September as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic. "He is a complete package."

There are detractors who point to perceived "stat-padding," or scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams, and a lot less money, than in England. Though Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

blocks.caption: Harry Kane has missed out on international honors with EnglandImage: Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Should Kane win the award, it will be a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga. Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain would make Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward, though. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.
Domestic trophies won but international success eludes
For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023, before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential," Defoe said. "He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean. … With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggests that he could get better still.

articles.title: Israel to close all West Bank land crossings on election day
articles.summary: After a deadly attack which killed two Israeli soldiers on Friday, the Israeli military has said all land border points between Israel and the occupied West Bank will be closed during Tuesday's…

image.caption: Evacuated Palestinian homes were draped with Israeli flags during the Israeli operation in HebronImage: Mahmoud Illean/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Israeli military said on Sunday that all land crossings between Israel and the West Bank will be closed during Tuesday's parliamentary election.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that, from Sunday, Palestinians would "not be permitted to enter Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley for work" — using terms used by many in Israel to refer to the occupied territories in the West Bank.
The army added that it would enforce "a ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers … as well as the closure of all land crossings throughout Election Day" on October 27.
The announcement came amid an ongoing Israeli military operation in the West Bank following a deadly attack by Palestinian gunmen near the city of Hebron on Friday.
Two Israeli soldiers were killed and three others injured in the attack, according to the IDF, which said the two suspected attackers were also killed.
The Palestinian militant group Hamas hailed the attack but did not claim credit for carrying it out.
Israeli army demolishes Palestinian buildings in Hebron
What have Israeli politicians said?
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to exact a heavy price for the attack which came just days before the poll in which he is facing a tough battle to secure a new term.
The Israeli army said it had been operating in 40 areas throughout the West Bank on Friday and Saturday, with locals reporting that soldiers had announced evacuations over loudspeakers late at night.
Israeli forces said they had "apprehended approximately 40 suspects, including terrorists affiliated with the Hamas and Islamic Jihad terrorist organizations."
The mayor of Hebron, Yousef al-Jabari, told broadcaster Al Jazeera that some 2,200 people had been forced from their homes since Israeli raids began on Friday.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz confirmed that figure, telling Israeli broadcaster Kan that "selected army units are currently operating there" and that Palestinians "will not be allowed to return … until we've finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron."

Israel's far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a Defense Ministry position overseeing civilian affairs in the West Bank, said he personally ordered "the immediate demolition of a row of illegal structures" in the territory following Friday's shooting.
"Anyone who messes with us will quickly understand that he will pay a painful price," he wrote on social media.
Can Netanyahu survive his last big fight?
What have Palestinians in Hebron said?

In the Hebron neighborhood of Ein Deir Baha, vacated buildings were marked by X's and the streets were deserted, except for a handful of Israeli military vehicles, reported the AFP news agency, which added that Israeli flags had been draped on a house apparently taken over by troops.
Higazi Shawer al-Tamimi, 70, a shopkeeper with a senior role in the neighborhood, told AFP he was awakened at 1 a.m. by soldiers who said he had to leave and gave him only a short time to pack.
He added that, for other residents, leaving the neighborhood was much more difficult. "My wife's mother, who is 90 years old and lives in the area, had to be carried out because she is ill," he said.
In Al-Tamimi's opinion, the West Bank operation is taking place because Netanyahu wants to win the election with "the blood of the Palestinian people."

Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister but his security-first reputation was shattered by the deadly attack by Hamas fighters on October 7, 2023, in which more than 1,200 Israelis were killed. The attack sparked an Israeli invasion of Gaza which has left over 73,000 Palestinians dead, many of them civilians.
Following Friday's attack, Netanyahu vowed the response so far would be followed by an operation on a scale not seen since Israel first occupied the West Bank in 1967.
