articles.title: FDR made it a blue bastion – now it’s Trump’s stronghold in California. Is it forever lost?
articles.summary:
Shasta has embraced the Maga movement with gusto – can Democrats ever win back the rural, working-class voters they once relied upon?

A crucial election was approaching and the country was…

blocks.text: A crucial election was approaching and the country was desperate. Despite promises that economic conditions were improving, nearly a quarter of the US was out of work as voters headed to the polls in 1932.

It was the darkest time since the civil war, a period so dire that in California’s capital people fought each other for work. In early 1931, a crowd of 200 men scuffled over a handful of temporary jobs moving back-breaking loads of granite, the Sacramento Bee reported.

That same newspaper urged its readers to find odd jobs to save fellow citizens from hunger and homelessness. Those who had already lost shelter set up along the banks of the Sacramento River, as unhoused people would do decades later, and were, in some cases, near starvation, according to the Bee.

The situation was often even worse in the remote and rural communities further up north, where opportunities were fewer and relief was slower. In Shasta county, which stretches from the northernmost reaches of the Central Valley to the state’s dense forests, residents were struggling.

blocks.caption: Loggers move timber using horses and ‘big wheel’ wagons near Mount Shasta in this 1930 photograph. A ‘donkey’ steam engine can be seen in the background. Photograph: Historical/Corbis/Getty Images

blocks.text: Shasta had been founded in 1850, as hundreds of thousands flocked to California in search of gold. The region became a productive center for gold mining, with newcomers scouring creeks and boring through mountains in search of the precious metal. It was a place of opportunity, a soon to be railroad hub that offered jobs in copper mining, agriculture and the timber industries.
Then came the depression.
In one mountain town, a group of jobless men were accused of setting a blaze with the aim of being hired to extinguish it.

Desperate people returned to the green hills that once yielded fortunes, hoping to find a bit of gold again. “Not getting rich, but I dug out $18.90 last month,” one young man told a reporter in 1931. “I eat, and that beats being jobless and hungry.”

Franklin Delano Roosevelt promised hope and help. He traveled to 41 states during his campaign, making a point to visit small towns and rural areas. When he stopped in Redding, the Shasta county seat, in September 1932, businesses closed and classes ended early so that everyone could see the New York governor’s remarks.

“I am not making this trip a political one. I am making it to learn the conditions and needs of every section of the United States,” he told a crowd of several thousand from the back of a train. “We are not making this fight against the Republican party but against Republican leadership which has brought the country to its present condition.”

blocks.caption: Franklin D Roosevelt speaks from the rear of a train alongside his daughter Anna in Redding in 1932. Photograph: National Archives and Records Administration

blocks.text: His message resonated. Despite Republican insistence that the party would carry California, the state went, as one newspaper declared, “Democratic and progressive with a vengeance”. That was especially true in Shasta, where just over 72% of voters backed Roosevelt.

Nearly a century later, it’s an election result that is difficult to imagine. Shasta is the de facto Maga capital of California, and a center of the US election denial movement. Roughly two-thirds of voters supported Donald Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. They took his political philosophy and ran with it, electing officials who promoted falsehoods about stolen elections and frequently clashed with the state.

During the pandemic, the area drew national attention for its hostility to Covid restrictions. The years that followed brought more turmoil that touched all corners of public life, documented in headline after headline – a journalist assaulted while covering a meeting of local conservative groups, a protester who faced jail time for holding a sign calling for the resignation of an elected official during a public meeting.

For more than a year, the Guardian has explored the political transformation that unfolded here over the 20th century. The story that emerged through conversations with longtime residents, historians, and political experts is one of a community that dramatically veered right amid the collapse of its major industries and became a hotbed for radical conservative politics.

And it’s a chapter in the story of the Democratic party. Shasta can be seen as a case study for how the Democrats have struggled to regain a crucial pillar of the base they once relied upon – rural America – even as they appear on track to win back crucial seats this midterm election.

The small settlement of Cottonwood is perhaps best known for its rugged western beauty, nearby fish hatchery and rightwing militia. It is a place of wide open spaces with sprawling cattle ranches and pristine views of the junction of the Sierra Nevada and Cascades.

Even in a deeply Republican county, the community stands apart for its conservatism. Along the roads, underneath majestic oaks, are old signs for measure B, a controversial ballot initiative voters approved in June that would end nearly all voting by mail while requiring voter ID and a hand count. The effort put the county in yet another legal battle with the state – a judge blocked the measure from taking effect as the litigation moves ahead.

blocks.caption: Cattle graze in a pasture near Cottonwood, with Lassen Peak in the distance. Photograph: Mason Trinca/The Guardian

blocks.text: A few miles away, inside a packed home office not far from the Sacramento River, Pat Carr has assembled a sort of museum showcasing a mostly forgotten history. Old photos of local luminaries with Democratic presidents line the walls, along with letters from White House officials and even a supreme court justice.
The documents paint a portrait of a deep blue region built by Democratic policies.

“When I try to explain that to people here now, they’re going, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me. It couldn’t have been like that’,” Carr, 82, said sitting in front of a table crowded with memorabilia. “Those of us that remember a heyday, we’re almost all dead.”

In the 20th century, Shasta residents played crucial roles in state and federal politics. They chaired California’s Democratic party, helped bring major infrastructure projects to the region, and they served in John F Kennedy’s administration.

Carr knows the history well – it was his family’s. In a photo of Roosevelt’s Redding visit, FDR stands alongside Carr’s grandfather, Francis. Carr’s father and cousin managed Kennedy’s Northern California campaign, and his uncle was the undersecretary of the interior department under Kennedy.

blocks.caption: Pat Carr at home in Cottonwood. Photograph: Mason Trinca/Mason Trinca for The Guardian

blocks.text: “The money was flowing out of Washington into the north state, and the guys that were getting it done were all Democrats,” Carr recalls.

The Shasta Dam is a 600ft tall monument to that era. Constructed with 15m tons of concrete, with a reservoir capable of holding back some 4.5m acre-feet of dark green water, the dam has helped make California an agricultural powerhouse as the keystone of the Central Valley Project.

It sends vast quantities of water from the state’s far north to more arid sections of the Central Valley for farming, and generates enough electricity to power as many as 710,000 homes. The federal government, which manages it, considers the dam critical infrastructure at a level just below the White House and the Pentagon, a tour guide said on a September morning.
During its construction amid the Great Depression and through the second world war, it provided thousands of badly needed jobs.

Roosevelt came to the White House with broad support and implemented an ambitious agenda that over his first term helped build a powerful coalition of labor unions, African Americans, the working class, liberal professionals and white southerners that became the backbone of his party.
Mere months after he took office, there were work camps established in Shasta county through the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC).

blocks.caption: The Shasta Dam. Photograph: Mike Kai Chen/The Guardian

blocks.text: The president’s administration put millions of Americans to work through programs such as the CCC, which enlisted jobless young men to build campgrounds, cut firelines and construct fire lookouts.

The agencies he created worked in virtually every county in the US, helped bring power to vast swaths of the country, and established much of the local infrastructure we now know. Redding, the largest city in the area, received federal dollars to build a fire station, post office, bridge and veterans memorial building.

“That won over the hearts of millions of ordinary people,” said Richard Walker, a professor emeritus at UC Berkeley and the director of the Living New Deal research project. “They felt that the government cared. Critically, they felt they participated. They were helping their own community, whether it was fixing streets and sidewalks or planting trees or building schools.”

The county had scored the most significant investment in the form of the dam, one of the largest public works projects of the era and one of the most important hydroelectric facilities in the world at the time, Walker said.

blocks.caption: Construction workers of the site of the Shasta Dam, circa 1940. Photograph: Frederic Lewis/Getty Images

blocks.text: Most of California’s water is located in the north, while 80% of the demand lies in the central and southern regions of the state. For decades, California had sought a solution to the imbalance and the winter flooding of valley communities. The state couldn’t afford to finance the project during the depression, but after lobbying from prominent Californians including Francis Carr, Roosevelt’s administration funded it.
“Things are more optimistic than ever before in [the] Central Valley. We are delighted with prospects of immediate work,” state senator John B McColl said in 1937 before construction began.

It employed almost 5,000 people at one time – bringing new residents. Construction was under way 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and was considered so vital that some workers received draft deferments during the second world war. The dam translated into enduring Democratic loyalty, said Bob Mulholland, a veteran Democratic strategist and longtime resident of northern California.

“I think there was a certain amount of that commitment or thanks for years, from the workers themselves and the kids, to FDR and the Democrats,” Mulholland said in an interview with the Guardian in 2025 shortly before his death.

The war brought significant growth in the timber industry, as did surging demand for housing in the years that followed. It was an era of opportunity and expansion in this part of the state, with ample jobs in the mills and unions for wide swaths of workers from loggers to retail clerks to bartenders. It echoed what was happening across the US.

“After the war, the United States experienced the greatest economic boom in human history and moreover, even as inequality was declining, the rich were still getting richer,” said historian Harvey Kaye, a professor emeritus of democracy and justice at the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay. “Everyone was doing better.”

blocks.caption: The agencies Roosevelt created established much of the local infrastructure we now know. Redding, the largest city in the area, received federal dollars to build a veterans memorial building, a fire station, and a post office. Photograph: Mike Kai Chen/The Guardian

blocks.text: By 1948, when Diane Kinyon was born, Shasta was one of California’s bluest counties and an important part of its Democratic base. Kinyon’s family had migrated to the area in the 1860s and for generations worked in the industries that helped build and feed California, from the railroad to ranching and logging.

Her parents were “diehard Democrats”, she said. Her father, a union man, was employed by the county road department, working his way up after starting as a mechanic, and also owned a pizza shop with her mother. Her father emphasized the importance of unions to Kinyon who later who spent decades as a union organizer.

“We knew we were union. We knew we were Democrats, and we knew what that meant was that you help people,” she recalled. “But I think on the other side, [those were Republican] values too. They just financially had a different way to get there.”

In the 1960s, the construction of Interstate 5, the nearly 1,400-mile (about 2,253km) highway that runs from Mexico to Canada, opened up the county, and brought more tourists, Kinyon recalled. Road work, along with reservoir projects, offered even more jobs.
The region’s extractive industries created challenges over the years – pollution from the mining industry damaged crops, seeped into waterways and poisoned fish.

Still, a sense of hope hung over the region, along with near constant smoke from wood waste burners at the mills, recalled Pat Carr and his brother Jeff, a farmer and retired teacher. It was a sweet wood smell rather than the acrid wildfire smoke California frequently endures today.
The industry was in full swing in 1960, when Kennedy ran for president, and Shasta was still a Democratic powerhouse.

Kennedy visited the area twice, following the same trail as Harry Truman in 1948, he said on one visit. He spoke in Redding in 1960, praising the Shasta Dam and telling the crowd “water is key to the American future” and that “this valley shows what can be done”.

Shasta went on to have some of the highest support for Kennedy of any county in the state. And James Kennedy Carr, the Carr brothers’ uncle, became the undersecretary of the department of the interior.

blocks.caption: President Kennedy with James K Carr, then undersecretary of the interior, in this 1962 photograph. The photograph is inscribed ‘JFK and JKC — Two fine ones!’ and signed by then interior secretary Stewart Udall.   Photograph: Courtesy of Pat Carr

blocks.text: While the US benefited from the legacy of the New Deal, major changes would soon alter the Democratic party and fracture the coalition Roosevelt built. The successes of the civil rights movement and the Democrats’ support of landmark legislation resulted in many white southerners beginning to abandon the party. Lyndon Johnson was the last Democratic presidential candidate to attract support from a majority of white Americans.
Meanwhile, conservatives and the corporate elite began what historian Kaye describes as a class war and crusade against the achievements of the “long age of Roosevelt”.

Business groups touted “free enterprise” in an effort to disempower unions and reduce government regulation, while corporations moved operations to the US south and abroad to cut costs and skirt regulations, Kaye has argued. Jimmy Carter embraced deregulation and austerity measures, Kaye said, and his policies ultimately weakened unions.

“The Democratic party basically turned its back on the working class,” Kaye said. “Republicans benefited from the Democrats abandoning the FDR tradition and the age of Roosevelt that had made them the majority party of the people from the early 1930s right through the early 70s.”

Shasta remained reliably blue for a little longer, but trouble was on the horizon. Mills had begun closing. For decades, wood products had been one of the top manufactured goods in the country, and far northern California was a key hub. The industry argued it was being hamstrung by increased regulation and environmental laws. But, Walker countered, by the late 70s the region had cut much of its prime timber and was being out-competed by new technology and production in Canada and the southern US.

Jeff Carr, 66, was a teenager at the time, and remembers the closures, and the hardship that followed. Instead of heading to the mills after graduating, people his age went into the military and some left town to attend college. Shasta was founded on extractive industries, he said, and it appeared it had largely used them up.

In November 1980, after nearly 50 years of almost uninterrupted support for Democrats, Shasta county, like the rest of California, backed Ronald Reagan for president. Voters also ousted the area’s long serving congressman Bizz Johnson in favor of a Republican.
It was a seismic shift, Jeff Carr recalled. And it echoed a change taking place across California.

“There’s one story here: California has gone to hell for Democrats,” Michael Berman, a Democratic consultant, told the Los Angeles Times in 1986. “Young people are registering Republican. And from what they’ve had to choose – between Jimmy Carter and Walter Mondale or Ronald Reagan – it’s not been a tough choice.”

The trend would ultimately reverse in much of the state, but in parts of California’s interior, including Shasta county, it proved a lasting change. Some locals began voting Republican and stayed aligned with the party. Meanwhile, a surge of new residents arrived from southern California, eager to escape to the more affordable north, and they leaned conservative. At the same time, there was an expansion in churches, including ultra conservative worship houses. Simpson University, an evangelical college, arrived in Redding in 1989.

Shasta was becoming more solidly conservative while the influx increased property values and drove up costs at a time when mills that had been critical to the economy were declining. The shift was shocking.
“None of us really saw that coming. I chalk it up to being complacent, being overly self-assured,” said Frank Treadway, a lifelong Shasta resident and Democratic organizer.

It manifested in countless ways. Treadway, 84, saw it in his coffee and tea shop where newly arrived conservatives would make a point to loudly discuss religion and politics, knowing he was active in the party. Jeff Carr heard it on ranches and job sites that suddenly rang with the endless soundtrack of conservative talk radio.

“With that fusion of religious fervor, it made politics extremely personal and a part of people’s fabric,” Carr said. “That’s when we began to see it: a real divide and the inability to meet on common-ground issues.”

A battle over wildlife highlighted the disintegration of this common ground. Even decades on, some Shasta residents shudder at mention of the spotted owl. Kinyon does not mince words: “The spotted owl screwed us.”

The timber industry had been in steep decline locally, but the federal government’s decision to list the northern spotted owl, which relies on old growth and mature forests for nesting, as a threatened species dealt another blow as the protection significantly restricted logging. The industry pushed a self-serving narrative, Walker argued, pinning the blame for its downturn on environmentalists who wanted to protect the small percentage of old-growth trees that remained.

While it was Republican George HW Bush’s administration that added the raptor to the list, following lawsuits, the Democratic party largely supported the proposal. It would become the source of years of resentment and further diminish the party’s popularity in the area.
“Not everybody is with me on the spotted owl situation,” Kinyon said. “As a Democrat I thought: we’re making a mistake.”

By the end of the century, California had turned into a blue bastion, while Shasta hardly resembled the community Roosevelt, Truman and Kennedy had visited decades before. The population had exploded, but the Democratic base had collapsed.

The transformation is emblematic of what happened throughout rural America as the loss of key industries drove economic decline, Walker said. These communities needed something akin to the New Deal, government intervention and investment to keep them viable and improved schools to allow students to better compete in changing labor markets. It never came – not from Democratic or Republican administrations.

“The government stopped caring. You’ve got very little government aid to workers whose factories were closing, whose lumber mills were closing, whose mines were closing. The basic foundation of their lives were shrinking,” he said.
On a sweltering afternoon in June 2016, Donald Trump stood before a crowd of thousands of supporters in Redding and promised a transformation.

“We are going to bring jobs back to this country. We need our jobs. We’re going to make it very expensive for companies to fire everybody and leave,” he said in front of a plane adorned with his name at the Redding airport. “You know, your area has lost one in three manufacturing jobs over a fairly short period of time. That’s a lot of manufacturing jobs.”

blocks.caption: Trump, then a Republican candidate, speaks at a campaign rally in Redding in June 2016. Photograph: Stephen Lam/Reuters

blocks.text: For Shasta, home to 180,000 people and now one of California’s most conservative counties, Trump’s words brought hope. He received more than 64% of the county’s votes that year and 65% in 2020. And Trump did deliver change here, but not the kind he had promised.
His refusal to admit he lost the 2020 presidential contest, coupled with the pandemic, ushered in an era of political extremism that reshaped public life in this region.

The latest shift began even before the election, amid a swell of outrage over California’s covid restrictions. There was growing discontent across the US during the pandemic, as seen in unruly school board meetings and city council sessions, but in Shasta it was particularly severe.

Some viewed the state’s strict rules as missteps and overreach, and further evidence that California’s Democratic leaders were out of touch with rural communities. The restrictions reinforced a feeling that had been building in past decades – that the region had been forgotten by Sacramento.

Many residents were aggrieved at what they saw as a sudden and lengthy intrusion into their daily lives. Photos of the state’s governor at a dinner party at the upscale French Laundry while the state was urging people to avoid such gatherings fueled further outrage.

The frustration over the pandemic and the state’s Democratic supermajority in the capitol intensified anger at the government and deepened allegiance to Trump. In Shasta, it also brought together disaffected residents and broad political groups including militia members, anti-vaxxers and secessionists. Reverge Anselmo, a Connecticut heir with a years-long grudge against the county, poured money into the growing anti-establishment movement. He also backed an effort to recall moderate Republican supervisors accused of not doing enough to push back against state pandemic rules.

blocks.caption: Woody Clendenen, barbershop owner and founder of the Cottonwood Militia, shaves customer Ben Duncan. Clendenen displays Trump 2020 and Maga hats alongside shotgun, rodeo posters and references to the US constitution. Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Leonard Moty, a former police chief who had served on the board for years, suddenly found himself not conservative enough for the political moment. Trent Copland, a retired teacher whose family settled in the county in the 1860s, was friends with Moty and considered him a reasonable Republican. They had clashing political beliefs, Copland recalled, but when Moty faced a recall election, he rushed to help.

In the end, Moty lost his seat, and the recall handed control of the county’s governing body to a deeply conservative majority aligned with the anti-establishment movement. It set off years of dysfunction.

In the following five years, local politics would be defined by animosity, with Democrats and moderate Republicans pitted against ultra conservatives. Public meetings have seen little meaningful conversation and instead verbal sparring and even arrests.

Jenny O’Connell Nowain, a former pre-school teacher with no criminal history, was detained and charged for silently protesting against an official who had alleged without evidence that elections in the community were being manipulated.
Visiting Shasta county in recent years, one might come away with the impression that fraudulent elections are the most pressing local issue.
“Now the big deal is election fraud, and there’s not a shred of proof that election fraud has ever taken place,’ said Copland. “But that doesn’t seem to matter. The facts don’t matter.”

Still, a small but visible group of local residents has insisted local races are compromised. Some elected officials have supported those claims, arguing without evidence there has been widespread interference in local contests. They’ve unsuccessfully sought to implement a hand-count system, a method considered too costly and error-prone for complex US elections but embraced by those who mistrust the integrity of the country’s voting.

blocks.caption: A sign supporting Prop 39, a statewide ballot measure that would require voters to show ID, in a front yard in Shasta county. Californians will vote on the measure on 3 November. Photograph: Mason Trinca for The Guardian

blocks.text: Last year, Shasta appointed Clint Curtis, a self-described election integrity advocate with no experience, to oversee its voting. Curtis accused his predecessors of interfering with elections – even though Republicans consistently win the county – and recently announced plans to hire a disgraced election clerk from Colorado for a job.

Longtime residents like Kinyon are frustrated by the significant time and resources officials have invested in trying to solve a problem that doesn’t exist while the area faces significant challenges.

Shasta county has one of the highest suicide rates in the state and high overdose rates. There is a severe lack of economic opportunity, residents say. Bethel, a conservative megachurch with about 11,000 members, plays a significant role in the local economy. The church’s school of supernatural ministry, which has been called a “Christian Hogwarts”, has attracted thousands of students and visitors, some of whom have stayed and started businesses.
The area relies heavily on federal funding – not in the form of massive infrastructure projects that once employed thousands – but through grants and social services.

Rural California is expected to take a significant hit with the Trump administration’s cuts to those grants and services, including about $1tn from Medicaid over 10 years. Last year, the head of Shasta’s largest healthcare provider warned the changes to Medicaid would have “crippling” impacts in a county where the local Medicaid provider serves nearly a third of the population.

It will take time for the full effect of the budget reductions to be seen, but they will have repercussions in the region for years to come. Experts have warned a new fund allocating $50bn for rural health is too small to offset the adverse effects.
Democrats have said they will reverse the cuts if they are victorious in the midterms.
Times may be dark for Democrats in Shasta, but there is also some hope.
Because of a redistricting effort undertaken in response to Trump’s push for gerrymandering in Texas, the region is poised to have its first Democratic representative in Congress in nearly 50 years.

Among conservatives, the redistricting measure, called Prop 50, has only fueled resentment against the California governor, Gavin Newsom, and intensified feelings that rural areas are not getting fair representation. Just over 70% of Shasta voters opposed it. But others celebrated the development, and are excited to have an experienced new congressman.

“I believe one of the best advocates that the North State will have gained is Jared Huffman,” Jeff Carr said, referring to the lawmaker slated to represent the region in January. He pointed to Huffman’s role as the top Democrat on the House natural resources committee and advocacy for farmers.

Local Democrats hope the party will be moved to invest more into organizing in the county. “We as Democrats [have looked] at Shasta county as a place where we gotta reduce our losses, not as a place we can win,” Mulholland said last year.

The California Democratic party concentrates resources in close races, meaning conservative rural areas receive relatively little support. Kinyon has long believed that if the state party invested more into local races, Democrats here could rally more voters.
“Our votes are important. Our people are. Give us some help.”
In the meantime, local Democrats are focused on the same sentiment Kinyon recalled from her childhood; community building and advocacy with food and clothing drives and support groups for immigrants.
“I think we’re making meaningful progress in Shasta county in the ways that we find people need help,” she said. “Those are the things that we work on here.”

Jeff Carr serves on the local Democratic central committee, alongside Kinyon, and says the local party is trying to aid people at risk of losing food, health and housing benefits under recent federal cuts.

More support from the state party wouldn’t necessarily change the outcome of races right away, but it would help improve the conversation, argued Francie Sullivan, one of the few Democrats to ever serve on Shasta’s governing board.

But what the region needs, like similar areas across America, is massive investment, Walker said, to create thriving communities. Joe Biden’s administration backed some significant rural projects, but Democrats have largely been poor communicators and failed to articulate what they were doing, he added.

“People in the rural areas like Shasta county have no idea what Biden was trying to do for them … They don’t think the government helps them,” he said. “There’s a lot of money that flows into Shasta county from the richer areas, but nobody trumpets it. They need more, and they don’t get it. And I understand their despair.”

blocks.caption: Name badges, newspaper clippings and political stickers cover a filing cabinet at Pat Carr’s home. Photograph: Mason Trinca/Mason Trinca for The Guardian

blocks.text: “If we don’t get a new New Deal of some kind it’ll continue,” he said. “The rural areas will continue to wallow in the mire of Magaism, and we’re going to be stuck with this horrible government. It’s a tragedy. It’s just a long, slow tragedy.”

Back in Pat Carr’s office, he and his brother pondered what it might take to turn things around in Shasta. Residents have previously lobbied the state to open a new university campus here, which would have a tremendous impact, Jeff Carr said. The region needs a change of perspective and a vision for its future economically, he said.
But whatever comes, they’re not going anywhere.

“There are other places that I could be that would be easier and the like. It’s well beyond family loyalty,” Pat Carr said from his property in Cottonwood, as the sun shone brightly over Lassen Peak framed in the window behind him. “I feel a duty almost to be here.”

articles.title: Israeli military conducts massive West Bank operation, days before Israel election
articles.summary: The Israeli military continued a massive military operation in the occupied West Bank on Sunday, displacing hundreds of Palestinians and placing major restrictions on movement in response to a gun…

image.caption: Palestinians transport bags of semolina past a military gate closed to vehicles during an Israeli army operation in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, on Saturday, a day after a Palestinian shooting attack in the area. (Mahmoud Illean/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

The Israeli military continued a massive military operation in the occupied West Bank on Sunday, displacing hundreds of Palestinians and placing major restrictions on movement in response to a gun attack that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others in Hebron on Friday.
The operation displaced more than 2,200 people, including nearly 300 children, according to Hebron officials

The operation comes as Israel enters the final days before a tense election, which is largely seen as a referendum on current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership and security policies during the past three years of war.

Most Palestinian workers with permits will not be allowed to enter Israeli settlements for work in the occupied West Bank on Sunday and Monday, and crossings into Israel will remain closed until after Israel's elections on Tuesday, the Israeli military said.

The military said it operated in more than 400 different locations over the weekend and arrested 40 Palestinians it claimed were affiliated with Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad. It said the operation is continuing at the same intensity on Sunday.

items: Netanyahu orders West Bank closure as Israeli soldiers, Palestinian gunmen killed in exchanges

blocks.text: Thousands of Palestinians displaced from Hebron
The Hebron municipality said the operation displaced more than 2,200 people, including nearly 300 children under the age of 18.

The military said that troops were conducting searches in the area where the gunmen operated and warned residents to evacuate Deir Bahha, the suspected gunmen's neighbourhood. After Friday's attack, Israel's military said it found weapons in the gunmen's car and that they were likely planning to attack Israeli civilians before being stopped at the checkpoint.
All entrances and exits to the city remained sealed, with the epicentre of the operation in Deir Bahha and another part of the city called Al-Jalda, according to Hebron Mayor Yousef Zuhair Al-Jabari.

"People cannot reach or enter the city, and they cannot leave it. The blockade has affected every aspect of life," Al-Jabari said. He added that the blockade is forcing businesses to close and has also shuttered a mosque.

items: Israel moving ahead with settlement plans that would split West Bank in two, rights group says

blocks.text: "The army told us that this area would be closed for 12 days. Now they're saying 12 days, but maybe they'll leave the area after two or three days," said Shadi al-Qawasmi, a Hebron resident who was displaced with his family. "This may be because of the elections or some political matter; no one knows except God Almighty."

The operation forced some families to navigate crossings on foot in order to leave Hebron after the roads were closed to traffic. At some military gates, people passed sacks of flour and gas canisters through the gates, while an elderly man pushed his wife in a wheelchair through an opening beside one of them. Another family attempted to navigate the gate to access medical appointments.
‘I accept that I’m next’: West Bank teen foreshadows his death
Netanyahu vows a strong response as elections loom
Hebron municipal officials said families had been displaced from nearly 500 apartments in Deir Bahha and surrounding neighbourhoods.

Six Israelis have been killed this year in attacks in the West Bank, which is experiencing a surge of violence. During the same period, 112 Palestinians have been killed, including the suspected gunmen, according to the Ramallah-based Palestinian Health Ministry.

A Palestinian man stands next to Israeli soldiers during an army operation in the West Bank city of Hebron on Saturday. The military said it operated in more than 400 different locations over the weekend. (Mahmoud Illean/The Associated Press)

Friday's attack sparked outrage in Israel, with Netanyahu and three members of his right-wing government giving statements from the site of the attack on Friday afternoon, vowing to respond forcefully. "We warned a few weeks ago about attempts by our enemies to harm us, our citizens and our soldiers ahead of the election," Netanyahu said. "We will act to destroy this place."
Netanyahu is under pressure to demonstrate a strong show of force against Palestinian attackers to bolster his image for Israelis concerned with security.

Roughly three million Palestinians and 540,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel occupied in the 1967 Mideast war. Hebron is one of its most tense cities and the only place where Jewish settlers live in the heart of a densely populated Palestinian area under Israeli military protection.

articles.title: Palawan fishers support calls to request recall of Chinese envoy
articles.summary: Fisherfolk in Palawan supported calls by lawmakers to request the recall of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan following his statement that Beijing could “easily win” if it resorts to force.

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 8:25pm

Fisherfolk in Palawan supported on Sunday calls by lawmakers to request the recall of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan following his statement that Beijing could “easily win” if it resorts to force against the Philippines.
In a press conference of the Atin Ito Coalition in Palawan, leaders of fisherfolk groups also condemned China’s continued aggression toward their livelihood in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).

“Hindi katanggap-tanggap ang pagbabanta ng kinatawan ng isang dayuhang bansa sa Pilipinas. Sinusuportahan namin ang panawagang pauwiin na sa China si Jing Quan,” said Rafaela David, an Atin Ito co-convenor and the Akbayan Party president.
(Threats from a representative of a foreign nation against the Philippines are unacceptable. We support the call to send Jing Quan back to China.)
“Hindi dapat bigyan ng puwang sa ating bansa ang mga katulad niya na nagbabanta sa ating bayan habang inaagawan ng kabuhayan ang ating mga mangingisda,” she added.
(Individuals like him who threaten our nation while robbing our fisherfolk of their livelihood should have no place in our country.)
The group emphasized that China’s actions in the WPS threaten their safety at sea, as well as their families’ livelihoods and food security.
It added that “every fishing trip disrupted by Chinese harassment means lost income and food off the table for families who depend on the sea.”

Atin Ito said the calls to expel Jing were backed by leaders of the Samahan ng mga Mangingisda kontra Korapsyon (SAMAKKO), Samahan ng mga Katutubo at Maliit na Mangingisda sa Dulong Timog Palawan (SAMBIL OG), Kalayaan, Palawan Farmers and Fisherfolk Association, Tinig ng mga Katutubo (TIKA), and Samahang Pagkakaisa ng mga Katutubong Tagbanua sa Marufinas.
Demands to expel the Chinese envoy grew following his remarks that Beijing could “easily win” should it use force against the Philippines, but it chose peace instead.
Senator Risa Hontiveros already filed a resolution calling on President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. to declare Jing Quan persona non grata or request his recall by the Chinese government.
Malacañang had earlier said that it would leave the matter to the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), noting that Marcos does not favor declaring any foreign envoy persona non grata.
The DFA formally summoned Jing Quan on Monday to convey the Philippines' "serious concern and strong objection" to his recent remarks. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: France: Hundreds arrested after nationwide protests
articles.summary: The French government says more than 1,000 people were arrested following nationwide protests on Saturday. Police and elite security forces were out in force across the country as clashes broke out.
articles.byline: Wesley Dockery, Richard Connor, Timothy Jones

image.caption: Police deployed tear gas and water cannons to disperse protesters at the end of an approved rally in ParisImage: Pedro Nunes/REUTERS

blocks.text: October 25, 2026
France reports more than 1,300 arrests after protests
French authorities detained 1,314 people during nationwide protests on Saturday, according to a provisional Interior Ministry tally.
The ministry said 53 police officers and other security personnel were injured, firefighters responded to 75 fires and 24 businesses were looted. It did not provide a figure for injured protesters.

Clashes broke out in cities including Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Tours, with police using tear gas. The ministry blamed groups including radical far-left activists for confrontations along or near protest routes.
Authorities counted 410,000 participants at 289 demonstrations and gatherings, down from 550,000 a week earlier. Other estimates put Saturday's turnout as high as 800,000.
The reported arrests and violence were substantially lower than on October 17, when authorities recorded 2,628 detentions and 1,144 injured security personnel.
The ministry said several investigations had been opened and described the subsequent night as calm.

articles.title: Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back: CBC's Marketplace Cheat Sheet
articles.summary: The CBC's Marketplace rounds up the consumer and health news you need from the week.

image.caption: Samantha Bradshaw, left, and Asif Mohammed each lost thousands when scammers called, claiming to work at their financial institutions. (Nelisha Vellani/CBC)

blocks.text: Marketplace·CHEAT SHEET
The CBC's Marketplace rounds up the consumer and health news you need from the week.
The consumer news you may have missed this week
Miss something this week? Don't panic. The CBC's Marketplace rounds up the consumer and health news you need.
Want this in your inbox? Get the Marketplace newsletter every Friday.
Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back
Bank scammer confronted by CBC Marketplace
Two people described the same financial scam to the police and their banks over the past year. The only difference was where they lived — one in Canada, the other in the U.K.
And that determined what happened next.
Asif Mohammed lost $7,200 this spring and never got it back. Meanwhile, Samantha Bradshaw was out £11,000 (nearly $21,000 Cdn) but her financial institution reimbursed the money within days.

That's because British banks are required by law to make most of their customers whole when money is lost to a scam — often returning the sum within days of making a claim. In contrast, Canadian banks have no such legal obligation, leaving scam victims here largely unprotected.
As CBC’s Marketplace found out, it also means British banks are incentivized to crack down on fraudsters in a way Canadian banks are not.
Read our full investigation from David Common and Nelisha Vellani.
Toronto Crime Stoppers pauses program after CBC investigation reveals details of data leak
Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database
Toronto Crime Stoppers is pausing its program effective immediately, said its chair, Sean Sportun, in a statement sent late Wednesday evening.

The news follows an exclusive CBC investigation from earlier that day revealing information from more than 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years was exposed in a massive data breach. It was the first time precise figures were made public showing the severity of the information exposed, as well as how many Canadian tipsters have been compromised.

Up until the investigation was published, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) and individual chapters had not spoken out about the extent of the breach, only saying they awaited a detailed report from Navigate360, the U.S.-based third-party company that manages its data through platform P3.

Toronto Crime Stoppers now says it has removed the "Tip Submit" feature from its website and will no longer accept or process any new information intended for the program. It has also advised Navigate360 to immediately suspend the intake function for the Toronto Crime Stoppers chapter from its platform.
In the statement, the organization advised the public not to send tips by phone, online or through its app "until we have a safer way to protect you."

"People in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous. This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry," Sportun said in a statement.
The Toronto Police Service also announced in a statement Wednesday evening that it has "temporarily suspended its use of Crime Stoppers" until further review.
MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada amid mounting harms
Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There’s a push to change that
For T.S., a 22-year-old Ontario man recovering from a gambling problem, widespread advertising for online casinos and betting during sports broadcasts is "frustrating."
"Imagine you're an alcoholic and there was a beer ad during every show you watched," he told CBC News.
His gambling started three years ago as a fun Friday night activity with friends, but it escalated.
One night last year he found himself locked inside a bathroom, losing it all — having bet away $14,000.
T.S., who CBC has agreed not to name, says he quickly sought treatment and hasn't gambled since. But during his spree, all those ads fuelled him to gamble more.
"It certainly … would trigger me to go back and place another bet."
Politicians in Ottawa are moving to curb the widespread advertising currently seen across sports broadcasts, social media and online video games.

The federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on Bill S-211, a law that proposes to rein in the ads across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.
A new analysis for CBC News shows Canadians continue to be bombarded with betting promotions during sports broadcasts.

The new analysis also confirms little has changed since a CBC Marketplace study in 2024 revealed viewers were bombarded with thousands of ads and product placements in five NHL games (up to three per minute).
Watch Marketplace’s 2024 investigation on how many gambling advertisements we see during sports games.

articles.title: Demand for UK government action 10 months after British man’s death in Grenada
articles.summary:
Police closed case of Andrew Frederick despite autopsy report ruling his death a homicide

A time-critical investigation into the death of a British man whose body was found in a ransacked…

blocks.text: A time-critical investigation into the death of a British man whose body was found in a ransacked property on the Caribbean island of Grenada has stalled because of diplomatic delays between the two countries.

Charity workers supporting the family of Andrew Frederick are demanding immediate government intervention to clear the path for a full investigation to begin almost 10 months after his death, which has been ruled a homicide by a pathologist.
The Murdered Abroad charity has called on the foreign affairs select committee to step in after Grenadian police found there was “no basis … that any homicide has occurred” and closed the case.

This was despite a report from an autopsy, done in the week he died, saying Frederick, 47, had suffered “blunt force trauma”, was tortured, including by removal of his toenail, and ruling the death a homicide.
Frederick’s body was found on 4 January. Since then, the family say they have been forced to focus on their fight for justice instead of coming to terms with their loss.

Murdered Abroad’s founder, Eve Henderson, said:“We understand there are challenges but [almost 10 months] on, this family is still being met with obfuscation. If a family this determined cannot get the FCDO [Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office] to put their diplomatic powers to good use, what hope is there for the 60 to 80 families bereaved by murder abroad each year?
“A minister must look urgently at how consular services treat these traumatised families or the foreign affairs select committee must step in,” she added.
A former Scotland Yard homicide commander who is supporting the family described Grenada’s actions as “incredible”.

“In the autopsy report … the pathologist, who is a qualified medical examiner, categorically states that he believes this is a case of homicide and that Andrew was tortured before he was killed,” David Johnston said. “And yet the police just choose to ignore that because it didn’t fit with their model. I mean, it’s incredible.”

After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK in August, where a second autopsy was carried out, during which it was discovered his organs were missing.
The family described this discovery as “shocking and devastating”.

In a statement, they said: “We were already heartbroken that Andrew’s life was cruelly taken, but nothing could have prepared us for what we would learn afterwards. For six weeks after his death, Andrew’s body was held under the control of the Grenadian authorities. When he was later examined in the UK, parts of his neck and all of his organs, including his brain, heart, and lungs, were missing.

“That discovery has been shocking and absolutely devastating for our family; we are still struggling to process it. It has added pain upon pain and left us with deep hurt with so many unanswered questions. Despite our multiple inquiries, no one has told us where they are, what happened to them, or why we were never told. No family should ever have to ask these questions.”

Last month a UK coroner asked the Metropolitan police to conduct an investigation. Weeks later a communication from UK authorities, seen by the Guardian, said a British high commissioner had raised Frederick’s case with officials at the highest levels of government in Grenada, and indicated that authorities there had agreed to cooperate with any forthcoming formal request for the UK to assist with the investigation.
That formal request was sent weeks ago but the family say they are still waiting for Grenada “to honour their verbal commitment to the British high commissioner and approve the request to cooperate”.

“Every day for almost 10 months we have had to live without Andrew and without answers. A formal request from the UK, asking Grenada to cooperate with its investigation into Andrew’s death, still sits unsigned. It is the best chance we have of finding the truth,” the family statement said.
Johnston said the initial handling of Frederick’s case and the further delays could have a detrimental effect on the investigation.

“In a homicide investigation we have a phrase that we refer to as the golden hours, which are the first real 24 hours from the notification, or the discovery, of a homicide [which] are the most important and crucial … because evidence diminishes and can be lost if a crime scene is not properly noted and properly managed.

“In the case of the death of [Frederick] that’s exactly what happened … the police, in my view, failed to properly identify and preserve the crime scene and to treat the crime scene in the manner it should have been treated,” he said.
Johnston added that cooperation between British and Grenadian police could help to “bring some stability to that investigation”.
An FCDO spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British man who died in Grenada, and are in contact with the local authorities.”
The Guardian has approached the Royal Grenada Police Force for comment but has not had a reply.

The family said: “With each passing day, our family’s heartbreak deepens. We need closure, and Grenada’s prime minister, who is also the minister of national security, can help make this possible. We appeal to him, with humanity and compassion, to sign the request without further delay.”
Additional reporting by Calistra Farrier

articles.title: There’s disappointment and hope among Albertans who supported the idea of independence
articles.summary: Now that the results of the referendum have come in, with three-quarters of Albertans voting to stay in Canada, we reached out to some residents who supported the other side to see how they feel and…

image.caption: We checked in with several people post-referendum. Clockwise from the top left, Vicky Bayford in Innisfail, Matthew Morin in Calgary, Brad Osadczuk in Jenner, and Daymond Khan in Calgary. (Elise Stolte/CBC; Submitted by Vicky Bayford; Submitted by Matthew Morin; Mantai Chow/CBC; Vincent McDermott/CB

blocks.text: Throughout the referendum campaign, CBC News used First Person writing, community focus groups and small engagement pop-ups to understand why Albertans were planning to vote the way they were.
We met many people on both sides of the debate.

Now that the results have come in, with three-quarters of Albertans voting to stay in Canada, we reached out to some of the community members who supported the other side to see how they feel and what they would like to see happen next.
There were many emotions — hope, disappointment, contentment.
Vicky Bayford lives in Innisfail, Alta., north of Calgary. She's pictured here in her backyard in 2026. (Submitted by Vicky Bayford)
‘This isn’t a hidden conversation anymore’

Vicky Bayford saw the results when she finished scrutineering early Tuesday morning. She had been hopeful, watching numbers near 50 per cent for Option 2 from her polling station in Innisfail, a town of nearly 9,000 people an hour’s drive north of Calgary.
Bayford said the provincewide tally of 25 per cent was disappointing, but not surprising.
“I’ve always known this was going to be an uphill battle.”

Bayford works in oil and gas, and has been heavily involved with separatism since 2020. She believes Option 2 lost because many conservatives decided to give Premier Danielle Smith a chance to make changes within Canada.
But Bayford also believes the last 18 months of work have been a boon to the independence movement, despite the loss.
“This isn’t a hidden conversation anymore like it was when I got involved in 2020,” she said. “Now at least it’s on the radar.”
Friendships were formed as supporters signed petitions and attended town halls. Pro-independence organizations will make sure that social aspect doesn’t go away, she said.

But there is something she does hope will change. Bayford wrote a First Person piece for CBC News during the campaign, and then sat down to discuss it with three other First Person authors on CBC's West of Centre.

items: Should Alberta separate? Here's why these Canadians feel the way they do

blocks.text: One of the authors, Matthew Morin, is gay.

“One thing he said really stuck out to me,” she said. “He made that comment that, you know, he agreed with a lot of the sentiments that Albertans are feeling, but he didn't know if there was a place for him in [the vision of] Alberta that he was seeing from the leaders of the independence movement.”
“That was pretty eye-opening to me,” she said. “This movement will never be successful unless we can get the consensus from Albertans that we're all Albertans.”
“I hope people start being a little more gentle with each other … and now that this is over, that we can just start having more calmer conversations.”
Matthew Morin works in the social service sector and lives in Calgary. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
‘I think the world can become more volatile’

Morin, the author that Bayford mentioned, wrote a First Person column for CBC News about how the precarity of life today — and the feeling that those in charge don’t care — is fuelling his interest in independence.
He thought much of the support for separatism in Alberta should be seen as a protest vote. Reached after the referendum, he said that’s why he’s not surprised at the results.
“People are angry and that's why the nine questions got over 50 per cent or around 50 per cent. But they’re not angry enough to look to for separation.”

“So we'll see where it goes. 'Cause I think the world can become more volatile,” he said. “If the government doesn't actually enact any tangible change [to benefit people’s everyday lives], then people will just continue to get more frustrated and angry.”

items: ‘What I expected’: Coffee crowd mostly relieved by remain victory in Alberta referendum

blocks.text: Post-referendum, political analysts have been wondering how the referendum results will affect Premier Danielle Smith’s leadership, and if the committed separatists within her party will agitate to push her out.
Morin is not a committed separatist, but has been a Smith supporter. He door-knocked for her in the last election and joined the UCP so that he could vote for her leadership.
“I thought she was grassroots and would make a difference,” he said. “And she's made some differences. I mean, some differences were good and some were bad. That's with any politician.”
But at the moment, he doesn’t stand behind her the same way.

“In my ideal world, the government will use [this mandate] as a way to build policy that informs lower immigration, more control over crime, increasing affordable housing and building more housing, increasing funding for social programs and resources.

“And that they’d understand that people are just frustrated and instead of saying that everything's fine, maybe standing up on a podium and saying 'we hear you,' which is not really what I felt like I got from a lot of the politicians.”
Alex Krull in his garage in Fort McMurray. He says he hopes to stay involved with the independence movement and is proud of what it accomplished. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)
‘We continue to be the rebel alliance’

Alex Krull came home after a 12-hour shift at an oilsands mine to catch the referendum results. He was disappointed votes in favour of having a binding referendum on separation didn’t hit 33 per cent, but still proud of everything the movement accomplished.

Earlier this fall, Prime Minister Mark Carney came to his workplace to announce the Pacific Link pipeline has been deemed to be in the national interest — and that’s due to the separatists’ agitation, he argues.

items: Northern Alberta shows higher support for separation, especially in rural areas

blocks.text: “It was very amusing as we're almost ground zero for separatism. A lot of us are high income, high tax paying, blue collar individuals. So we're definitely not your typical liberal supporters. But yeah, there he was.

“I've been following the mainstream media quite a bit since the referendum and they're completely dismissing the impact that our movement had on federal-provincial politics. They're saying things like the federal Liberals were already moving in this direction,” he said.

“I would strongly contend that. I think that our movement brought a lot of attention to the province, and we've seen a lot of capitulation from Ottawa on topics that I don't think we would have had, had we not had this form of rebellion.”

Krull volunteered with the independence campaign in Fort McMurray, collecting signatures to get the question on the ballot. The experience left him feeling that ordinary Albertans can make a difference, and he plans to stay involved, watching from the sidelines to see where he can help. That might be with a separatist party in the future, depending on how the political situation evolves, he said.

“Danielle Smith is in a dilly of a pickle ‘cause a big chunk of her support are separatist. So she's come out staunchly stating that the UCP going forward is a federalist party and that's how it is. So I think in 2027, Alberta, UCP has a big problem,” he said.

“But as far as the separatist movement, I think we continue to apply the pressure; we continue to be the rebel alliance against the Ottawa empire. Without that resistance, the status quo will overwhelm us, and I guess that's what democracy is.”
Brad Osadczuk ranches near Jenner, Alta. He says he supports provincial autonomy. (Mantai Chow/CBC)
‘If we’re not ready for change, we’re not ready for change’

Brad Osadczuk is a rancher near Jenner, Alta., about 200 kilometres east of Calgary. He was driving his empty cattle liner back from a feedlot, where he left a load of calves, when he took a phone call from CBC News.

Osadczuk is separatist curious. He says Monday’s results didn’t surprise him, but he was disappointed because he wanted to at least advance to the next step and have a serious look at what an independent Alberta could mean.
“I’m a businessman, so I like to see the details of a deal,” he said. “It may not ever work, [but] I would have loved to see what it would look like.”

Osadczuk spoke with CBC News during the campaign about his frustration with Ottawa — how much power is centralized in the east and how the bureaucracy is out of touch with the reality on the ground. He said he hopes this vote will help Alberta keep pushing for more authority.

“The feds see the results of this referendum, too,” he said. “I hope that maybe we can see some more goodwill and some work towards what Alberta would like out of this federation. I hope that there was a message sent.”
As for what happens next?
“We just keep living our lives. … If we’re not ready for change, we’re not ready for change.”

“I’m really sorry that people see this referendum as divisive. I see it as 100 per cent democracy. This was a government serving the people, not serving an agenda,” he said, adding that he hopes emotions will now settle down.
“I’m so tired of divisiveness.”

Daymond Khan, a member of the citizen action group at Southside Victory Church in Calgary, shared how his concerns over Canada's shifting identity have influenced his views on Alberta separatism. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
‘We can continue to stand for what's right’

During the campaign, Daymond Khan met with CBC News as part of a focus group at Southside Victory Church in Calgary, where he said the feeling that Canada was losing touch with its traditional Christian values pushed him to favour separatism.
But after the vote, he says he’s content with the outcome. He voted for Option 2, but never expected it to win and never wanted Alberta to actually leave.
“I'd like to see Alberta treated better within our federation, and I'd like to see the general direction of our nation and our federal government change,” he said.
And he’s already seeing positive signs.

“Economically, we see the federal support for the West Coast pipeline, which will hopefully help to turn the tide on seeing more major projects and investments in Canada,” he said. “Then on the moral side of things, we saw medical assistance in dying not get expanded to people who are just struggling with mental health challenges.
“I think that's a great decision by our leaders in Ottawa to not open that piece up.”

He believes the vote is giving Alberta more leverage. He says he takes to heart something Southside Victory’s Pastor Craig Buroker said recently in a sermon that the name Alberta is a variant of Albert, a name that means “noble and bright.”
“That was a good way to frame the calling of Alberta in our country and in general. So I'm confident that we can continue to stand for what's right and not necessarily be quiet about it.”

articles.title: El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages
articles.summary: Nayib Bukele says bodies delivered to soldiers are "not our men" amid search for Salvadorans abducted last week.

blocks.text: Four bodies handed over to special forces on a mission to Haiti to recover Salvadoran hostages are "not our men", El Salvador's president has said.

Nayib Bukele said a nongovernmental organisation delivered the human remains to one of Haiti's airports claiming they were four El Salvadoran air technicians, but that one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's army uniform.
He had dispatched a military contingent, reportedly of hundreds of soldiers, on Thursday after the four men vanished after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups".
The hostages had been part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), which is tasked with tackling worsening gang violence in Haiti.

The men had been travelling back to their camp in an armoured vehicle when they were attacked in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets. No gang has so far claimed responsibility.

Bukele previously said the Salvadoran military operation in Haiti had the sole purpose of returning the four men alive. Approximately 450 soldiers had so far been deployed, according to Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste.

Bukele said the bodies the mission had received included one of a man of "considerably greater height than that of our air technicians", a person "who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours", and that among the remains were identification cards and uniforms from other countries.
He posted pictures showing the ID card of a GSF member and a corresponding national ID card from Chad in Africa.

Bukele's comments poured skepticism on an earlier report in the New York Times, citing people close to the Salvadoran mission, that the bodies found on the outskirts of the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, on Saturday were thought to belong to the missing men.
The newspaper reported that the bodies delivered to the military contingent had been badly burned, meaning a medical examination would be required to identify them.
It cited one unnamed source briefed on the situation as saying the ID posted by Bukele in fact belonged to a soldier who had lost it when he had been injured.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of its president in 2021.
The multinational force dispatched to quell the violence and push back the armed gangs has struggled to penetrate areas where they hold sway.
More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year, the UN said at the start of October.
Bukele said the four GSF members had primarily been there to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
When they were abducted, helicopters were deployed and multiple attempts were made to reach the location, but these efforts were hampered by fighting in the area, the Salvadoran armed forces said.

articles.title: Serbia election: Can student-led opposition end Aleksandar Vucic's grip on power?
articles.summary: Nearly two years after a deadly railway station collapse sparked mass anti-corruption protests, Serbians are voting in a closely fought election that could end Aleksandar Vucic's grip on power.

image.caption: Voters cast their ballots at a polling station in Belgrade in Serbia's closely contested parliamentary electionImage: Zorana Jevtic/REUTERS

blocks.text: Voting was well underway in Serbia on Sunday in a closely contested election that could bring an end to more than a decade of rule by long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
Polls suggest a tight race between the SNS and the newly formed, youth-backed Students' List, which emerged from a mass student protest movement.
The protests were sparked by the deadly collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi ‌Sad in 2024.

The disaster killed 16 people and stirred widespread anger over alleged corruption, poor construction standards and a lack of accountability for public infrastructure projects. Protesters accused the government of allowing corruption and political patronage to undermine public safety, allegations the authorities have rejected.
Demonstrations demanding accountability have since snowballed into Serbia's largest movement since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.
The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election

What began with university students staging blockades and marches soon drew support from teachers, farmers and other sections of Serbian society, turning a demand for justice over the disaster into a broader challenge to Vucic's grip on power.
Vucic faces tough election challenge
SNS won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics ever since. Vucic himself first came to power as prime minister in 2014 before becoming president in 2017.
After calling snap elections last month, Vucic stepped down as president to run for prime minister.

blocks.caption: Under Serbia's constitution, Vucic cannot run for a third presidential termImage: Jelena Djukic Pejic/DW

blocks.text: His second presidential term was due to expire in May 2027, and Serbia's constitution prevents him from serving a third term.
Critics have accused him of concentrating power, undermining independent media and weakening democratic institutions. He and his party deny the allegations.

The student movement has sought to channel the energy of the street protests into an electoral challenge, presenting itself as an alternative to both the ruling party and Serbia's established opposition.
Turnout higher than last time
By 1 p.m. (1200 GMT), 41.1% of eligible voters had cast their ballots, up from 26.6% at the same stage in the December 2023 parliamentary election, according to independent election monitor CRTA.
After voting at a kindergarten on the outskirts of Belgrade, Vucic said he hoped the election would proceed smoothly.
"We will heed the democratic will of the citizens. You can win or lose an election. Either way, we will act responsibly," said Vucic, who is seeking to become prime minister.
Cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic heads the Students' List but is neither the movement's leader nor its designated candidate for prime minister.
"I hope that today will pass in a democratic atmosphere, in peace, and that we will legitimately elect a new government in Serbia," he said after casting his ballot in Novi Sad.

The election is being closely watched in Europe. Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership, but its accession process has been hampered by concerns over democratic standards and the rule of law.
Vucic has also maintained close ties with Russia and refused to join Western sanctions against Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine.
The vote comes six months after Peter Magyar's victory in Hungary , when he defeated Vucic's ally, Viktor Orban.
Polling stations close at 8 p.m. local time (1900 GMT).

Ryanair closes base, cuts routes at Berlin's international airport

blocks.caption: Ryanair has closed its base at BER airportImage: Jörg Carstensen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Low-cost Irish airline Ryanair has closed its base at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER), and removed 12 routes there at the start of its winter timetable.
The move was announced in April and confirmed in October, with the airline having long complained about high taxes and fees at German airports.

Six of the 12 deleted routes, from BER to Palermo, Marseille, Triest, Reggio Calabria, Tallin and Pisa, can now no longer be directly reached on flights from the airport, the airline and the airport operator FBB said.
The other six — Gran Canaria, Fuerteventura, Lanzarote, Bologna, Thessaloniki and Vilnius — are served by other airlines flying from BER.

The seven Ryanair aircraft that were based at the BER airport have been reassigned to airports in European Union countries that, according to Ryanair, have got rid of aviation taxes or reduced airport charges.
Ryanair is to still fly to and from Berlin using planes based elsewhere.

The operators of BER have pointed out that despite Ryanair's move, eight more destinations can be reached from the airport than last winter, as other airlines have expanded their services at the airport.

articles.title: 4 ways US foreign policy could change if Democrats win in November
articles.summary: Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump's foreign policy

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, USA – Nonpartisan analysts say Democrats stand a good chance of winning the US House of Representatives and possibly the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, which would give them a slice of power in Washington after two years of Republican control.
Democrats argue that Republicans have allowed President Donald Trump‘s administration to declare war and control spending, even though the US Constitution reserves those powers for lawmakers.
Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump’s foreign policy.

Trump did not secure approval from Congress before he launched the war with Iran on February 28, and Democrats have voted repeatedly to end the fighting unless he does so. One of these resolutions passed with support from a handful of Republicans, but Trump’s administration ignored it.

With control of the House or the Senate, Democrats could cut defense spending to pressure Trump to obtain permission from Congress to continue the war. They could also require administration officials to testify publicly about their plans.
Trump has largely halted direct US financial and military aid to Ukraine, despite broad support from Democratic and Republican lawmakers as it fights a Russian invasion.
Most recently, he has angered members of Congress, including many Republicans, by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russian energy only weeks after signing them into law.
With a victory in both chambers in November, Democrats would be able to decide what gets voted on and when.
That could allow them to approve new aid to Ukraine, which likely would pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to overcome a Trump veto.

They could also target other Trump activities. For example, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, who could head the House Foreign Affairs Committee if Democrats win control, has introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump’s plan to bring Russian diesel back into the global market.

Support for Israel has plummeted among Democrats over its conduct in the Gaza war, which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians. The ongoing violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s close alliance with Republicans have also been factors.
Democrats could limit or end military aid to Israel, which amounted to $3.8 billion in the most recent fiscal year. That is more than was provided to any other country.

Nearly half of House Democrats voted this summer to ‌cut off aid to Israel. Some of those who voted against that effort, such as Meeks, have backed limits on providing weapons like heavy bombs to Israel.

Democrats are far more likely than Trump’s Republicans to limit military spending. Trump asked for an unprecedented 67% increase in the military budget this year, to $1.5 trillion, but Democrats blocked it in the Senate, citing his refusal to consult Congress about the Iran war and his steep cuts to social programs.
Trump has also withheld or canceled billions of dollars in foreign aid approved by Congress. Many Democrats have been angered by the cuts and say they will try to restore funding.

articles.title: DOH logs 8% rise in flu-like illnesses; vaccines to roll out next week
articles.summary: The Department of Health (DOH) recorded an increase in influenza-like illness (ILI) cases this week and will begin rolling out influenza vaccines next week, Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 6:08pm

The Department of Health (DOH) recorded an increase in influenza-like illness (ILI) cases this week and will begin rolling out influenza vaccines next week, Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said Sunday.
Mercado said the DOH recorded 11,137 ILI cases last week, an 8% increase from the 10,278 cases recorded during the September 3-16 period.
“There were 11,137 cases recorded last week, compared with 10,278 cases from September 3 to 16,” Mercado told Super Radyo dzBB.
However, Mercado said the cumulative number of cases from January through last week remained lower than the total recorded during the same period in 2025.
According to the World Health Organization, influenza-like illness is a clinical syndrome characterized by symptoms such as fever and cough, and can be caused by various respiratory pathogens.
Mercado said respiratory droplets from coughing and sneezing, as well as contact with contaminated surfaces, can contribute to the spread of respiratory infections.
“Cases tend to rise during colder weather as people gather in close quarters. This is also the season when many celebrations take place,” he said.
Mercado said the DOH would roll out influenza vaccines next week, prioritizing vulnerable sectors.— MCG, GMA News
