articles.title: Storm Boelo: warnings in place in Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of England as high winds batter UK
articles.summary:
Met Office reports gusts of 80mph in exposed coastal spots and advises people in affected areas to stay indoors

Strong winds have battered Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent

blocks.text: Strong winds have battered Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England overnight as Storm Boelo hit the UK.

It was the second named storm in as many days, after Storm Austen brought strong winds to parts of the UK on Friday. The Met Office said wind speeds reached 60-70mph, affecting areas in an amber warning zone that came into force at 9pm on Saturday.

The warning covered Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, with gusts reaching more than 80mph in exposed coastal spots. The island of Tiree in the Inner Hebrides was hit by 82mph winds at about 4am on Sunday, according to the forecaster.
The Met Office advised people in affected areas to secure loose items in gardens and to stay indoors as the storm posed a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.

The Met Office chief forecaster, Jason Kelly, said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north. Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.

“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts. People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”

Several events have already been cancelled this weekend due to the inclement weather. Visit Liverpool said the River of Light event, featuring illuminated artworks, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”, while London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations on Sunday were also cancelled on the advice of independent health and safety experts.

Edinburgh Castle is closed on Sunday because of the high winds and adverse weather, while the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire has also closed for the day, after its Fountains by Floodlight event on Saturday evening was cancelled.
There was disruption on the railway network on Saturday night and delays and cancellations were expected to continue into Sunday.
The railway line between Preston and Blackpool North in Lancashire was blocked after heavy rain led to flooding, while in Scotland trees came down on the tracks near Dumfries.
Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, and it reminded people living near rail lines to firmly secure objects in their gardens.
after newsletter promotion
Strong winds also disrupted flights, with hundreds delayed or cancelled at several UK and Ireland airports, including Dublin, Heathrow, Manchester, Edinburgh and Glasgow.
The Environment Agency had issued 66 alerts for spots across England where flooding was possible by 7am on Sunday, as well as 10 warnings stating that flooding was expected.

Cumbria police said they had received a number of calls overnight to localised flooding and fallen trees blocking roads across the county, and urged motorists to drive with care while emergency services worked to clear the obstructions.
The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings, which cover parts of England farther south, as well as north Wales and the whole of Northern Ireland.

Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday, bringing 76mph winds to St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, 74mph recorded at Aberporth in south Wales, and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.

articles.title: Brazil votes in tight runoff between leftist Lula and right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro
articles.summary: The high stakes election will decide whether Brazil will move toward the right or retain a leftist government.

image.caption: The election pits left-of-center veteran politician Lula da Silva (R) against right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro (L)Image: Douglas Magno/AFP/Agustin Marcarian/REUTERS

blocks.text: Voters in Brazil head to polls on Sunday for a presidential runoff election between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro.
In the first round earlier this month, Bolsonaro surpassed Lula by more than 2.2 million votes. More than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million abstained.
However, Sunday's runoff election is expected to be neck-and-neck, with recent polls showing Lula closing the gap.
Candidates need more than 50% of the vote to become president.
Brazil election: Voters in Rio split over crime and policing
Election to determine Brazil's direction
The high-stakes election is set to determine Brazil's political direction, pitting left-of-center veteran Lula, 80, against right-wing Bolsonaro, 45, who is an ally of the US.
If Bolsonaro wins, it will signify a shift to the right for Brazil and could determine the extent to which the US will be able to grow its influence in Latin America.
Lula has campaigned to continue his social policies to boost employment and reduce poverty, while Bolsonaro has pledged a tougher course against crime and a political fresh start.
Flavio has also pledged to free his father, who is under house arrest for attempting a coup in 2022, if he is elected.
However, if Lula, who has opposed the US President Donald Trump over trade and security, secures a fourth term, it is likely to pose hurdles for Washington.
The 80-year-old was previously head of state from 2003 to 2010, and became president again in 2023.
Deforestation in Brazil's Amazon falls to record low
Flavio Bolsonaro has sat in the Senate since 2019 and is running for the presidency for the first time.
The rematch between Lula and Bolsonaro comes against the backdrop of corruption scandals, economic downslide and accusations of US interference, which Washington denies.
Around 159 million people are eligible to vote in the election.
Preliminary results are expected on Sunday night.

articles.title: Signs suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine minister
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Forensic analysis of found images continues as Meghan’s father denies possessing child sexual abuse images

All signs point to Thomas Markle Sr being a “possible sex offender of…

blocks.text: All signs point to Thomas Markle Sr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” although a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”, the Philippine interior minister has told the Guardian.

Authorities in the south-east Asian country are analysing digital images allegedly belonging to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex that were said to have been found at his former home in Cebu. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities last week that he had apparently discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images.

“In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles,” said Jonvic Remulla, the interior minister. “Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week.”

Remulla said a statement would be released once the data had been analysed, without giving a specific date. “Please give us a week to determine the contents and to come up with a definitive picture,” he said. “We will release a statement then.”
Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.
Philippine police are also investigating a laptop found at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr had been living until he returned to the US earlier this year.
In a statement given to Agence France-Presse, Remulla said the Philippine national police inspected Markle’s former home and found a “trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop”.
“The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him,” he said.
Markle told the Mail the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
He said: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

Meghan has said she is “deeply distressed” over the allegations, which were first reported in the Sun. She said she had broken off contact with her father to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.

On Saturday, the Metropolitan police confirmed they gave a letter to Meghan in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, but said they did not pass it on to other law enforcement agencies. Scotland Yard is considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.

In a statement, a Met spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019 we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS [Metropolitan Police Service] Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.
“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

In a statement on Friday issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
She later said she had misremembered the year in which the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.

A spokesperson for the duchess said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.
“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.”

Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu. Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

articles.title: Teodoro warns PMA of ‘weaponization of information’ as warfare moves beyond battlefield
articles.summary: The Philippine defense chief says technological advances, geopolitical developments, disruptions to supply chains, and other changes can emerge quickly and carry consequences for the security of…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – Wars are no longer fought only with guns, ships, and aircraft. Information itself can be weaponized, and future military leaders must know how to deal with it.

Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr. raised that warning during the Philippine Military Academy’s 128th Foundation Anniversary on Saturday, October 24, pointing to the “pervasive weaponization of information” as one of the security challenges that military institutions can no longer afford to treat as secondary.
Teodoro said technological advances, geopolitical developments, disruptions to supply chains, and other changes can emerge quickly and carry consequences for the security of states and individuals.

Some of these changes, he said, are not even the result of carefully planned government action but may come from technological breakthroughs or decisions by major global players that force everyone else to adjust.
The military, he said, must be able not only to respond but also to build leaders capable of managing organizations through that uncertainty.
For the Philippines, Teodoro said, that means strengthening the institutions needed to protect “our most sacred sovereignty, territorial integrity, and dignity as a Filipino people.”

Teodoro is among the most vocal in the Philippine government over China’s actions against the Philippines in the West Philippine Sea, enough for China to bar him from entering the country as well as from engaging in “any transaction, cooperation or other activities” with organizations or individuals in China.
Teodoro said the changing security environment also affects what PMA is expected to produce.
“We have to produce in this academy war fighters, make no bones about it. Every graduate of this institution is a war fighter,” he said.

He was quick to explain that he was not referring only to soldiers engaged in combat. “War fighting is not confined to combat operations and kinetic operations. War fighting spans the whole gamut of activities that will preserve the national objectives of any state,” he said.
That includes intelligence, analysis, logistics, personnel support, and the people who keep operations going behind the front line.
“Every person in uniform is a war fighter. Every member of the civilian human resource team of the Department of National Defense and the Armed Forces of the Philippines is a war fighter,” he said.
For PMA, this means doing two difficult jobs within the cadets’ four years at Fort del Pilar.

The academy must give them an education that can meet Philippine standards and stand alongside peer institutions in countries the Philippines works with. At the same time, it must produce junior officers ready to serve in the Armed Forces and, beginning three years from now, the Philippine Coast Guard.
Those graduates, Teodoro said, must leave with the proper military ethics, duties, responsibilities, and basic tactical skills required of their respective services.
“That is a tall order,” he said.
Teodoro also had a message for defense planners: Think bigger. Move faster.
“The Philippines cannot afford to be conservative in its planning,” he said.

If the country plans cautiously while similarly situated states are more ambitious, he said, the Philippines risks falling behind. That is particularly dangerous when sovereignty and national security are involved.
“Ambitious plans needed to have been laid down on the ground years ago,” Teodoro said. “But we cannot recoup the past. We can only make the present faster.”
Then came one of his sharpest lines: “And today is not fast enough. Tomorrow is certainly unacceptable.”

Teodoro said he had extensive discussions with PMA Superintendent Lieutenant General Michael Logico on the academy’s growth plans, infrastructure, curriculum, Corps of Professors, and the future design of the Cadet Corps, building on goals left by former superintendent Vice Admiral Caesar Bernard Valencia.
Teodoro also questioned a habit he said he has seen in AFP education and training systems.
“Education is for knowledge. Training is for skills,” he said.
The two, he argued, should not simply be fused together. “Without knowledge, you cannot form skills. You cannot train skills.”

Military officers need a continuing and current body of knowledge across different fields, he said, because conflict has become increasingly multidisciplinary, unpredictable, and difficult to structure neatly.
That knowledge can then be translated into skills.
Teodoro also took issue with educational opportunities being awarded without sufficient regard for merit, particularly in advanced study and research.
“The opportunity for acquiring knowledge should be democratic,” he said.
Once that opportunity has been made available fairly, however, he said “individual merit and excellence” should determine educational qualification.
Teodoro also challenged the idea that PMA education and training should remain confined to its Baguio home.
“Fort Del Pilar houses the Philippine Military Academy. But the Philippine Military Academy should not be solely in Fort Del Pilar,” he said.
The Philippines has too many different operating environments, he said, for future officers to depend on a single training venue.

He linked this to the government’s push to secure military reservations for AFP use and to address infrastructure gaps that have affected operations, particularly in the maritime domain, as well as logistics, internal security, external defense, and disaster response.
Teodoro said the Armed Forces must be ready to enforce Philippine laws across the country’s vast maritime domain and deal with state actors that may not always follow international law.
That, he said, is why the defense establishment cannot afford timid planning.

The task for PMA is no longer simply to teach cadets how to fight the wars previous generations knew. It is to give them enough knowledge, skill, and judgment to understand what the next threat looks like, especially when it may arrive not as a bullet, but as information. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Gadi Eisenkot campaigns on Moroccan roots in challenge to Netanyahu
articles.summary: As Israel prepares to vote, Gadi Eisenkot is leveraging his Moroccan heritage in Likud strongholds such as Sderot. From historical divides to October 7, identity and trauma are redefining the city's…

image.caption: Gadi Eisenkot election ads use the term 'a prime minister of our own' in Moroccan ArabicImage: Felix Tamsut/DW

blocks.text: Ahead of Tuesday's elections, party advertisements greet people arriving by train to the outskirts of the western Israeli city of Sderot.
Campaign posters with various slogans promote the right-wing Likud and the far-right Otzma Yehudit parties. However, one poster is seen more than any others: that of's liberal Yashar party.
Its slogan, "Rosh Memshala Dialna," combines the terms "prime minister" in Hebrew and the words "of our own" in Moroccan Arabic.
And there is a good reason why Eisenkot's campaign in Sderot and other cities on Israel's sociopolitical periphery focuses on his Moroccan roots.
Eisenkot's Mizrahi background

Sderot — located in the Negev desert, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) to Tel Aviv's south and just a kilometer away from the Gaza border — is a city with a large Moroccan Jewish community. In recent decades, the city has become symbolic of Moroccan-Jewish culture in Israel, finding its expression in music, cinema and state politics.
Israel elections: Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's challenger?

Historically, Sderot is considered a bastion of the Israeli right, and especially a stronghold of Prime MinisterBenjamin Netanyahu's Likud. In 2022, Likud received more than 40% of the votes in Sderot, compared with 23% nationwide. Other members of Israel's far-right coalition received a lot of support there in the last election.

This pattern reflects deeper historical divisions in Israel between Ashkenazim, or Jews of European origin, and Mizrahim, or Jews mostly from Middle Eastern and North African backgrounds. According to estimates, half of Israel's Jewish population is of Mizrahi origin, amounting to about 4 million people.
Mizrahi Jews have faced discrimination and neglect since the early days of the Israeli state. This inequality still shapes the economic and social reality in Israel ― and its political discourse.

The issue has received special attention in the 2026 campaign. Eisenkot, Netanyahu's major challenger, is of Moroccan origin and grew up in Eilat, a city with a large North African Jewish population. Eisenkot's Yashar party accused Likud of sidelining its Mizrahi politicians. The campaign slogan, "Netanyahu: Let the Mizrahim give interviews,” mocked that omission.

blocks.caption: A sticker campaign in Sderot called for a Mizrahi prime ministerImage: Felix Tamsut/DW

blocks.text: On live television, the right-wing journalist Yinon Magal — one of Netanyahu's most vocal supporters — claimed that Eisenkot was being controlled by elitist Ashkenazim and called him a "monkey."
Netanyahu, who is of European origin, condemned the remark.

Morocco-born Daniel Ben-Simon, an award-winning Israeli journalist and a former member of parliament, told DW that Eisenkot's embrace of his roots might have been forced upon him by Magal's comments — but it has historical value nevertheless.

"People don't use terms like 'Dialna' with pride," Ben-Simon said, referring to Eisenkot's embrace of the Arabic term "of our own" in campaign posters. He said Israeli society had long tried to erase the Arab identities of North African Jews.

Eisenkot's embrace of his identity serves as a way of "leaving the frame" set by society. "By using such a term, you're creating a new identity: an Israeli-Moroccan identity," Ben-Simon said. "Eisenkot is the first to allow this double identity to be expressed and still feel at home."
Israel's historical divide

After Israel's founding, the ruling socialist party, Mapai, whose leadership was largely Ashkenazi, pursued discriminatory policies against Mizrahim. Mizrahim were often expected to "Europeanize” rather than preserve their own culture, heritage, or Arabic language.
Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel's election?

These inequalities also took a material form. In the state's early decades, while European immigrants often received better housing and jobs, many Jews from Arab-speaking countries were sent to Ma'abarot, or temporary transit camps, often in remote areas with little infrastructure. Many later became "development towns,” which remained underfunded compared with Israel's central regions. That in turn resulted in poverty. Sderot, in the south, is one of the best-known development towns.

For many Mizrahim, limited access to jobs, education and infrastructure symbolized long-standing exclusion by the Mapai establishment. Likud, founded as a right-wing alliance in 1973, used this frustration effectively under Menachem Begin. Mizrahi support for Begin helped produce the Mahapach, or upheaval, when Likud first defeated the socialist camp and took power. Since then, Mizrahim have often been associated with Likud, even though the party has never had a Mizrahi leader.
Sderot's changing demographics

Over the past two decades, Sderot's proximity to Gaza has made the city a frequent target of rocket attacks launched by the militant group Hamas. During the Hamas-led terrorist attacks on October 7, 2023, the city of Sderot was hit especially hard. More than 50 people were killed. In the three years since the attack, the city's population has grown by about 5,000 people, bringing it to 40,000, with many young families making the town their home, both as a result of idealism and government benefits.

blocks.caption: The Sderot memorial for the victims of October 7Image: Felix Tamsut/DW

blocks.text: Walking around the town, it's hard not to notice that the so-called national-religious community is becoming increasingly dominant. This community tends to vote for Bezalel Smotrich's far-right Religious Zionism party, a main member of Netanyahu's coalition. Though votes for Smotrich and his party are de facto votes for Netanyahu's bloc, the prime minister's Likud party itself could suffer losses in Sderot.

Regardless of the election's results, the perception of Sderot as a city of Moroccan Jews is not bound to change anytime soon. Ben-Simon said Eisenkot's election could serve as an opportunity for reshaping Moroccan Jews' future identity in Israel.
"The connection cities like Sderot have to their Moroccan roots would grow stronger as a result of an Eisenkot win," Ben-Simon said.

articles.summary: The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said on Sunday that it would comply with the Supreme Court"s (SC) directives on unprogrammed appropriations (UA) in the 2026 national budget.

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 5:21pm
The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said on Sunday that it would comply with the Supreme Court’s (SC) directives on unprogrammed appropriations (UA) in the 2026 national budget.

In a statement, the DBM said it would adhere to the high court’s directives while continuing to implement provisions of the 2026 General Appropriations Act (GAA) that were unaffected by the ruling, in accordance with the Constitution and other applicable laws.

“The DBM will observe the applicable Supreme Court directives concerning these provisions, without prejudice to the government’s right to seek reconsideration through appropriate judicial processes,” the department said.
“Unaffected provisions remain implementable, subject to their respective legal bases, funding conditions, and established budgetary procedures,” it added.
The DBM also said that funds released so far from the 2026 UA were strictly for foreign-assisted projects, which are governed by a separate funding rule that was not invalidated by the Court.
On Tuesday, the SC declared unconstitutional provisions allowing UA in the 2024, 2025 and 2026 national budgets, citing budget increases made by Congress.
Malacañang said it “respectfully disagrees” with certain portions of the ruling, adding that the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) had been tasked with filing a motion for reconsideration.
“Magalang nating hinihiling sa Korte Suprema na muling suriin ang kanilang desisyon,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said.
(We respectfully ask the Supreme Court to review its decision.)

The OSG confirmed that it had received a copy of the SC decision and said it respected the ruling. However, it would challenge certain portions, “particularly the guardrails prescribed for the exercise of budgetary powers.”

The DBM said it would continue coordinating with the OSG and other concerned government agencies to assess the ruling’s “legal, fiscal, technical, and operational implications” and determine the appropriate next steps.
It added that the government would seek to safeguard fiscal stability and ensure the continued delivery of government services authorized by law. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Prague honors Roma resistance fighters against Hitler
articles.summary: More than 1,400 Roma fought against the German Nazi occupation in Czechoslovakia. A new exhibition in Prague showcases the stories of partisans and soldiers whose fates barely received any attention…

image.caption: Since the end of WWII, the role of Roma resistance fighters was largely unknownImage: Luboš Palata/DW

blocks.text: For more than half a million Roma in Czechia and Slovakia, October 15, 2026, marks an important milestone.

That day, an exhibition on a largely forgotten chapter of Czech history opened at the Museum of the Romani National Revival in Prague. The exhibit explores the role of Czech and Slovak Romani resistance fighters during the Nazi German occupation and the dismantling of Czechoslovakia from 1938 to 1945.

Until now, Czech and Slovak Roma appeared in the history of World War II almost exclusively as victims of the Holocaust against Roma and Sinti. In the so-called Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, Nazi Germany murdered approximately 90% of the Czech Roma during World War II.

However, what is less well known is that a large number of Czech and Slovak Roma fought against the German occupiers as partisans in resistance groups and as soldiers in the Czechoslovak Underground Army, or Defense of the Nation, ON.

blocks.caption: The organizers of the exhibition hope that people will bring their children and grandchildren to show that Roma and Sinti have their own heroesImage: Luboš Palata/DW

blocks.text: Roma have heroes, too

The exhibition at the Museum of the Roma National Movement therefore marks a turning point in how the Roma are viewed during World War II. At least that is the hope of museum director Emil Scuka, a lawyer, former prosecutor and one of the best-known Czech Roma activists.

"We were not only victims; we were also heroes," Scuka said in his speech to several hundred attendees at the exhibition opening, most of whom were Roma from Czechia and Slovakia. "Many people, not even among the Roma themselves, are aware that we Roma fought against Nazism," he noted. In his view, "organizing and opening the exhibition was something my generation owed to these Roma heroes and today we are repaying that debt."
Scuka called on those present: "Bring your children and grandchildren here so they can see for themselves and realize that the Roma have heroes too!"

He also pointed out that this topic had been completely marginalized in Czech and Slovak historical writing for decades and that the Roma had therefore decided on their own to document the fates of their war heroes.
The exhibition presents the detailed life stories of 100 of the most significant Roma partisans and Roma soldiers from the Czech underground army and resistance groups who fought against the Nazis.
"We found over 1,400 Romani fighters in the archives. From among them, we selected the 100 most interesting stories for this exhibition," said exhibition curator Radoslav Scuka at the opening.
Unseen heroes — Sinti and Roma resist Nazis
Groundbreaking research on Roma resistance fighters

Among these figures is Anton Facuna, a sergeant in the American intelligence agency Office of Strategic Services (OSS), who was flown to Slovakia in October 1944 on a secret mission. Slovakia had been a puppet state of Hitler from 1939 to 1945.

Another is Josef Serinek, known by the nickname "Black Partisan from Vysocina," who managed to escape from the Nazi concentration camp for Roma in Lety and subsequently founded and commanded the large Capajev-Cerny partisan unit in the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands.

In 2022, Czech President Milos Zeman posthumously awarded him the Medal for Heroism. Toward the end of his life, Serinek shared his memories with historian Jan Tesar, who later wrote the three-volume book "Ceska cikanska rapsodie", which translates to Czech Gypsy Rhapsody.

Except for Tesar's book, the history of Roma resistance against Nazism has not been researched by Czech and Slovak historians to this day. "I am not aware of any scholarly historical work that deals with Roma resistance against Nazism," Prokop Tomek, a historian at the Military History Institute in Prague, told DW.

"The number of 1,400 Roma who took part in the fight against Nazism as members of the resistance or in the foreign army does not strike me as an exaggeration and corresponds to the proportion of the Roma population in Czechoslovakia," Tomek said, adding that the "exhibition on the Roma resistance against Nazism during the war is undoubtedly groundbreaking."

blocks.caption: The life of resistance fighter Anton Facuna is one of around 100 examples on displayImage: Luboš Palata/DW

blocks.text: Fears of revealing one's Roma identity

To this day, many Roma in Czechia and Slovakia do not publicly acknowledge their ethnic identity. This is partly due to experiences with the Holocaust during the Nazi era that have been passed down through generations. Czech historians and politicians continue to debate the extent to which the Czech authorities of the Protectorate were complicit in the extermination of the Czech Roma.
However, one thing is certain: the police registration of all Roma, which had been enshrined in law in Czechoslovakia since 1927, facilitated the extermination of the Roma by the German Nazis.
According to estimates by the Czech government, approximately 250,000 Roma live in the country today. In the 2021 census, however, only 21,000 people identified as Roma.

Of all ethnic groups in Czechia, which has a population of 10 million, the Roma are among the three largest ethnic minorities in terms of numbers. However, they are the most socially disadvantaged, have very little political representation, and are therefore scarcely present in Czech politics.
Roma, Sinti persecuted in WWII still fight for recognition
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia looks to US for an AI edge as Yemen's Houthis up pressure
articles.summary: The US is helping Saudi Arabia fight the Houthi group in Yemen with AI-assisted targeting. But AI is not a magic bullet, experts say, and there are technological, political and human rights issues to…

image.caption: Almost 200 people, mostly children, were killed at a school when the US military used AI-assisted targeting in Iran in late FebruaryImage: Atta Kenare/AFP

blocks.text: Under attack from the militant Houthi group in neighboring Yemen, Saudi Arabia has asked numerous allies for help.
That includes the United States, even though media report that US President Donald Trump refused when Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman asked him to take direct military action against the Houthis.

However the US is providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence, which includes a targeting tool that uses artificial intelligence, or AI. A September report by US broadcaster CNN, quoting several unnamed American officials, said that between 100 and 200 US soldiers were in Saudi Arabia as part of new joint force command to facilitate this.
The US personnel were helping the Saudis "use a targeting tool that allows military officers to see in real-time what is happening on the battlefield," CNN reported.
Officials said the system in Saudi Arabia was similar to that known as the Maven Smart System, or MSS for short, which the US military has also used as it sought targets in Iran, Iraq and Syria.
UK sends warplanes as Saudi Arabia seeks more help against Houthis
What is Maven?

MSS came out of what's known as Project Maven, the US's flagship artificial intelligence program for the military, first launched in 2017. MSS itself is an AI-enabled digital platform that "aggregates, organizes and visualizes vast streams of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data," analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington explained in a June text.

The software system identifies patterns in data coming from, for example, live satellite feeds or drone cameras and then labels potential targets such as possible rocket launchers, tanks or suspicious vehicle convoys.

Previously human military analysts would have had to look at a wide array of different sources to try to find those, the CSIS researchers wrote. It was difficult and, in the case of hours of satellite or drone footage, almost impossible. But MSS now brings hundreds of sources together, analyses them all, then flags possible targets. It also calculates the best method of hitting the target.
Tech commentator Bilawal Sidhu, a former Google product manager, has described the MSS set up as like a "Google Earth for war."
Using the MSS dramatically speeds up what is known as "the kill chain" — that is, the time it takes to detect a target, decide if it's dangerous and then order a strike.

When the US military used MSS while attacking Iran in late February, the AI-powered system facilitated hits on more than 1,000 targets within the first 24 hours of the war. Previously American soldiers were hitting about 100 targets a day.
A faster kill chain?
Up until recently, the long-simmering civil war in Yemen had been comparatively calm following an informal ceasefire negotiated in 2022.

The Houthi rebel group has held large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2015. Yemen's internationally recognized government and other groups held territory across the south and east. That latter is supported by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

blocks.caption: The Houthi group has been fighting in a civil war in Yemen as well as against Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states since 2015Image: Mohammed Huwais/AFP

blocks.text: The Houthi's latest military campaign, which began in September, has seen the group take further control of Yemen's coast. They also ramped up attacks against Saudi Arabia again, hitting the country's main airport and oil facilities. So far, though, military campaigns against the Houthi group by Saudi Arabia, the United States and others have all failed to significantly weaken the group.

This is partially because the Houthis take a "zero-sum approach," Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House, told DW recently. The group's founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too "soft," and that poverty and hardship are a divine test, al-Muslimi said.
"They don't care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital," she said. "It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice."
MSS's major issues
There are certain technical issues users have noted with the MSS in the past that could also prove problematic in Yemen.

The Houthis tend to be highly mobile, using truck-mounted ballistic missiles and small drone swarms as they operate from hills and canyons in rugged countryside. It's possible that fighters might be long gone before they can be attacked even with the help of AI-assisted targeting.

blocks.caption: Iraq in 2003: During the US invasion of Iraq, about 2,000 US military personnel were responsible for targeting; in a 2024 army exercise using MSS, only 20 were neededImage: Jamal Saidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Though MSS is known to work best in relatively unpopulated areas, factors such as changes in desert terrain, dust storms, high wind, snowfall and dense foliage — and even deliberately planted decoys — can reduce its success rate.
There is also a worrying ethical aspect to shortening the kill chain. A human is always supposed to verify the target that the AI-assisted tool has identified and decide how to react.

But it doesn't always work that way. For example, among the sites MSS targeted in Iran on the first day of the war was a school. An American missile killed almost 200 people at a primary school in southern Iran, most of them children aged between seven and 12.
Could AI defeat the Houthis?

In its military campaign in Gaza, Israel — arguably the Middle Eastern country with the most advanced military-use AI — has also used AI-assisted targeting. An Israeli system known as the Gospel, or Habsora, is the closest to MSS in the way it works.

But, as has been documented elsewhere, including by Israeli and British journalists and in the recent documentary Naza, the use of such AI targeting tools have also been highly problematic because of the numbers of civilian casualties that can result.

blocks.caption: The school a US missile hit had previously been part of an Iranian naval base, yet was listed online as a school and playgrounds were visible on satellite imageryImage: Vantor/REUTERS

blocks.text: "On the one hand [in Gaza], AI has enhanced commanders' situational awareness, lessened the human costs of tunnel mapping, improved the speed of military strikes, and boosted the survivability of troops," analysts Frederic Wehrey and Andrew Bonney wrote for War on the Rocks, a specialist media outlet. "Yet the benefits afforded by such functions have been overshadowed by mounting civilian deaths reportedly resulting from this technology's safeguards being loosened or eliminated."

All of which is why Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist based in Australia who has researched the impact of Israel's AI-assisted technology, doesn't believe similar technology will lead to the defeat of the Houthi group.

"I don't think there's much evidence at all that using an AI tool is going to make much difference on the ground, except for causing huge amounts of civilian casualties," Loewenstein, who authored the book, "The Palestine Laboratory: How Israel Exports The Technology of Occupation Around the World," told DW. "And I think what the US and the Saudis will find is that the Houthis have an incredibly high tolerance level for destruction."
Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis

articles.title: This Nova Scotian just ran his first marathon. He trained for it by eating donairs
articles.summary: David Wadden ran and biked to 59 donair shops in the Halifax area this year to eat donairs and rate them as part of a charity fundraiser. But that wasn't the hard part. After eating the donair, he…

image.caption: David Wadden recently completed the 42.2-kilometre marathon at the Valley Harvest Marathon in Nova Scotia's Annapolis Valley. Part of his training regimen involved running and biking to 59 donair shops, where he'd eat a donair. He later posted videos rating the donairs. (Paige Wadden/Submitted by Da

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

David Wadden ran and biked to 59 donair shops in the Halifax area this year to eat donairs and rate them as part of a charity fundraiser. But that wasn't the hard part. After eating the donair, he faced the ungodly task of running or biking back home.
David Wadden trained by running and biking to 59 donair shops, raising more than $2,000 for Feed Nova Scotia
Growing up in Cape Breton, David Wadden thought donairs were fixtures at pizza shops worldwide.

It wasn't until he moved to Halifax that he learned the beloved official food of the city — spiced meat served on a pita with onions, tomatoes and a sweet garlicky sauce — was not a global thing. Well, not yet at least.

This realization, coupled with the fact that he couldn't name a favourite donair spot to friends visiting from out of town, got him thinking about how to incorporate a journey of donair discovery, exercise and raising money for charity.
"Thinking of exercise, I went to running, donair and marathon, kind of shove those two words together, and then once we had the name Donair-Athon … the ball really started to roll," said Wadden, 29.
Wadden ran and biked to 59 donair shops in the Halifax area this year to eat donairs, rate them and post videos about the experiences. He's raised more than $2,200 for Feed Nova Scotia doing so.
But that wasn't the hard part. After eating the donair, he faced the ungodly task of running or biking back home.

David Wadden rated the donairs on factors such as meat and pita quality, and tracked the results in a publicly available spreadsheet. He even weighed the donairs to calculate the price per pound. (Submitted by David Wadden)
This unorthodox training regimen resulted in Wadden running a 42.2-kilometre marathon two weeks ago at the Valley Harvest Marathon in Nova Scotia's Annapolis Valley.
Wadden said after eating the donairs, sometimes he felt great, sometimes not.

items: Halifax declares donairs the official food of the city

blocks.text: "There was the odd time where I felt better after the donair, I don't know why," he said. "But most of the time I was a little sluggish getting back out and running. I didn't have any incidents, which was nice. I kind of expected maybe more bathroom breaks needed or, heaven forbid, a throw-up."

While running after eating a donair is an achievement on its own, even more impressive is that Wadden did not have a background in running prior to this. He used to do indoor rock climbing, but had to find a new outlet after a shoulder injury.
Wadden has an innate curiosity. He used to post videos to YouTube of himself learning new skills, such as how to juggle or cook the perfect steak, so this project is an extension of that attitude.
A rotating spit of donair meat is seen at a King Of Donair restaurant in Halifax on Tuesday, Nov. 14, 2017. (Andrew Vaughan/The Canadian Press)
Wadden said he selected Feed Nova Scotia because he wanted something food-related that was local.

"I think it's the broader idea of helping the community," said Wadden. "I was lucky enough never to have those issues myself, but I always had family that … would fundraise for these different charities."

Thomas Coldwell, Feed Nova Scotia's director of philanthropy and engagement, said every year there are hundreds of "third-party events" where people like Wadden fundraise for the charity or hold food drives. He said they're important for the charity.
Coldwell said he's not sure if others have pitched donair-themed events to the charity.

items: Why this Smithsonian astronomer has a donair website
How a recipe for wild game donair ended up on an NRA website

blocks.text: "Well, I love a donair, but I'm not sure I could happily bike after eating one, so it's great to see someone like David who's using their skills and putting out wonderful videos showcasing the Halifax donair … and also to tie it in with food insecurity and support fundraising," said Coldwell.

Besides the out-of-pocket costs for the donairs at roughly $12 each, Wadden said he also had to buy running equipment. Despite the social media views, he said he hasn't made any money from the project.

Wadden said he came up with the idea for the project about a year ago. Before he could actually do the Donair-Athon, though, he had to spend a few months training to get ready for it, dealing with complications such as shin splints and knee pain.
How Wadden prepared for the marathon

Starting in February, he'd do one donair excursion a week. In March, he upped the frequency, running two days a week and throwing in a third donair trip by bike, eventually landing on running three days a week.
On the off days, he'd supplement the regimen with things like yoga or strength training. All told, he said he ran more than 500 kilometres and biked more than 300 kilometres through the Donair-Athon.
Wadden said the highlight of the venture was meeting with people at the donair shops and doing the marathon itself.
His least favourite part was the shin splints.
"They were not fun one bit," he said.
Prior to the Donair-Athon, Wadden said he only ate donairs once every couple of months, which explains why he couldn't suggest a favourite place to out-of-towners.
Wadden said he's had enough donairs for 2026, but might resume eating them in the new year.
Future marathons?
While he rules out doing another full marathon, a half-marathon may be in the works.
"I told myself once I finished this, I'm done [running]," said Wadden. "And now that I've finished the marathon, I really want to get back out there.
"I'm going to see if I can fit it in because I do want to keep doing other stuff, but I definitely have a new love for running that I didn't think I would get."

articles.title: Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
articles.summary: Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute

blocks.text: CAMPAIGN. A person uses a smartphone next to a campaign van for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party at Hatikva market during Netanyahu's visit, ahead of Israel's national election, in Tel Aviv, Israel, October 22, 2026.
Hannah Confino/REUTERS
Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute

items: In Dimona, Israel, disenchanted voters are actively campaigning for centrist Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main rival, as the election approaches on October 27, following a decline in Likud's popularity after the October 7 Hamas attack.

Despite a strong historical support for Likud among Mizrahi voters, a significant portion of former supporters are now considering alternatives, with 13% of voters undecided and 55% of 2022 Likud voters indicating they may not vote for the party again.

Eisenkot's personal story and military credentials resonate with voters, particularly in areas like Dimona, but Netanyahu remains a formidable opponent, leveraging his long-standing influence and development efforts in the region.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

DIMONA, Israel – In the remote Negev Desert town of Dimona, long a bastion of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, disenchanted voters are going door-to-door campaigning for his top rival, hoping to bring down the veteran prime minister in Israel’s election on Tuesday, October 27.

The ballot is Israel’s first since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, surprise attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the militant group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran.

The October 7 security breach saw Likud’s popularity plummet. Opinion polls for months have predicted Netanyahu’s coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties losing its majority. But his top rival, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears.
Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground.
“We must have change. Bibi has to go,” said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most his life. “Bibi has brought disaster to Israel.“
Assayag is part of a cohort of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot’s party Yashar, which is neck-and-neck with Likud in the polls.
It’s a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the previous 2022 election cast a ballot for Likud.

“I will never betray Likud,” said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and the blame he receives from detractors for October 7 was unfair.

Right-wing Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced centre-left Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations.

Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the centre to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong.

“Most people here vote for Likud just because that’s how they were raised,” said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. “The change will come when people start to think about their children’s future rather than their parents’ past.”

While Netanyahu has a hard core of supporters that can’t be won over, the prize is undecided voters who “understand that we are in a state of crisis” and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot’s Dimona campaign.
Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.

Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided.
It is in places just like Dimona where Eisenkot stands a chance to bite a chunk out of Likud’s base, said Amotz Asa-El, a political scientist at the Hartman Institute.

A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins from the Mizrahi community that “appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud’s traditional electorate,” said Asa-El.
In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters.

At a town hall during a visit to Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a leader of Mizrahi descent. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son.
But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds.

“Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love,” he said.
Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears.

But even some who are sympathetic to Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel’s youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms.
“It’s time for him to go,” said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. “He’s done a lot for Israel but it can’t go on. I won’t give my vote to someone almost 80-years-old.” – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 4:47pm

A flotilla composed of ships and aircraft from the Philippines, United States and Japan recently conducted the 22nd Multilateral Maritime Cooperative Activity (MMCA) in the West Philippine Sea from 19 to 24 October 2026.

A statement from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said the Philippine Navy and Philippine Coast Guard were joined by the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF) and United States Pacific Command (USPACOM) in the activity.

The Philippine side was represented by the guided missile frigate BRP Miguel Malvar (FFG6), an AW109 helicopter, a C-208B aircraft, and a search-and-rescue (SAR) aircraft, while the Philippine Coast Guard fielded BRP Gabriela Silang (OPV 8301).
The USPACOM sent the cutter USCGC Bertholf and an MH-65 helicopter, while the JMSDF deployed the guided missile destroyer JS Kirisame and an SH-60K helicopter.

The AFP said the participants conducted Communications Exercise (COMMEX), Division Tactics (DIVTACS), Photo Exercise (PHOTOEX), Deck Landing Qualification and Vertical Replenishment (DLQ/VERTREP), Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) and Search and Rescue (SAR) serials to strengthen logistics, maritime-security, and emergency-response coordination.

It added that, “the successful conduct of the 22nd MMCA reaffirmed the Philippines’ commitment to strengthening maritime cooperation with Japan and the United States and promoting a free, open, and rules-based maritime environment. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: 'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
articles.summary: That Girl Boina's post about why she had closed her beauty parlour struck a nerve with other small business owners.

blocks.text: When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.

Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.

The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.

She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"

Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.

In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.

The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.

The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.

A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.

The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.

At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.

The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.

The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.

At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

articles.title: Senate vows to scrap lump-sum funds in 2027 budget after SC ruling
articles.summary: The Senate has vowed to eliminate lump-sum funds from the 2027 national budget, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday, following a Supreme Court ruling declaring certain provisions of the…

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 4:35pm

The Senate has vowed to eliminate lump-sum funds from the 2027 national budget, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday, following a Supreme Court ruling declaring certain provisions of the 2024 and 2025 national budgets unconstitutional.
The high court also ruled on provisions allowing unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 budget.
“The bottom line is that the Supreme Court said appropriations cannot exceed the budget proposed by the president,” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.
“For 2027, we will ensure that there are no lump-sum funds because they are unconstitutional,” he added.

Gatchalian said a significant portion of the 2024 and 2025 budgets was allocated to the Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs (SAGIP), which was identified as a source of funding for flood control projects.
The senator said, however, that unprogrammed appropriations would remain in the budget, provided they comply with the conditions set by the Supreme Court.
"There will still be unprogrammed appropriations. The Supreme Court did not say these are prohibited or unconstitutional. It merely set parameters, which we will follow,” Gatchalian said.
He said the Senate would also carefully review the allocation for foreign-assisted projects, which had been reduced, with funding transferred to unprogrammed appropriations.
"This is the funding used to build subways and railways. It is important because, without funding, we cannot complete these projects,” he said.
"That is something we are studying carefully. I believe next year's projects are important because we need to accelerate economic growth,” he added.
According to Gatchalian, unprogrammed appropriations account for about 2% to 5% of the total national budget.

Meanwhile, lawyer Camille Ting said the doctrine of operative fact would apply following the Supreme Court's declaration that the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts (GAAs) were unconstitutional.

“Under this doctrine, good-faith projects already implemented and no longer reversible remain valid. Applying this doctrine, irreversible programs in the 2024 and 2025 GAAs whose beneficiaries acted in good faith are valid,” she said.
Ting added that the ruling would not require the return of funds spent on such programs.
“There will be no funds returned in that case,” she said.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

India carries out major operation against international drug cartel
Union Home Minister Amit Shah says Indian agencies have carried out a major crackdown on an international narcotics cartel.

The home minister said 18 people were arrested across 38 locations in the northeastern states of Assam, Mizoram and Manipur on October 23 during a crackdown on an alleged international narcotics cartel.

Shah said Operation Trident uncovered hawala transactions worth ₹100 crore (around €9.4 million). Authorities also froze 1,424 bank accounts, seized properties worth ₹17.82 crore and 500 detonators, and recovered ₹12 lakh in cash, he said.
According to Shah, the network trafficked narcotics across the borders of India, Myanmar and Bangladesh through what he described as the "Death Triangle Corridor."
"India will hammer until the last nail is driven into the coffin of drug cartels," Shah said.

articles.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
articles.summary: The tech billionaire accuses Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using the network for military activity.

blocks.text: Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.
Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".
Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations.
The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.
"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."
He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."
Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram that Ukraine "physically cannot use" commercial Starlink for long- and middle-range drone strikes.
There was no immediate comment from the country's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h (249mph). Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.

Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.
Zelensky initially agreed to do so on the proviso that Russia cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Moscow disregarding this.

The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
