articles.title: Brazilians vote in presidential election runoff pitting leftist Lula against far-right Bolsonaro
articles.summary:
Incumbent president lost in first round to senator and son of convicted ex-president

Brazilians are going to the polls on Sunday in a highly unpredictable runoff in which the leftist…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Brazilians are going to the polls on Sunday in a highly unpredictable runoff in which the leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is attempting an unprecedented comeback against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who won the first-round vote.
Bolsonaro’s surprise victory despite not leading most polls made him the favourite three weeks ago, but since then Lula’s campaign has gained ground, and the two go into the contest virtually tied.

The gap between them was the narrowest ever recorded in a first round, at less than 2% of the vote, and the 81-year-old president has spent much of the runoff campaign focused on turnout – abstention reached a record high in the first round and disproportionately affects his voters – and on stoking fears over what a return to power by a member of the Bolsonaro family could mean.

A congressman for more than 20 years with few bills passed, the 45-year-old Bolsonaro is the eldest son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup to overturn his 2022 defeat to Lula.

The senator has promised that if elected he will pardon his father, and with an even more conservative congress taking office next year he has vowed to “change the constitution and re-democratise this country”, sending chills through those who fear he could follow in his father’s authoritarian footsteps.

blocks.caption: Lula attending a closing campaign rally in São Paulo on Saturday. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

blocks.text: “We’re facing two completely different projects for the country,” said voter Nuno Rau, 63, an architect and writer. “One points towards the end of social rights and the end of democracy itself; on the other side is someone who fought for income distribution and free public education. I may have criticisms of Lula, but there is no way to choose Bolsonaro,” he added.

Aparecida Moreira, a 62-year-old lawyer, will vote for Bolsonaro mainly because of the “iron fist” security policy he proposes, including building five “mega-prisons” inspired by those of El Salvador’s populist autocrat Nayib Bukele.

“I agree with Bolsonaro’s idea of chemical castration for rapists, because there is no crime worse than rape,” said Moreira, adding that voting for Lula would be the same as voting for the “dictator” Alexandre de Moraes, the justice who, despite not having been appointed by Lula, is widely associated with him by Bolsonaro supporters because he oversaw the former president’s conviction.
Both Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula drew large crowds to their final campaign rallies on Saturday in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo and Belo Horizonte.

blocks.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro dancing at a rally in São Paulo on 18 October. Photograph: Alexandre Meneghini/Reuters

blocks.text: With each side of supporters virtually “crystallised”, the election will be decided by the small number of voters who identify with neither candidate.
Bolsonaro began the runoff campaign with a lead and the support of most other defeated candidates, but instead of growing, he stagnated in the polls while Lula gained support.

Many analysts saw this as the result of part of the population suddenly waking up to the “fear” of a Bolsonaro returning to power, as well as controversies including the fact that the senator is under investigation in two federal police inquiries over alleged corruption and money laundering.
Lula, by contrast, radically changed his digital strategy and benefited from student-led protests across the country, most of which did not even involve the president.

“In the first round, Lula’s campaign failed to connect with the population, but now it has been civil society movements that have driven his growth,” said the political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.

blocks.caption: Lula attending a closing campaign rally on Saturday. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

blocks.text: Whatever the result, the race is expected to be decided by a narrow margin in Latin America’s largest country, with an electorate of 159 million.

Many analysts believe that if Lula overturns his first-round defeat, Bolsonaro could follow his father’s example from four years ago and refuse to concede, and that Donald Trump, a longstanding ally of the Bolsonaro clan, could refuse to recognise the result.

“Trump wants to ‘colonise’ all of Latin America in pursuit of its own interests,” said Telles, adding that, with rightwing candidates having won all seven presidential elections held in Latin America since Trump began his second term, Brazil is one of the few countries in the region still offering any resistance to the US president.
“So a Bolsonaro victory would mean losing Brazil to a model of autocracy backed by the US,” she added.

articles.title: Is this Quebec-developed fruit the 'apple of the future'?
articles.summary: Quebec apple producers say it’s been a good season, harvest- and sales-wise. They say it has much to do with U.S. tariffs and new varieties developed in — and for — Quebec.

image.caption: After nearly 25 years of work, the Orléans apple — developed on Île d’Orléans, Que. — is hitting grocery store shelves this fall. Producers hope it might be able to replace the popular Honeycrisp. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal
Quebec apple producers say it’s been a good season, harvest- and sales-wise. They say it has much to do with U.S. tariffs and new varieties developed in — and for — Quebec.
Local apple producers say it comes amid increasing demand for Quebec-grown produce
The Orléans apple — developed on Île d’Orléans, Que. — is hitting grocery store shelves this fall, but has been in the works for nearly 25 years.

Beginning back in 2002, producers handpicked pollen from Honeycrisps and Empire apple flowers, and then spent years crossbreeding them until they arrived at the bright red and crisp Orléans. While it has been available in Quebec orchards for about two years, it's only now hitting grocery store shelves.
"I have some clients coming here asking especially for that kind," says Karen Morin. She thinks it just might be "the apple of the future."
The co-owner of the Verger du Roy in Portneuf grows 57 different types of apples, but Morin says the Orléans is growing more and more popular this year with apple pickers.

"It's a mix of Honeycrisp and Empire, so these two together, it's like a bomb. It's really, really good, so sweet [and] still really crispy," says Morin. "In the future, our children, it won't be the Honeycrisp anymore that will be the top one, it will be the Orléans."

Morin says that, while apple preferences can vary from generation to generation, people are always looking for apples that stay crisper longer. She believes that's why the Orléans apple is increasing in popularity.

Karen Morin says the Orléans apple has been growing in popularity for the past two years with apple pickers, but many people still aren't aware of the latest apple varieties coming to the market. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)
"It's like on the top of the list for firmness, and it's almost top of the list for sugar content," says
Benoit Caron, the owner of La Maison de la Pomme. Caron planted 20,000 Orléans trees at his orchard in Frelighsburg about five years ago.
"It's not the first apple created in Quebec, but it's the first one that we can supply at least 10 months a year because of [its] conservation," says Caron.

He adds that this particular variety is great as a snack, "but it's also a really good apple for cooking. It will hold itself together. So if you do apple custard or apple pie, you will have the nice apple slice that will stay together."
More supply and more demand for Quebec produce

Jérôme-Antoine Brunelle, the executive director of the Producteurs de pommes du Québec, says it's good to have new varieties to appeal to all the different types of consumers, but that the demand for Quebec produce has also been growing recently.
"If these new varieties can help us gain market shares from imported apples and that we can source more of Quebec-grown apples to consumers, it's a win for everyone," he says.
Brunelle says recent tensions with the U.S. and tariff woes did have an impact. "Consumers had more of an interest in locally sourced food," he says, and apples were no exception.

There’s been a bigger interest for locally sourced apples for the past two years, "and it doesn't seem to be slowing down," says the executive director of the Producteurs de pommes du Québec, Jérôme-Antoine Brunelle. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)
"That interest for locally sourced fruit helps us out, and we see that Quebec consumers are more conscientious of where their food comes from," says Brunelle.
He says he is aware, however, that producers and grocery stores must make sure Quebec apples are clearly identified as such in produce aisles to attract more consumers .
Different regions, different apples, different ciders

Claude Jolicoeur, an author who's published three books about apples and cider production, wants to increase the number of apple varieties in Quebec, specifically for cider. "And eventually maybe to have an appellation ‘regional cider,'" he says.

Jolicoeur says this could bring Quebec cider production to another level, similar to wine production in Italy — where different grape varieties, grown in different regions, produce different types of wines, with distinct flavours.
Morin, for instance, says Quebec-grown apples can also taste like other fruits, such as bananas, pineapples, strawberries, and even chestnuts.
"You can compare apples with apples, but they're different," she says.

Regardless of their provenance or flavour, cider apples would not be the same ones as those picked in orchards, or bought at the grocery store, however. "When you want to sell apples in a grocery store, that apple has to be beautiful," says Jolicoeur.
In the cider context, however, he notes, "no one is going to see the apple, so what it looks like is not important at all."
Jolicoeur hopes Quebec cider and apple producers will grow more and more Quebec apple varieties in the coming years.
However, apple producers reiterate, in the meantime, several apple varieties are already available year round, not only in the fall — including the brand new Orléans.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah-Kate Dallaire is a regional journalist with CBC News in Quebec City. She can be reached at sarah-kate.dallaire@radio-canada.ca

articles.title: People are using AI to 'dumb down' their smart TVs. Is that a good idea?
articles.summary: Viral social media posts are showing people how to use AI to hack smart TVs to remove unnecessary apps and programs and disabling some tracking features in an effort to make them run more smoothly.…

image.caption: Some people are using AI agents to 'dumb down' their smart TVs. Tech experts say there are better ways to make your TV less annoying. (CeltStudio/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: World·New

Viral social media posts are showing people how to use AI to hack smart TVs to remove unnecessary apps and programs and disabling some tracking features in an effort to make them run more smoothly. While some are rejoicing, others warn the AI solution could cause bigger problems. They note there are easier, safer ways to simplify a cluttered TV.
Tech experts say to proceed with caution when tinkering with your devices
It's a very 2026 paradox.
Some tech users, fed up with constant surveillance, ads and other distractions, are using artificial intelligence to "dumb down" their smart devices.

Viral social media posts are showing people how to use AI coding prompts to hack and "debloat" smart TVs by removing unnecessary apps and programs and disabling some tracking features in an effort to make them run more smoothly.
While some are rejoicing, others warn the AI solution can cause bigger problems — and say there are easier, safer ways to simplify a cluttered TV.

items: A fridge hack spoiled food in hundreds of French supermarkets. Cybersecurity experts say it's a wake-up call
Is your TV spying on you?

blocks.text: "My TV was updating all the time with different security features and that's because of all the apps and data collection that's required," Toronto-based tech analyst and cybersecurity expert Ritesh Kotak told CBC News.
"So yeah, here is a big push to make the TVs not as smart."
International team of researchers looked at how IoT devices interact with home networks
An easy fix?
Some people have posted their coding scripts — sets of programming instructions carried out by AI agents — on the internet for others to copy.
One, called "dumbtv," was created by its developer to fix a Fire TV that had "become painful to use" because of constant ads on the home screen and apps taking too long to open.

Kotak says people are essentially using AI agents to help them identify their TV's IP address, then blocking certain traffic, like ads on TV home screens and analytics that get sent back to the company that makes the TV.
Some say they had success with asking a Claude AI agent how to hack their TV and talk them through the process so they could do it themselves, an example of a process called "vibe coding."
introducing dumbtv - no spying - no ads from tv - fully customisable to setup just point your agent to this repo - https://t.co/prQLD17Wa4 https://t.co/c6R8EhljiA—DevMuzzammil
But that hasn't worked for everyone. Some users are skeptical that Claude would even respond to that suggestion, and one said his attempt actually made his Android TV unusable.

Experts have urged people not to use these AI solutions, warning they could cause bigger problems. They also point to existing apps like Kyu Launcher and AT4K Launcher that can achieve similar results without the risk.
People 'starting to get fed up'

Tech-savvy individuals have long been hacking devices to customize them, but vibe-coding has opened that capability to a much wider audience, says London, Ont.-based tech analyst and journalist Carmi Levy.
For example, some people have used similar strategies to dumb down their smartphones, with the goal of making them less distracting and addictive.
But Levy warns that vibe coding is not for the "faint of heart," because people can inadvertently destroy their devices, void warranties or install the wrong kind of software.

items: A cure for scrolling? Focus apps are popular, but experts warn more tech can add stress
Why the 'dumb phone' may be having a moment

blocks.text: "It's definitely a 'your mileage may vary' type of scenario. Sometimes it'll work, sometimes it won't. Sometimes you'll end up breaking the very device that you're trying to update."
Levy says in the case of smart TVs, many of these changes can be made by simply tweaking the settings on the TV itself.
He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back

While he doesn't necessarily recommend enlisting AI agents to do the job, Levy says this emerging trend is an understandable response to the surveillance and data collection that's increasingly invading consumer products.
"Every device that we buy has to be smart, every device we buy has to have an app and it has to collect all sorts of information," he said.
"I think, frankly, people are starting to get fed up with all of this data collection. And they're starting to react to this surveillance economy."
Security concerns

Kotak says one way to address these concerns is to use a Fire Stick or other multimedia streaming device loaded with the apps you want that plugs into a TV's HDMI port. Because these tools (which also include the Apple TV device) have their own Wi-Fi adapters, you can leave your TV offline so it will basically just function as a monitor for the streaming device.
He cautions that users should also consider that hacking their smart TV while leaving it connected to the internet could end up making them more vulnerable to outside attacks.

items: AI-driven 'worms' that learn on the fly are the latest potential threat to your devices, researchers say
Canadian hacker pleads guilty in Snowflake data breach case, stealing data and extorting people for millions

blocks.text: Those annoying updates that keep popping up on your TV, he notes, are usually security-related.

"It's important to understand that a lot of smart TVs now also have microphones in them … My fear would be that is it possible for hackers to take over some of those features on your television," Kotak said.
"If your TV is going to be connected to the internet, and you're blocking certain services and you're not doing those updates, you may be making yourself vulnerable."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Netanyahu 'fighting for his political life' in 1st Israeli vote since Oct. 7. He might still survive
articles.summary: There are few Israeli analysts willing to write off the country's longest-serving prime minister in Tuesday's election, despite the catastrophic impact of the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

image.caption: A campaign banner for Benjamin Netanyahu is seen in Jerusalem. Few Israeli analysts are willing to write off the country's longest-serving prime minister in Tuesday's general election, despite the catastrophic impact of the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023. (CBC)

blocks.text: On the cusp of Israel's first election since Benjamin Netanyahu presided over the most devastating security failure in the country's history, the Israeli prime minister is still hawking himself as the security candidate of choice and counting on it to work.

And it might. There are few Israeli analysts willing to write off the country's longest-serving prime minister in Tuesday's vote, despite the catastrophic impact of the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed about 1,200 people and led to 251 being taken hostage.

In an election already short-handed in terms of pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs, opinion polls in the weeks ahead of the vote have consistently suggested neither side will win the 61 seats needed to form a majority in the Israeli Knesset.

"We are back to where we were Oct. 6 [2023] in terms of the fact that the nation is split almost in the middle, electorally speaking," Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) in Jerusalem, said in an interview with CBC News.
"This means that we might come out with indecisive results. We may also have a minority government, but [then] the question, if there is a minority government, how long will it last?"

Netanyahu greets supporters in Jerusalem. The deaths of more than 74,000 Palestinians in Israel’s war against Hamas — a figure from health officials in Gaza — have not been the subject of much debate in the mainstream of Israel's election campaign. (Nico Hameon/CBC)
It could also mean a lengthy period of coalition building, during which Netanyahu would serve as a caretaker prime minister.

"Israel has moved to the right ever since Oct. 7, and maybe that is part of the answer to why the current government in the polls hasn't collapsed completely," political scientist Reuven Hazan of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said in an interview earlier this month.

items: Israelis are leaving the country in record numbers. Could a looming election accelerate the trend?

blocks.text: Hazan doesn't believe that Netanyahu, 77, and his far-right coalition partners will ultimately regain power, but he also said that "they should be doing a heck of a lot worse in the polls than they are."

Well-documented allegations that Netanyahu was repeatedly warned by regional allies and members of his own intelligence services that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel but ignored them have filled newspaper columns and media broadcasts in Israel and abroad.
What Netanyahu knew before the Oct. 7 attacks

The repeated pleas to Netanyahu by families and friends of Israeli hostages held in Gaza to agree to a deal with Hamas for their early release rather than insisting on "total victory" first have left Israel with some of its deepest scars.

The deaths of more than 74,000 Palestinians in Israel’s war against Hamas — a figure from health officials in Gaza — have not been the subject of much debate in the mainstream of Israel's election campaign. But the country's increasing isolation on the world stage has.

Israeli lawyer and longtime peace campaigner Daniel Seidemann said it's as surprising to many Israelis as it is to outsiders that Netanyahu might stand a chance of returning to office given the allegations stacked up against him.
Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and longtime peace campaigner, estimates Netanyahu still has strong, core support of about 30 per cent of the population. (CBC)
"It's a function of a number of things," he said in an interview from his Jerusalem office. "Number one, Netanyahu's hard-core supporters have to be described as a cult."
"Absolutely nothing that can be discovered about Netanyahu will pierce the armour of their devotion to the cult leader. That is probably about 30 per cent of Israel."

Netanyahu is currently being tried on allegations of corruption, including fraud, bribery and breach of trust. And he's steadfastly refused to appoint a commission of inquiry into the failings of Oct. 7, despite public pressure.
Some question reliability of Oct. 7 warnings

The IDI's Hermann said Netanyahu supporters contend that any leader could have made similar mistakes. In polling done by the institute, she said, 43 to 46 per cent of Jewish Israelis questioned whether the warnings delivered to Netanyahu were reliable.
Hermann said 60 per cent of those surveyed about what the prime minister did or didn't know believe the allegations have surfaced close to the election as part of an agenda to topple him.
"He is honest," Monel Bercovich said at a campaign event in Jerusalem on Friday, when asked why she backs Netanyahu.
Monel Bercovich says she's backing Netanyahu in the election because he's 'honest' and has taken a tough stance on Iran. (CBC)
She also mentioned his tough stand on Iran amid speculation that Israel might launch another round of strikes against it.
"To go to Iran and to do all the wars and all the things with [U.S. President Donald] Trump."
Hermann agrees with Seidemann that Netanyahu — nicknamed Bibi by those both for and against him — enjoys an unusual relationship with core supporters.

"Some of Netanyahu's voters actually love him," she said. "I mean it is something that comes from their stomach or their heart if you wish. [It's] a phenomenon which we don't have on the centre and left."
Rival vows Oct. 7 review
There's very little of a "left" left in Israeli politics, and much of the anti-Netanyahu side — or "change bloc," as it's known — arrayed against him would be described as centre-right and right.

Netanyahu's strongest challenger in the general election is former Israel Defence Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, whose political party is called Yashar, which means "straight" or "honest" in Hebrew.

items: Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election

blocks.text: Hazan, of Hebrew University, said Eisenkot's military background will appeal to voters concerned about security, particularly in the face of what many Israelis view as an existential threat posed by Iran.

"In other words: the security of this country, keep us safe in our homes. That's what they're looking for. But essentially, his entire campaign has not been on security issues. It's been on social issues, that this country is hemorrhaging, that we need to unite."
Gadi Eisenkot, centre, leader of the Yashar party and a former Israeli military chief, visits the Western Wall in Jerusalem's Old City on Thursday. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
Eisenkot, 66, joined Netanyahu's unity government in the days immediately after Oct. 7, but resigned eight months later.
His youngest son, a master sergeant in the Israeli military, was killed in Gaza during the war, and, unlike Netanyahu, he has pledged to create an Oct. 7 commission of inquiry if elected.
Ultra-orthodox conscription issue
Eisenkot has also distinguished himself from Netanyahu by making compulsory conscription for Israel's sizable ultra-Orthodox community a campaign issue.

Military service is mandatory in Israel for Jewish men and women once they reach 18. Until recently, the ultra-Orthodox — or Haredi — community enjoyed an exemption dating back to the founding of the state in 1948.

Israel’s Supreme Court refused to extend the exemption two years ago, despite Netanyahu's efforts. He's relied on the support of ultra-Orthodox coalition partners to stay in power over the years, and their vote will be key next week.
How Haredi draft dodgers became a key Israeli election issue
But the exemption is a much harder sell for the rest of the country in the wake of Oct. 7.

"I think for the last few years, we saw how tough it is and how our security situation is not as secure as we thought," said 27-year-old Yonatan Lambert, who was sent to serve in Gaza and will not vote for Netanyahu.

items: Ultra-Orthodox Israelis rally against plans for military conscription

blocks.text: "If you decide that you want or don't wanna be part of the army — or part of the country — you shouldn't get anything from the country," Lambert said, a reference to subsidies paid by the Israeli government to yeshivas, where ultra-Orthodox men study full time.

"[The ultra-Orthodox] know that they will never have it so good as they do under Netanyahu," said lawyer and peace campaigner Seidemann, a view he shares of Netanyahu's other coalition partners: hardline Jewish nationalists underpinning Israel's settlement expansion in the Israeli-occupied territories.
Military exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox — or Haredi — community are a much harder sell for the rest of the country in the wake of Oct. 7. (CBC)
'Total devotion of the right-wing settler base'
Israeli settlements, including in the occupied West Bank, are considered illegal under international law.

Images of increased violence by Israeli settlers attacking Palestinians and their property as they seek to bring in their annual olive harvest have horrified onlookers and increased Israel’s isolation internationally.

"In the past, Netanyahu, with all of his bluster, was risk averse," Seidemann said. "He was attentive to international engagement in ways that he did not usually disclose, but he was capable of exhibiting restraint.

"That's not the Netanyahu that we have now. He is in a semi-messianic disgruntled mode. He is fighting for his political life, and he has decided that the way he can survive politically is by having the total devotion of the right-wing settler base."
A campaign poster for Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's national security minister, shows him superimposed over the images of shackled Palestinian prisoners on their knees. (CBC)
That base includes Itamar Ben-Gvir, a Jewish settler from Hebron convicted in the past of incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organization.
Appointed by Netanyahu as the country's national security minister, Ben-Gvir's campaign posters show him superimposed over the images of shackled Palestinian prisoners on their knees.

items: Netanyahu orders West Bank closure as Israeli soldiers, Palestinian gunmen killed in exchanges

blocks.text: Seidemann likens the increase in land appropriation and settler attacks in the West Bank over the past month to an "end-of-season fire sale" ahead of the election.
"There's a sense that ... let's do whatever we can now, because it's an opportunity that may not repeat itself," he said. Then again, depending on Tuesday's results, it might.

articles.title: Egg freezing is becoming significantly more popular in Canada
articles.summary: Over the last decade, egg freezing has become significantly more popular. According to data from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society (CFAS), there were 2,663 retrieval cycles for the purpose…

image.caption: An employee demonstrates the work process before freezing eggs in a fertility research lab at Cha Fertility Center in Bundang, South Korea, April 30, 2022. (Heo Ran/Reuters)

blocks.text: Health·New

Over the last decade, egg freezing has become significantly more popular. According to data from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society (CFAS), there were 2,663 retrieval cycles for the purpose of freezing, or banking, eggs reported in 2025. Compare that number to 2013, when there were only 217 such procedures logged.
Experts say plenty of reasons are behind the surge, including the high cost of living and career ambitions
U.S. congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 36, made headlines in August after she decided to publicly document her egg freezing journey online.
"My hope is that by sharing my experience, it can help others and perhaps normalize not keeping women’s bodies in the shadows," Ocasio-Cortez said on Instagram.
Her decision to freeze her eggs reflects a growing trend marked by women in their 20s and 30s pursuing one or more cycles of the procedure — a trend that doctors are seeing here in Canada, too.

"We can laud AOC for documenting her egg freezing journey because that was helpful," said Dr. Rhonda Zwingerman, the chief medical officer at Toronto-based clinic Twig Fertility, because transparency from well-known people can help those considering similar journeys.
U.S. congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez shared multiple videos on Instagram, documenting her experiences while freezing her eggs. (Instagram/@aoc)

Over the last decade, egg freezing has become significantly more popular. According to data from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society (CFAS), there were 2,663 retrieval cycles for the purpose of freezing, or banking, eggs reported in 2025. Compare that number to 2013, when there were only 217 logged. The number of banked eggs has also shot up. In 2013, some 775 eggs were stored. Last year, there were more than 22,000 reported frozen eggs.
There are plenty of reasons behind the surge, experts say, with their patients citing high costs of living, career ambitions or even a lack of a partner as motivations for preserving their fertility.

"There is definitely a rise in elective fertility preservation," CFAS president Dr. Mohamed Bedaiwy told CBC News. ("Elective" refers to procedures taking place for non-medical reasons, unlike those that take place ahead of cancer treatments that put fertility at risk, for example.)

Across Canada, people are opting to have children later — another reason behind egg freezing. In 1976, the average age of mothers at the time of birth was 26.7. By 2022, the average age at the time of delivery had climbed to 31.6, according to Statistics Canada.

But even as more people delay pregnancy, their fertile windows remain finite. A woman's fertility — marked by egg quality and quantity — declines steadily, with a noticeable shift typically occurring at 32 and a faster decline starting at age 35.
Canadians are having fewer kids than ever
By freezing eggs, patients keep their options open, Zwingerman told CBC News.

Despite the surging interest in egg freezing, doctors warn that they can't guarantee a successful pregnancy down the line, with odds depending on the number of eggs retrieved and the age of the patient at the time of retrieval.

items: Egg Freezing in an Age of Uncertainty

blocks.text: "If you're in your early 30s and you freeze 20 to 25 eggs, there's about a 75 per cent chance you'll have a baby," Zwingerman said.
"There are many ways to define success," she said. "To me, it's successful if you're able to retrieve somewhere around the number of eggs you anticipate a person should get based on their age."
Egg freezing isn't cheap
Some patients choose to undergo multiple cycles to increase their chances. Still, a single cycle is expensive — let alone two or three.
"That's one of the main barriers," Bedaiwy said. "Those who can afford it can do it, but those who cannot are deprived of that opportunity."
Costs vary from clinic to clinic, but doctors who spoke to CBC News said that one cycle of egg freezing typically costs around $8,000, with another $2,000 to $8,000 for medication.

items: Spain's soccer federation will fund egg freezing. Is this a win for female athletes?

blocks.text: Some clinics, like Zwingerman's, include a price breakdown on their sites.
"Depending on the dose of drugs someone needs, an entire cycle with treatment and all of the medication, along with a year of storage, could cost $11,000 to $16,000 ballpark," Zwingerman said.

Generally, public funding for fertility treatments, such as IVF, varies from province to province and doesn't cover elective egg freezing, but sometimes workplace benefits cover a cycle, or at least the medication required.

Around the world, patients typically have to foot the bill when underdoing elective egg freezing. But there are signs that that's changing, at least by some employers in certain industries, like big tech. Several sports bodies, such as Spain's soccer federation, Chelsea FC women's team and the WNBA, have introduced measures to cover fertility treatments, including egg freezing. Still, the move isn't without controversy.

items: Some employers pay for egg freezing. Is that about helping you build a family or something else?

blocks.text: Beyond costs, Zwingerman said other barriers exist, too, like geography or inflexible work environments.

"There are a lot of people who live exceedingly far from a clinic, so I would love to see financial support for those of us with labs in big cities to build outreach facilities further out," she said.
For those interested in or simply curious about egg freezing, Zwingerman says booking a consultation at a fertility clinic is a good first step to learn about the procedure and everything it entails.

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis found that only about 11 per cent of reported people who froze their eggs had gone back to thaw them. But Zwingerman said she believes that figure will climb in the coming years.
"The key is don't wait," Zwingerman said. "There are published research papers that show people regret not doing it more than doing it."
Why are more British Columbians freezing their eggs?
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Anya Zoledziowski is a Peabody-winning multimedia journalist from Edmonton who's covered social and climate justice, Indigenous affairs, gender, politics and more, and has been recognized by several national and international awards. She’s currently pursuing her PhD in journalism studies.

articles.title: Ontario municipal elections: A look at 7 mayoral races as voters head to the polls
articles.summary: Monday is municipal election day in Ontario, and people across the province will get a chance to pick their next local leaders. Most polling stations will be open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., and…

image.caption: Most polling stations will be open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. for Monday's Ontario municipal elections. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Monday is municipal election day in Ontario, and people across the province will get a chance to pick their next local leaders.
More than 11.8 million Ontarians are eligible to vote, according to the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).
Most polling stations will be open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., and residents can find information about where to cast their ballots on their municipality's website.
Across Ontario, about 6,663 candidates vying for 2,800 positions, including mayor, city councillor and school board trustee, the association says.
Here, CBC looks at the mayoral contests in seven cities: Toronto, Ottawa, Thunder Bay, Oshawa, Mississauga, Hamilton and Cambridge.
Toronto

While dozens of candidates are vying to be Toronto's next mayor, it has largely been a two-way race between incumbent Olivia Chow, who was elected in 2023, and her main challenger, two-term city councillor Brad Bradford.

items: Here’s how Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford plan to hire more cops

blocks.text: A Liaison Strategies poll last week said the pair were in a "statistical dead heat" heading into election day. Bradford was in the lead with 49 per cent support while Chow had 47 per cent among decided and leaning voters surveyed. The poll has a margin of error of +/-3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
The two top candidates had a final chance to make their case to voters in a debate on Thursday, outlining their plans on affordability and other issues.
You can follow all of CBC's coverage from Toronto here.
Chow vs. Bradford: Toronto’s final mayoral debate in 3 minutes
Ottawa
Ottawa's mayoral race is also a close one, with incumbent Mark Sutcliffe holding a single-digit lead over Jeff Leiper, a three-term city councillor.

items: How to watch CBC Ottawa's live election night special
Ottawa voters ask: What can cities do to bring down the cost of housing?

blocks.text: A Quorus Consulting Group survey released last week put Sutcliffe at 28 per cent support compared with 24 per cent for Leiper. The survey did not have a margin of error, but a comparable random sample poll of the same size would have a margin of error plus or minus 3.5 per cent, 19 times out of 20.
Other candidates trailed by a significant margin, with Neil Saravanamuttoo at seven per cent and Alex Lawson at four per cent, the survey showed.
For all our coverage from Ottawa, follow along here.
From taxes to transit, mayoral candidates faced off in CBC Ottawa debate
Thunder Bay
Ten mayoral candidates are on the ballot in Thunder Bay — but that doesn't include Mayor Ken Boshcoff, who is not seeking re-election.

items: Northwestern Ontario mayoral candidates share top priorities ahead of Election Day

blocks.text: The candidates vying to replace him are Trevor Giertuga, Maureen (Moe) Comuzzi, Volker Kromm, Peter Mark John Diedrich, Donald Baxter, Shane Judge, Aldo Ruberto, Peter Panetta, Wolfgang Schoor and Doug Vincent.
Whoever wins faces the city's $30.6 million annual infrastructure deficit .

An informal survey, launched by CBC Thunder Bay at the end of August, found that homelessness and public safety were the top issues for residents. Roads, infrastructure and traffic were also high on people's lists of priorities.
For all CBC's election night coverage from Thunder Bay, check out this page.
Thunder Bay, Ont., mayoral candidate rejects strong mayor powers
Oshawa
In Oshawa, nine candidates are competing to replace Mayor Dan Carter, who is not seeking re-election. That includes three sitting councillors: Tito-Dante Marimpietri, Jim Lee and Derek Giberson.

items: Oshawa’s voter turnout in 2022 was 18 per cent. Here’s your guide to voting this year

blocks.text: As in Thunder Bay, homelessness emerged as a major campaign issue in Oshawa, as regional data shows the city has the highest homeless population in the Durham Region.
It will be interesting to watch voter turnout, too. In 2022, just 18.4 per cent of eligible voters — about two in 10 people — cast a ballot.
For our election coverage from Oshawa, see our Durham page here.
Oshawa’s mayoral race is wide open. CBC’s Durham team gives you a primer
Mississauga
Mississauga residents will get to choose from more than a dozen mayoral candidates.
But it's shaping up to be a four-way race between incumbent Carolyn Parrish, former mayor Bonnie Crombie and city councillors Alvin Tedjo and Dipika Damerla.

items: New poll puts Crombie in lead for Mississauga mayor as early voter turnout increases

blocks.text: A poll published last week showed Crombie — mayor from 2014 to 2024 before leaving for a brief stint as leader of the Ontario Liberal Party — in the lead with 35 per cent support among decided and leaning voters.
Tedjo had 31 per cent followed by Parrish with 28 per cent and Damerla at four per cent. The margin of error was plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Mississauga set a new record for advance voter turnout, the city said earlier this month. More than 44,000 people cast their ballots between Oct. 6 and 11 — an increase of 57 per cent compared with advance voting in 2022.
You can follow along here for Mississauga election news throughout the day.
Leading candidates in Mississauga mayoral race face off in final debate
Hamilton
Hamilton also reported strong turnout in advance polls ahead of election day. It said on Oct. 21 that at least 34,996 ballots had already been cast, surpassing the 30,893 advance votes cast in 2022.

items: More Hamilton voters cast advance ballots this municipal election than in 2022

blocks.text: Incumbent Andrea Horwath is seeking re-election against 12 other candidates.

Those challengers include local community organizers, city councillor Rob Cooper and Keanin Loomis, a former president of the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce who lost the 2022 race to Horwath by about 1,600 votes.
Stay on top of all our election updates from Hamilton, here.
Get to know the 2026 Hamilton mayoral candidates
Cambridge
Six candidates, including incumbent Jan Liggett and Coun. Scott Hamilton, are in the race to be the next mayor of Cambridge, just outside of Kitchener.

items: Cambridge candidates share their top issues in this municipal election

blocks.text: For all our coverage from Cambridge and the wider Kitchener-Waterloo region, see here.
Cambridge mayoral candidates share their plans for transit and the LRT

articles.title: A ‘reset’ or ‘one and done’? First Nations and first ministers set to hold historic meeting
articles.summary: The Assembly of First Nations national chief says Monday's historic meeting between First Nations and first ministers is a chance to redefine the relationship between First Nations, premiers and the…

image.caption: Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak is shown at the organization's 2026 annual general assembly in Ottawa on July 16. She says at the very least, she wants a commitment for regular meetings with the prime minister and premiers. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics

The Assembly of First Nations national chief says Monday's historic meeting between First Nations and first ministers is a chance to redefine the relationship between First Nations, premiers and the prime minister, even though it will take place under a cloud of skepticism.
Even with key premiers absent and format restrictions, both sides look for progress

The Assembly of First Nations national chief says Monday's historic First Nations-First Ministers' Meeting is a chance to redefine the relationship between First Nations, premiers and the prime minister, even though it will take place under a cloud of skepticism.
Not all 13 premiers are attending the one-day political conference in Ottawa. Premiers from Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec are expected to be absent.
Some First Nations chiefs say they're concerned about how the Privy Council Office is organizing the closed-door meeting, which won't be livestreamed to their community members.
"I'm doubtful that it will meet our expectations," said Nishnawbe Aski Nation Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler.
"It seems to me that Canada is the one that's driving the agenda."

items: First Nations leaders praise high Alberta referendum turnout despite ballot box barriers

blocks.text: But with this being the first-ever first ministers' meeting dedicated to First Nations and their priorities since the high-level gatherings started 120 years ago, there is also hope tangible progress can be made even if the leaders attending have only a few hours together.

"A lot of our previous national chiefs and First Nations that have come before my time have always been disrespected and left out of these meetings,” Assembly of First Nations (AFN) National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak told CBC News.
"We have to reset our relationship."

Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, AFN national chief, left, looks on as Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at the organization's Special Chiefs Assembly in Ottawa on Dec. 2, 2025. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
The Prime Minister's Office says the goal of the meeting is to see outcomes and that the federal government will make an announcement on Monday for new community supports in First Nations.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, who was the first woman elected as grand chief of the Cree Nation Government in Quebec, said her role will be to encourage the participants to continue working together.
"This is the first step in, I think, a new relationship, path forward," Gull-Masty said.

items: Some Indigenous leaders call premiers' meeting positive but inclusion remains an issue
Carney government is stalling on Indian Act reform bill, advocates, lawmakers charge

blocks.text: "We're looking to build this relationship to advance things in Canada, and that means that everybody has to be included."
At the very least, chiefs gathering on Monday say they're looking for a commitment that the event will be the start of regular meetings between First Nations and first ministers.
"This is not a one-and-done meeting," AFN Ontario Regional Chief Abram Benedict said.
Stalled Indigenous bills raise questions about Carney’s priorities
Tensions over inclusion in major projects

The meeting is expected to cover a wide range of issues from more than 630 First Nations across Canada, including infrastructure and health-care needs. But much of the focus will likely be on economic development and major projects.

Benedict said he wants to make sure first ministers understand that First Nations have to be involved in decisions about projects from the outset, not after work has already started — something that he said still happens too often despite commitments from governments.

items: First Nations chiefs vote to oppose Carney government's proposed major projects reforms

blocks.text: "There are two different pathways through the large project development: It's either with First Nations or without First Nations," he said.

"One will seed a successful collaboration that brings benefit not only to our nations but to the province and to the nation in which we live in. And the other one will be met with resistance and court challenges."
AFN Ontario Regional Chief Abram Benedict wants to address concerns over project development with the prime minister and premiers at Monday's meeting. (Pierre-Paul Couture/CBC)

Fiddler, who represents 49 First Nations in northern Ontario, said he wants to find a resolution for chiefs shut out of discussions on the Ring of Fire — a 5,000-square-kilometre area in Ontario's James Bay lowlands that the province and Ottawa want to see mined for critical minerals.
But he's not sure any of those concerns can be conveyed given the way the meeting is structured.
Backlash over access casts shadow
As of Friday, First Nations chiefs told CBC News that each AFN region would be given three minutes to deliver opening remarks on Monday.
With more than 130 First Nations in Ontario alone, Fiddler said he doesn't think the format is conducive to a constructive discussion.
Fiddler is flying from Thunder Bay, Ont., to attend the meeting, but as of Friday he didn't know if he would be able to participate in the main meeting room or even be allowed to speak.
"I find it very disrespectful," he said. "Their approach is unacceptable."

Nishnawbe Aski Nation Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler, who represents 49 First Nations in northern Ontario, says he's concerned too many restrictions at the meeting will prevent progress. (Ivanoh Demers/Radio-Canada)

The AFN said there will be an observation room for chiefs who aren't in the main meeting room. Fiddler said he was told they would have to surrender their cellphones to ensure no one records the meeting.
First ministers' meetings are traditionally held behind closed doors, but Woodhouse Nepinak said she would prefer to see this one fully televised.
"It's so important to Canadians. It's so important to First Nations," she said. "The more transparent and open we are with each other, the better."

items: Chiefs, Opposition call for Alberta government to drop appeal of decision that quashed separation petition

blocks.text: Gull-Masty said the meeting was planned by the Privy Council Office with the AFN. She describes it as a first conversation between first ministers and First Nations.
"I'm actually looking forward and very excited to see how this conversation is going to unfold," she said.
"It's going to be a defining opportunity for everybody who comes to that table."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Olivia Stefanovich is a senior reporter in the CBC's Parliamentary Bureau based in Ottawa. Connect with her on Instagram and X @CBCOlivia. Confidential story tips always welcome: olivia.stefanovich@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Brazil heads to polls in runoff between leftist Lula and Bolsonaro Jr.
articles.summary: Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days

blocks.text: ELECTION CAMPAIGN. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate seeking re-election, waves a flag during a closing campaign rally ahead of the presidential runoff, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 24, 2026.
Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS
Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days

items: Brazilians are voting in a runoff election on October 25, 2026, between leftist President Lula and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro's first-round victory surprised many.
Polls indicate a tight race, with Bolsonaro leading slightly, but historical trends suggest that candidates who come second in the first round rarely win the presidency.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

SAO PAULO, Brazil – Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday, October 25, in a tight runoff vote that could shift Latin America’s largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.

The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round.

A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.

The election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety, and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro’s 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if he is elected.

Trump has called the case a “witch hunt” and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While many of those were later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices.
Lula has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying.

On economic issues, despite falling inequality, and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds.

Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has also promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses.
Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days.
Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote.
Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%.
The senator’s first-round win sent Brazil’s markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms.

His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In Bulgaria, record low voter turnout triggers a November 1 presidential run-off in a poll colored by divisions over Ukraine war
articles.summary: Low voter turnout has triggered a run-off for the Bulgarian presidency. The vote was colored by strong divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine, and Sofia's relations with the Kremlin.

image.caption: Despite a few plus ones, voter turnout was historically low in Bulgaria's presidential electionImage: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Record low turnout in Sunday's Bulgarian elections mean voters are expected to head to the polls on November 1 to cast ballots in a presidential run-off.
Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 8 p.m. (0500-1800 GMT), with official results expected within 48 hours, but voter turnout was less than 40%, far short of the 50% required.

Voters were choosing between candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and relations with Moscow and the vote came as drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast brought home the significance of the conflict in Ukraine for the former Soviet satellite state.

Although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the head of state in Bulgaria can appoint interim governments during political crises, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and is able to veto legislation.

blocks.caption: Bulgarians are deciding on who should officially reside here in SofiaImage: Dzhanan Mehmed Ismail/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Who are the main candidates in Bulgaria's presidential election?

Frontrunner in the elections is incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who took over the position this year after current Prime Minister Rumen Radev stepped down to take part in the parliamentary elections that led him to power.
Yotova, 62, who surveys show as having 41-47% of the vote, favors dialogue with Moscow as the way to bring peace to Ukraine and opposes military aid to Kyiv.
A win for Yotova would give a boost for Radev, who also advocates dialogue with Moscow. Victory would make Yotova Bulgaria’s first elected female president.
Her main challenger is Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, who is polling at 28-31%.

Gyurov, 50, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition, is an outspoken critic of Radev's foreign policy and strongly supports the Euro-Atlantic ties of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state. As caretaker prime minister, Gyurov signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv.
The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%.

blocks.caption: Yotova (R) appointed Gyurov (L) as caretaker premier, a post he held from February to March 2026Image: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Altogether 27 pairs of candidates for president and vice president are competing in the first round, with nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin.
Top rivals vote, turnout low

After casting her ballot in Sofia, Yotova called for peace, stability and unity, urging an end to divisions among Bulgarians. Her main challenger, Gyurov, voted in Blagoevgrad, calling for a Bulgaria that looks ahead and offers families greater economic security.
Turnout was estimated at 15.1% by 3 p.m. local time (1300 GMT), according to polling agency Myara, Bulgarian media reported.
To win outright, a candidate must secure more than half the valid votes, with more than half of eligible voters taking part. Otherwise, the top two candidates advance to a runoff on November 1.
What are the main issues in Bulgaria's presidential election?

The war in Ukraine triggered by Russia's unprovoked invasion is one of the central themes in the election, particularly after four merchant ships were allegedly hit by drones off Bulgaria's coast this month in suspected spillover from the conflict. The attacks have prompted Bulgaria to seek assistance from its allies to strengthen maritime security.
Satellite internet antennas from the Starlink network — an important part of Ukraine's defense capabilities — were also set on fire near the capital, Sofia.
While Radev has said that the attacks seemed to be to the advantage of Russia and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government has declined to blame the incidents directly on Moscow.
The strikes have nonetheless raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict.
Rising energy prices and inflation that have caused economic hardship to many in Bulgaria, the EU's poorest member state, are also a main issue addressed by candidates.
Many voters are also looking to stop government corruption, a persistent concern in the country, and hope for a stable government after multiple elections and coalition breakdowns in recent years.

articles.title: What schools will do amid intense heat during El Niño
articles.summary: How prepared is the Department of Education for the potential effects of El Niño?

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The education sector will not be spared when El Niño worsens in the coming months. Across the country, temperatures are expected to be warmer than usual, which would pose another threat to students’ learning.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara previously said government protocols would ensure that El Niño’s effects are mitigated in public schools.
How exactly is the Department of Education (DepEd) preparing for the impact of the weather phenomenon? Pending formal guidelines, here’s what we know so far:

In an interview with Rappler on Friday, October 23, Education Undersecretary Malcolm Garma said the DepEd is concerned that lost school days may increase due to high heat index levels. The heat index, or the temperature that the human body perceives, is measured using the air temperature and the relative humidity in a place at a given time.
Garma noted that the DepEd’s existing class suspension guidelines, issued back in June, already spell out learning continuity plans for schools.

The DepEd said that under Level 1-Hayo, face-to-face classes continue during manageable conditions. Schools can set scheduled water breaks, shift outdoor activities to early morning or shaded areas, and allow students to wear comfortable clothing or Physical Education attire.
At Level 2-Hinay, schools may adopt modified class days with structured home-based or hybrid learning.

Level 3-Hinga may be implemented when temperatures can cause heat cramps or heat exhaustion or there is loss of water supply. Learning packets, short activities, and broadcast resources may be used to reduce academic demands.

Once the heat index reaches 42°C and above, academic activities are suspended at Level 4-Hinto, focusing on safety checks and psychosocial support referrals, according to the class suspension guidelines.
Garma said self-learning modules, activity sheets, and other materials needed for alternative learning will be prepositioned before the peak months of intense heat.

In case actual conditions turn out to be worse than projected, Garma said school heads can adjust class schedules or recommend granular suspensions of face-to-face classes. But he added that the situation must be properly assessed.

“Hindi naman ‘yung school head ay basta-basta na lang siyang magpapauwi o magsu-suspend. So kailangan mai-vet ito ng [schools] division office…or [they should] even coordinate with the local government unit. Para sa gano’n, talagang hindi naman maabuso din ‘yung pagsususpende ng klase,” the DepEd official said.

(The school head cannot just decide to send students home or suspend classes. This must be vetted by the schools division office or they should even coordinate with the local government unit. This is to prevent abuse of class suspensions.)

“While we are looking after…the welfare of our learners, we also have to ensure that learning continues. At alam naman natin na pinakamainam pa din na learning delivery natin ay kung school-based ito or face-to-face (And we know that the best learning delivery is school-based or face-to-face),” he added.
Garma said the DepEd has ordered schools to make hydration facilities and equipment, such as safe drinking stations and water dispensers, accessible to learners and personnel.
The DepEd also told schools to repair water leaks immediately and coordinate closely with local water concessionaires for rationing contingencies.

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian earlier raised the possibility of deploying community water depots to public schools. These depots are rainwater catchment equipment with built-in filtration systems to provide potable water during shortages. Garma said the DepEd welcomes such proposals.

Regarding health, Garma said school clinics will be ready to address medical concerns like heat stroke or dehydration. Additional support from local government units (LGUs) and the Department of Health will also be tapped for emergency response.

With El Niño also threatening agriculture and food supply, schools division offices and schools were directed to develop contingency menus for the school-based feeding program, partner with LGUs and cooperatives for local food sourcing, and maintain buffer stocks of shelf-stable commodities.
Garma said public schools can use their funding for maintenance and other operating expenses to buy additional ventilators like electric fans.
But the DepEd’s long-term solution is structural intervention.

“For old classrooms, we cannot change their designs; we can only do mitigation. But for those classrooms under construction and for future ones, we’ll make sure that there will be structural intervention such as high ceilings, insulated ceilings, and wide airflow,” he said in Filipino.
Garma also said the DepEd is exploring the possibility of institutionalizing the use of solar power in schools to reduce electricity costs and possibly provide air-conditioning.

The DepEd said its upcoming formal guidelines for El Niño-related measures will mandate schools to conduct integrated school-level risk assessments covering water supply reliability, classroom thermal safety, electricity resilience, and fire hazard prevention.

The set of guidelines is also expected to prohibit schools from charging or requiring parents to buy cooling equipment, connectivity, or specialized attire as a condition for alternative learning modalities. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Win Gatchalian: Marcoleta, Estrada suspensions on hold pending motions
articles.summary: The suspension of Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada will be held in abeyance pending the final resolution of their motions for reconsideration, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said…

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 2:56pm

The suspension of Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada will be held in abeyance pending the final resolution of their motions for reconsideration, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.
Gatchalian made the statement after confirming that the Senate had received the suspension orders from the Sandiganbayan.

“Nakakuha rin ako ng sulat galing kay Sen. Jinggoy at Sen. Marcoleta na i-hold muna in abeyance ang suspension dahil ang balita namin... magpa-file sila ng motion for reconsideration,” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.

(We also received letters from Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta asking that their suspensions be held in abeyance because we received reports that they would file motions for reconsideration.)
“Kapag nag-file ng motion for reconsideration, hindi muna sinususpinde until maging final na ang kanilang motion for reconsideration,” he added.
(If a motion for reconsideration is filed, the suspension will be deferred until the motion is finally resolved.)

Earlier this month, the Sandiganbayan’s Fifth Division ordered Estrada placed under preventive suspension for 90 days in connection with the plunder and graft charges he faces over his alleged involvement in the flood control projects scandal.
It was the second 90-day preventive suspension imposed on Estrada after the anti-graft court’s Second Division issued a similar order in June in connection with separate graft charges.

Meanwhile, the Sandiganbayan’s Third Division ordered Marcoleta placed under preventive suspension also for 90 days in connection with a plunder charge over alleged undeclared campaign contributions worth P75 million.
Gatchalian said Marcoleta and Estrada, along with Senator Loren Legarda, were not receiving their salaries because of their absences from office.

Earlier, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said criminal charges against Legarda and Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste were expected to be filed soon over an alleged failure by Leviste’s solar company to deliver contracted power supply.
Remulla, however, declined to give a timeline for the filing of the cases.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Win Gatchalian, Ping Lacson to authorities: Conduct safe arrest of Bato dela Rosa
articles.summary: Authorities should conduct a safe arrest of Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, who is now considered "armed and dangerous" by law enforcement officials.

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 2:30pm
Authorities should conduct a safe arrest of Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, who is now considered "armed and dangerous" by law enforcement officials.
Senator Sherwin Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB that the safety of Dela Rosa and the authorities tasked with arresting him are equally important.
"Sa enforcement agencies, dapat maging ligtas 'yung pag-aresto kay Sen. Bato," Gatchalian said Sunday. "Hindi pwedeng maging bayolente o may karahasan na mangyari."
(Enforcement agencies must conduct a safe arrest of Sen. Bato. No violence or cruelty should occur.)
"Importante ligtas siya at ligtas din ang law enforcement agencies... Importante na magkaroon ng maayos na pag-aresto sa kanya," he added.
(It's important that he and our law enforcement agencies are safe. It is important to have an orderly arrest.)
'Due process'
In a statement on Sunday, Senator Panfilo Lacson shared the same sentiment, saying that Dela Rosa's arrest should be carried out peacefully and without tragedy.

"He (dela Rosa) has his faults, as we all do. But whatever accusations he faces, he is entitled to due process, a fundamental right guaranteed to every Filipino, and for that matter, to every human being," Lacson said
The Department of the Interior and Local Government has raised a P50-million reward for the arrest of dela Rosa, Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic" Remulla announced Friday.
Remulla's announcement came after he said Dela Rosa is under the protection of a group in Mindanao, with whom the government is initiating negotiations. He did not identify the said group.
He said an operation to get the former Philippine National Police chief could result in 10,000 deaths.
For Gatchalian, the government should assert its authority as he described the group to be more bolder than the former.
"Parang ang lumalabas, itong armed group ay mas matapang pa sa gobyerno," Gatchalian said.
(It seems like the armed group is more bold than the government.)
"Ang gobyerno, hindi dapat nakikipag-negotiate sa armed group lalo kung ang armed group ay terrorist group," he added.
(It's not right that the government is the one negotiating with the armed group, especially if that armed group is a terrorist group.)

Dela Rosa is charged before the International Criminal Court as a co-perpetrator with former president Rodrigo Duterte for cases of murder and attempted murder tied to the war on drugs of the latter's administration.
Both Duterte and Dela Rosa have denied the allegations against them.
Dela Rosa left the Senate before dawn on May 14, hours after a shooting incident in the chamber's premises.
Gatchalian said he has yet to communicate with Dela Rosa after his last appearance in May. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Malversation, graft charges filed vs 2 ex-DPWH execs over GenSan right-of-way scam
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman files charges against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano Suan Jr., and several other DPWH personnel and…

blocks.text: The Office of the Ombudsman in Quezon City on March 6, 2026.
Jire Carreon/Rappler

The Office of the Ombudsman files charges against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano Suan Jr., and several other DPWH personnel and private individuals

items: The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft cases against two former DPWH officials, four personnel, and seven private individuals related to a road right-of-way scam in General Santos City.
Evidence was found against former DPWH officials and personnel for falsifying documents and inflating claims for land compensation, resulting in over P491 million in fraudulent payments.
The Ombudsman also ordered the dismissal of former DPWH Region 12 legal officer Ansare Mariga Busran in a separate administrative decision.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft cases against two former Department of Public Works and Highways officials, four DPWH personnel, and seven private individuals over their alleged involvement in a road right-of-way scam in General Santos City.

The Office of the Ombudsman said in a press statement on Sunday, October 25, that it “found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction” against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano B. Suan Jr., and DPWH personnel Tomas Marquez Rodriguez, David Lucena Padlan, Paisal Amerol Padate, and Ansare Mariga Busran.

The Ombudsman also included seven private individuals in the cases filed before the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan: Wilma Mamburam, Nelson Ti, Evelyn Paloso, Rudy Hadji Ong, Marisa Seguirre, William Uy, Paul Michael Bagio.

“The Ombudsman filed 18 informations for Malversation of Public Funds or Property through Falsification of Public Documents under Article 217 in relation to Article 171 of the Revised Penal Code, and another 18 informations for violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act,” the Office of the Ombudsman said.

In 2018 and 2019, the National Bureau of Investigation submitted three investigation reports to the Ombudsman in relation to the DPWH Region 12 payment for right-of-way for 18 parcels of land allegedly affected by the construction of the Digos-Makar National Road in Lagao, General Santos City.

The witness, Roberto Catapang Jr., had admitted in his 2017 affidavit that he was involved in a syndicate that was allegedly “in collusion with respondent public officers, collected money from the government purportedly as payments for the acquisitions, by fabricating and submitting fake documents.”

Investigators found that the claimants, which were paid a total of P491,931,120.20, had presented falsified documents. The DPWH Region XII technical working group had approved the disbursement of the amount to the claimants.

“Investigators also uncovered the alleged unlawful use of a 2009 appraisal value of P3,500 per square meter to determine compensation for properties taken by the government in the early 1990s, resulting in inflated right-of-way claims,” the Office of the Ombudsman said.
The press statement also said that in a separate administrative decision, the Ombudsman ordered the dismissal from service of former DPWH Region 12 legal officer Ansare Mariga Busran. – Rappler.com
