articles.title: Nigeria: Tinubu launches reelection bid amid economic woes
articles.summary: President Bola Tinubu promised "a better tomorrow" for Nigerians while kicking off his next electoral campaign, while also blaming his rivals for poverty plaguing Africa's most populous nation.

image.caption: Tinubu said his administration is confronting Nigeria's economic crisisImage: Marvellous Durowaiye/REUTERS

blocks.text: Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu on Saturday formally launched his campaign for a second term.
"We have prosperity, consistency, growth, recovery and opportunity," Tinubu said at a rally in the northwestern state of Kaduna.
"You grant me the privilege to promise you once again, there is that promise of a better tomorrow," he added.
Africa's most populous country will hold its next presidential election in January 2027. The campaign is expected to focus on Nigeria's economy and security challenges.
Tinubu's tax gamble: Progress or pain for Nigerians?
Nigeria's worsening cost of living
After taking power in 2023, Tinubu sparked anger by scrapping decades-long fuel subsidies — a move that has fueled Nigeria's inflation.
On Saturday, the incumbent president dismissed criticisms about his economic policies.
"I hear my opponents talking about hunger and poverty. Who created it? They did," Tinubu said at the crowded rally. "They created the hunger, they created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it."

Earlier this month, the 74-year-old acknowledged Nigeria's economic issues. In his Independence Day address, he argued that his administration's reform "did not create the weaknesses in our economy," but actually "confronted them."
Tinubu's government announced potential price caps on fuel soon after.
Security threats to play big role in Nigeria's election
Apart from grappling with a cost-of-living crisis, Nigeria continues to struggle with armed bandits and kidnappers.
On Friday, gunmen killed at least 20 people in an attack on a village in the country's northeast.
The nation has also been fighting a long-running jihadist insurgency, sparked by Boko Haram's 2009 uprising.

blocks.caption: Thousands of supporters showed up in Kaduna for Tinubu's first election campaign of the seasonImage: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another three-man race
Tinubu's main challengers are expected to be former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and former state governor Peter Obi.
In the 2023 presidential election,Tinubu only managed to secure less than 36.6% of the valid votes cast, with Abubakar at 29% and Obi at 25.4%.
Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?

articles.title: Four people injured after drive-by shooting outside boxing event south of Brisbane
articles.summary:
Offenders still at large after shots fired from vehicle outside licensed premises in Loganholme

  • Get our breaking…

blocks.text: Four people have been injured after a drive-by shooting outside a venue hosting a boxing event.
Police said they responded to reports of shots being fired from a vehicle outside a licensed premises in Loganholme, south of Brisbane, at 8.15pm.
“The involved vehicle was witnessed leaving the scene,” police said.
Fitzys Loganholme on Bryants Road was scheduled to host the Logan City Titles Fight Night on Saturday.
Four injured people were taken to hospital, police said, and their condition was being assessed.
The offenders are still at large but police said they did not believe there was an ongoing threat to the public.
Police were urging anyone with information about the incident to contact them.

articles.title: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
articles.summary:
Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November

Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.
The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU.

Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.
In an interview with the Sunday Times he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”
The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.
The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.
“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times.
“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.
“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.
He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.
The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.
In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics.
Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.

Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.
It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.
Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.
But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.
Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.
The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”

Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.
“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

articles.title: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
articles.summary: The ultra-Orthodox community is resisting being drafted into the Israeli army. But will they now bring down the Netanyahu government?

blocks.text: BySebastian Usher

blocks.caption: Sebastian Usher

blocks.text: Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police.

The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service.
The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed.

This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050.

As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service.
Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ultra-Orthodox Jews have staged many protests against being drafted into the military

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Ultra-Orthodox Jews have staged many protests against being drafted into the military

National security and the economy are two of the key issues this election. That means the division between the ultra-Orthodox and the majority of Israelis who believe they are not contributing their fair share to either is starker than ever.

With no outright majority likely for any current political alliance, and the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in doubt, the role of smaller parties - including Haredi parties - will once again be crucial in deciding who will govern Israel.
To have any chance of staying in power, Netanyahu needs to keep the ultra-Orthodox parties on side, however much pressure there is within Israel for their special status to be diminished.
A group apart

From the ultra-Orthodox perspective, their social contract with the Israeli state is increasingly coming under pressure. Their all but exclusive focus on the study of Judaism's religious texts - such as the Torah, the Jewish Bible - means their education system is separate and many Haredim are not part of Israel's workforce.

For the ultra-Orthodox, the biggest issue of all is holding on to the exemption from serving in the IDF for students at traditional religious - or yeshiva - institutions. This dates back to the earliest days of the Israeli state when the Haredim were a miniscule community of survivors struggling to rebuild from the near extinction of the Holocaust.

But as Israel has become more embattled after the attacks of October 7, fighting wars on several fronts, their near complete absence from the country's conscription army has become more controversial.

Religious students and their rabbis believe that if young ultra-Orthodox men enter the military, they will be exposed to influences and behaviours that may decisively turn them away from their community. Beyond that, they believe that their staying true to the traditions of their community is vital for the very survival not only of Israel but the Jewish people.

When asked not long after October 7 why the ultra-Orthodox didn't contribute more to the military in such an emergency, one of the community's most senior leaders, Rabbi Dov Landau, said that not only should religious students not serve in the army, but they shouldn't even visit the wounded or attend the funerals of soldiers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Haredi birth rate is higher than in the rest of Israeli society

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The Haredi birth rate is higher than in the rest of Israeli society

The rabbi said that in a time of such danger, only Torah students could protect Israel spiritually. "Salvation only comes through Torah learning, orderly Torah learning. And any neglect of or disruption to Torah learning, woe and alas for what will happen… The more Torah learners multiply, the more Torah learners increase their learning, the better. They protect us."

It would be a considerable understatement to say that this view is not shared by wider Israeli society. Polls have shown public support for conscripting the ultra-Orthodox surge throughout the war in Gaza. Many see it as a dereliction of responsibility by the Haredi community, made all the more galling by the fact that such a stance comes at the expense of taxpayers. The IDF has bemoaned a deficit in manpower, while many Israelis have had to serve hundreds of days in the past three years.

Dahlia Scheindlin is a leading political consultant and pollster in Israel. She says this issue is critical for Netanyahu and is key to understanding this moment in Israeli society against the backdrop of the war in Gaza, particularly among the political right. "Really the most burning, more immediate issue is the right-wing communities who are furious at the government for protecting the blanket exemption from the IDF at a time when, especially among the right, but really everybody in the Jewish community in Israel, is serving and many dying in these wars."

Two years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that the exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from serving in the military was effectively null and void. That could have meant that those dedicated to full-time religious study would now be drafted.

The reaction from the Haredi community was one of fury. Hundreds of thousands of Haredim held protests, blocking the main highways. And as with the incident in Modi'in, they tried to prevent the arrest of religious students for evading conscription. Protests have continued off and on, and densely-populated Haredi areas are often the backdrops for confrontation with the security forces.
Consequences at the polls
This is a row that is playing out in the election.

There are two parties that have traditionally represented the Haredi community. One is United Torah Judaism – or UTJ – and represents Ashkenazi Jews, or Jews of European origin. The other is Shas, which was formed later and represents the Sephardi and Mizrahi – Jews from North Africa and the Middle East. They share a core agenda, which puts religious study above all else, including any questions around relations with the Palestinians.

Both UTJ and Shas have been part of Netanyahu's coalition - and they used their political clout to find ways to try to block enforcement of the Supreme Court ruling. On several occasions, they threatened to pull out of the alliance and bring the government down. UTJ acted on this but continued to support the government from outside, while Shas remained within the coalition.

Centre-right politician Gadi Eisenkot, who's shaped up as Netanyahu's main rival in this month's election, does not support their stance. He has made clear his belief that the idea of the ultra-Orthodox constituting a separate state within Israel with its own rules has become increasingly toxic. "A country that sends its best sons and daughters to fight and sacrifice their lives cannot tolerate a reality in which a state within a state exists," he said.
All this has meant that the issue of conscription exemption for ultra-Orthodox men is the number one priority on the electoral agenda of both Shas and UTJ.

A recent remark by a UTJ parliamentary candidate, Eliakim Stark, has raised the temperature further. He compared the plight of ultra-Orthodox men evading the military draft to the persecution of Jews during the Holocaust. It triggered furious rebukes from opposition leaders from across the political spectrum.
Daniel Goldman, an activist who specialises in Haredi issues, says that the two main Haredi parties feel increasingly embattled and less open to compromise.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters have blocked key highways

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Protesters have blocked key highways

He says the ultra-Orthodox don't believe that the state really needs their boys to bolster numbers. "It's at least partly down to the fact that the Haredi parties see the state as wanting to take their boys out of the community and change them from ultra-Orthodox to either regular religious or secular, God forbid, as they perceive it," he says. "And so in that environment of tension, they've actually hardened their positions."

Yitzhak Goldknopf from the UTJ, a former minister, has gone so far as to issue an ultimatum: "The Haredim will not change their way of life because there is an army and a war... If there is no choice and they must leave the country, they will leave."

But this is having a clear impact on the electoral fortunes of the Netanyahu coalition - of which Shas in particular has long been a key part. Without them, Netanyahu's alliance would fall short of the more than 60 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.

Dahlia Scheindlin, the Israeli pollster, says that the refusal to give up the draft exemption by Shas and UTJ is damaging Netanyahu's coalition. "It is one of the main reasons why the coalition is unable to win back the kind of support that they had in 2022 when they won 64 seats," she says. "They're currently polling at about 50 to 52 seats."

All Netanyahu's challengers advocate for ending the ultra-Orthodox exemption and cutting funds to institutions or individuals who refuse the draft. On the left, Yair Golan has called for an immediate mobilisation of those who are eligible.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Benjamin Netanyahu is relying on Haredi support which may not materialise

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu is relying on Haredi support which may not materialise
So, despite statements from Shas and UTJ that they would switch allegiance from Netanyahu if he were to dilute his support, there seems for now nowhere else for them to go.

Anshel Pfeffer has been a leading commentator on the Israeli political scene for years - now mainly as the Economist's correspondent in Israel. He says Netanyahu's position looks shaky. "There are two things that are bringing together the current opposition bloc," he says. "One is obviously they want to replace Netanyahu and the other is they are capitalising on this really hostile environment nowadays towards the ultra-Orthodox, mainly over the issue of the draft to the army.
"Netanyahu has been willing for many years, to basically give the ultra-Orthodox whatever they want. They're not going to get that from the opposition."
A potential compromise?
Into this arena of resentment and intransigence, a new Haredi party has emerged this year, presenting itself as a break with the traditional mindset of Shas and UTJ.
Essentially, the Haredi Public Party is offering a compromise in which the ultra-Orthodox would contribute more to Israel as a whole while maintaining the core of their identity.
For the first time in the ultra-Orthodox community, it is also fielding two female candidates.

One of them, Ziva Ginz, explained to the BBC her party's position on the military draft. Key to it is men serving being allowed to remain culturally Haredi. "Anyone whose life is genuinely devoted to full-time Torah study should be able to continue learning. Everyone who isn't sitting and studying for a full day should serve alongside the rest of Israeli youth, in frameworks where a young man can enter as a Haredi and finish as a Haredi," she says.
But it may be too soon for such efforts at compromise to make an impact this election.
Anshel Pfeffer says that it's difficult to sway the base vote in the ultra-Orthodox community, where most still essentially follow what their rabbi says they should do.

"And once people are voting for other parties, they won't necessarily do so for another Haredi party," Pfeffer explains. "That's why we're seeing people like [far-right leader and National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir making inroads in the Haredi community, because he's the only non-Haredi party leader who actually talks to young Haredi. Basically, every other party in Israel doesn't even try."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ben-Gvir is making inroads with Haredi voters

blocks.text: Ben-Gvir is making inroads with Haredi voters
This is reflected in the polls, which show his Jewish Power party is making gains.

If Ben Gvir's actions are increasingly seen as tainting Israel's international image with his support for policies such as annexing the occupied West Bank, his hard-right message is attracting a bigger core of support within the country. His ultra-nationalist ethos is not one that traditionally overlaps with policies of the Haredi parties, but they share a position on the right of Israeli politics.

So for some ultra-Orthodox voters looking for a new political home, Ben Gvir represents the nearest alternative. His self-portrayal as a strong man unafraid to take an extreme position against those he perceives as Israel's enemies in the face of international condemnation may attract some already leaning to the far right in the Haredi community.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gadi Eisenkot has been firm in his support for Haredi Jews serving in the military

blocks.text: Gadi Eisenkot has been firm in his support for Haredi Jews serving in the military
No alliance appears close to achieving a majority, however, so there is bound to be a lot of horse trading to secure a workable coalition after the vote.
Netanyahu will naturally apply his exceptional political skills to trying to find one way or another to stay in power.

As ever, that leaves the smaller parties with the ability to play the role of kingmaker. That's a role that the ultra-Orthodox parties have been known for in the past. But this time they may not be the decisive factor.

"The truth is, any small party can become a kingmaker," Dahlia Scheindlin says. "I don't think it would take too much to lure the Haredi parties away from Netanyahu... The thing is, though, I don't think the opposition parties will want to lure them in unless they have some promise that they're really prepared to make serious concessions on the draft. The opposition parties are absolutely staking their platforms and their promise to the voters on that issue."
This time, rather than being the kingmakers, it may turn out that the ultra-Orthodox parties help bring down the king.

articles.title: Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'
articles.summary: The meticulously-planned visit takes in three countries in nine days - but is not without jeopardy.

blocks.text: Image source, Aaron Chown - WPA Pool/Getty Images
ByDaniela Relph
Senior royal correspondent
Royal tours are unpredictable beasts.
The planning is meticulous and dates back months, sometimes years, but there is always jeopardy.

King Charles III's visit to the Caribbean, which starts on Tuesday, takes him to three countries in nine days: the Bahamas, Guyana and finally Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm).

It also throws him directly into the heat of the debate over the payment of reparations - compensation from countries that took part in the slave trade - alongside questions of whether the King should be apologising for the UK's role in what he has previously described as an "appalling atrocity" that leaves an "indelible stain" on history.

"This is the biggest risk of his reign so far with so much just outside of his control," said author and historian Sir Anthony Seldon. "Questions about slavery, reparations and apologies mean the moral integrity of the monarchy is being questioned."

blocks.caption: Map of the Caribbean and northern South America showing a three-stop itinerary: The Bahamas (27-28 October), Guyana (29-30 October), and Antigua and Barbuda (31 October-3 November). Red numbered markers indicate each stop

blocks.text: The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade.
A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government.
The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.
Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.
But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.
This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.
Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.
Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022.

Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.
Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge shook hands with children through a wire fence during a visit to Trench Town on their 2022 tour

blocks.text: Image source, Chris Jackson-Pool/Getty Images
The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge shook hands with children through a wire fence during a visit to Trench Town on their 2022 tour

blocks.caption: Image caption, A woman holds a sign in protest as she waits for the arrival of William and Catherine on their tour

blocks.text: Image source, Toby Melville - Pool / Getty Images
A woman holds a sign in protest as she waits for the arrival of William and Catherine on their tour

The leadership in the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda will celebrate the King and his work in protecting rainforests, creating cultural ties and reinforcing relationships around trade, energy, and agriculture.
But they do so against a backdrop of change.
The leaders of all three countries have voiced their support for reparatory justice.
In Antigua and Barbuda and the Bahamas, where the King is head of state, the conversation about becoming a republic has significant support.
Elected officials in the former no longer have to pledge allegiance to the King ending a 40-year tradition of swearing loyalty to the monarch.

"He pulled off an extraordinary triumph with President Trump in his US visit earlier this year and stood up to him and put him in his place in a way that no leader has done - while not incurring his wrath," said Sir Anthony. "If he can deal with the delicate nature of this trip for him personally, for the British monarchy, and the future of the Commonwealth, it could be an enormous success."
The Sussexes surprise return
Timing also matters for royal tours.
This Caribbean tour has to cut through a sea of royal distractions.
The King has spent much of the past three months in Scotland, where he is based over the summer.
It should have been a quieter time in the royal calendar, but it has been quite the opposite.
The surprise return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to the UK has been noisy. The level of coverage Harry and Meghan get is unsettling and, at times, irritating for the Royal Family.
The King's youngest son has not yet seen his father in person, but they are said to have talked.

Then enter Earl Spencer, the King's former brother-in-law, with his memoir, Swan Song, criticising the King's response to the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. It triggered a strong pushback from the Palace.

And in recent days, the serious claims made about Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, have drawn his daughter into a complex tale involving global police forces, sexual abuse allegations and further family trauma.
An impactful and successful Caribbean tour is a chance to switch focus.
But if royal stories back home are running hot, it can be hard to focus minds on the King's engagements over four thousand miles (6,437km) away.

blocks.caption: Image caption,  Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has received a lot of coverage

blocks.text: Image source, Mark Cuthbert/Getty Images
Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has received a lot of coverage
Former Foreign Secretary David Lammy, who has strong family ties to the Caribbean, has accompanied the King on a number of trips outside the UK.

"He is our head of state. He is amongst some of the most recognisable figures in the world. For a small country like Guyana, the validation of a state visit is huge," said the Tottenham MP whose father came to the UK from what was then British Guiana and who also has relatives in Antigua and Barbuda. "My mother would forever recall the Queen's visit in 1996."
But there was also a recognition of that royal trip jeopardy.
"Knowing Guyana, Antigua and Barbuda as well as I do, he will be overwhelmingly received positively," Lammy said. "But these are lively democracies in which of course there will be some dissent."

A transatlantic flight, three countries over nine days and about 36 separate engagements when you're closing in on your 78th birthday is an intense schedule. It is also a reminder that the King is still dealing with a cancer diagnosis and having regular treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated its position that he is on a "positive trajectory".

Queen Camilla will only accompany the King on the Antigua and Barbuda leg of the visit for Chogm and a number of other engagements, including some around her own areas of interest – literacy and supporting efforts to end violence against women and girls.
The Queen, who will be 80 next July, is known to find the pace and hot conditions of some royal tours gruelling.
This is a trip that comes with potential pitfalls but also the possibility of great reward for the King.
"The King can be an extraordinarily empathetic and in tune figure," Sir Anthony said.
"He could play a blinder here."
Additional reporting by Felicity Baker

articles.title: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and Tyapa
articles.summary: For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year journey from Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.

blocks.text: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and Tyapa
Image source, Wild Ireland press handout
Tyapa (left) and Bu (right) were previously kept in small cages in the Republic of Dagestan in Russia
ByMike McBride
BBC News NI

After years in cramped cages, two brown bears are adjusting to their new life following a remarkable rescue mission that spanned multiple countries, was disrupted by two major conflicts and involved more than 100 people.
For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year rescue journey from the Republic of Dagestan in Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.
One bear had spent their life forced to perform in a circus, while the other was confined to a cage so small they could not stand upright.
Today, the bears are now adjusting to a totally different world among the trees and grass at Wild Ireland, a sanctuary for rescued animals in County Donegal.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tyapa is slowly settling into her new surroundings in Burnfoot, County Donegal

blocks.text: Tyapa is slowly settling into her new surroundings in Burnfoot, County Donegal
Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin first learned about Bu and Tyapa in 2021 and committed to bringing them to safety in Donegal.
The sanctuary, located in Burnfoot, opened in October 2019 and provides a safe space for animals, including brown bears, monkeys, wolves, and lynx.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin says the bears' health improvements since their arrival have been remarkable

blocks.text: Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin says the bears' health improvements since their arrival have been remarkable
McLaughlin said the two bears were in extremely poor health when they were first rescued.
Former circus bear Bu had spent years confined to a small indoor cage after being forced to perform.

McLaughlin said Tyapa had lived in a cage measuring just 2.5m by 2.5m by 2m, which was too low for him to stand upright and had no roof, which left him exposed to the harsh winters and blistering summer heat.
The bear had no water dish and relied on a hose for drinking water. McLaughlin said he was being raised to be killed for an eventual taxidermy display.
When the bears were rescued, both were severely malnourished and showed signs of psychological trauma.
Blood tests also revealed serious kidney problems associated with prolonged dehydration.
How do you transport two large bears?
Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made the original transport route through Ukraine impossible, said McLaughlin.

An alternative route through the Middle East was then explored, but plans were disrupted again in February 2026 when the escalating conflict involving Iran led to airspace closures and flight disruptions across the region.

More than 100 people were involved in the rescue operation, including volunteers, lawyers, veterinarians, animal transport specialists, cargo teams and officials in Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Ireland.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The bears travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in the Republic of Ireland on 3 August 2026

blocks.text: The bears travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in the Republic of Ireland on 3 August 2026
In late October 2025, Dima and Yana Kim, who work at Tiger House, a sanctuary near St Petersburg that cares for former circus tigers, embarked on a 36-hour drive to Dagestan to rescue the bears.

Bu and Tyapa had to be cut out of their rusting steel cages, sedated and placed in secure transport crates for the journey back to Tiger House, where they received veterinary treatment and underwent quarantine.
After months of preparation and repeated delays, the bears eventually travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in Ireland in August.
Health improvements since arriving
Since arriving at Wild Ireland, McLaughlin said both bears have gained weight, their coats have improved, and follow-up blood tests have shown that their kidney function has returned to normal.
He said their habitat provides woodland, water and room to explore, as well as sheltered areas where they can retreat or move out of public view if they would like some privacy.
"These bears have suffered trauma and the first step of that recovery process is get them back out into the forest, get their paws into the soil and on the grass and get them exploring.
"We hope they can now have a full and happy life."
Working with bears isn't your normal 9-5
Working with bears is certainly not your everyday job, but for Wild Ireland team member Chloe McElhatton, it's one she absolutely relishes.
Chloe has been working at Wild Ireland for just over a year. She studied zoology at Queen's University Belfast, completing a four-year degree before joining the team.
"This is obviously a very unique job, and it's quite different from what most people would do," she said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Chloe McElhatton is part of the bear team at Wild Ireland and says looking after bears is not your average 9-5 job

blocks.text: Chloe McElhatton is part of the bear team at Wild Ireland and says looking after bears is not your average 9-5 job

"We've done a lot of work hiding food around the bear habitats, encouraging them to search and forage for it themselves and this promotes their natural behaviours and helps them become more comfortable in that new open space," she said.
"Over time, we've seen their confidence build, and you can see great changes, both physically and mentally, in both of them."
What do visitors think of the bears?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Liam, who is from France, says the two bears are big and impressive

blocks.text: Liam, who is from France, says the two bears are big and impressive
Liam, who is from France, said the bears were one of his favourite animals to see when visiting the park.
"Very big and very impressive," is how he summed up Bu and Tyapa.
"I saw chickens, some wolves and some monkeys and then the bears which were definitely my favourite."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Chris Roberts is a regular visitor to Wild Ireland and came to visit hoping to see a glimpse of the two new bears

blocks.text: Chris Roberts is a regular visitor to Wild Ireland and came to visit hoping to see a glimpse of the two new bears
Chris Roberts is from Manorcunningham, about 20 minutes from Wild Ireland, and has been visiting the site ever since it first opened in 2019.
"I've lost count of how many times we've been here, but we really wanted to come down today to see if we could catch a glimpse of Bu and Tyapa.
"It was fantastic to see them in the flesh.
"We absolutely loved it and are delighted to see them doing so well, especially considering their backstory and the awful conditions they were once kept in."

articles.title: A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?
articles.summary: More than a million people flocked to Busan to catch a glimpse of the female dusky shark they called Bukangi.

blocks.text: A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?
Watch: BBC follows operation to rescue shark stranded in South Korean canal
ByJake Kwon
Seoul correspondent Reporting fromBusan, South Korea
As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.

He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.
South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.
With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.
The first task was to determine the species.
Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans.
The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal.
The shark had to return to sea.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The dusky shark was first spotted in the canal in mid-September

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The dusky shark was first spotted in the canal in mid-September
A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid.
They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.
Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.
As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.
Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".
People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.
Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online.

blocks.caption: Map of the coast of Busan, South Korea, where a shark was spotted in a canal near Bukhang (North Port) Waterfront Park.

blocks.text: City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot.

A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.
Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals.
Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A poster encourages support for a baseball stadium "on behalf of Bukangi"

blocks.text: Image source, Hosu Lee/BBC
A poster encourages support for a baseball stadium "on behalf of Bukangi"
More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.
The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port.

"It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for her… It's a lot of fun."
But officials couldn't leave Bukangi in the canal.
As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.
Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kim Joo-eun and her nieces were among Bukangi's many visitors

blocks.text: Kim Joo-eun and her nieces were among Bukangi's many visitors

At the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.
But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.
On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.

At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.
The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests.
It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The canal leading up to the Busan port where Bukangi was stranded

blocks.text: The canal leading up to the Busan port where Bukangi was stranded
With each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace.
On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".
When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!"
"I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jeong protesting against Bukangi's "eviction", alongside a man demanding officials "protect Bukangi's right to self-determination"

blocks.text: Jeong protesting against Bukangi's "eviction", alongside a man demanding officials "protect Bukangi's right to self-determination"
Others thought it was time for her to return home.

"I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."
People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said.
"She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bukangi became a sensation, drawing the curious and the concerned

blocks.text: Bukangi became a sensation, drawing the curious and the concerned
Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south.
"This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."

Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi.
On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.
This left her trapped between the two layers.
Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.
Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Staying in the canal is dangerous for Bukangi, says marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo

blocks.text: Staying in the canal is dangerous for Bukangi, says marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo
There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign.
Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters.
She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.

But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media.
For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea.
Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul

articles.title: 'They’re the nicest people': Obama mocks Trump for hitting Canada with tariffs
articles.summary: Former U.S. president Barack Obama slammed the Trump administration's tariff regime on Saturday, noting the absurdity of engaging in a trade war with Canada.

blocks.text: World·New
Former U.S. president Barack Obama slammed the Trump administration's tariff regime on Saturday, noting the absurdity of engaging in a trade war with Canada.
'These are the people who gave us maple syrup and Martin Short': ex-president
Obama mocks Trump over trade war with 'the people who gave us maple syrup'
Former U.S. president Barack Obama slammed the Trump administration's tariff regime on Saturday, and mocked the absurdity of engaging in a trade war with long-time ally Canada.
"The big trade war he's starting now is with that well-known evil empire: Canada," Obama said at a Cleveland rally for Democratic candidates in Ohio.
"These are the people who gave us maple syrup and Martin Short.… They're the nicest people," he joked. "They're our friendly neighbours to the north, and he's picking a fight with them?"

Obama, who has been stumping for Democrats ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, also criticized Donald Trump's tariffs policy more generally, saying they have had the expected negative effect on U.S. consumers who bear the brunt of the rising costs.
Those rising costs have hampered Republican chances in the midterms, especially in border states, leading Trump to announce on Friday that he plans to lift tariffs on some Canadian products.
Trump to lift some tariffs on Canada before U.S. midterms
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said on CBC's Power & Politics that Ottawa isn't expecting a deal before before the Nov. 3 vote.

The U.S. and Canada have been engaging in retaliatory tariffs since Trump first launched his levy campaign last year — ostensibly to combat alleged fentanyl trafficking and trade imbalances — and trade talks broke down in August.
Trump repeated lashes at Canada
Trump has routinely used Canada as a punching bag in his campaign rally speeches.
"At some point, we're making a deal that's gonna be amazing," Trump said during a stop in Highland Heights, Ky., on Oct. 17.
"But for years we've lost billions and billions of dollars, and they just felt so emboldened."
He was cheered when he called former prime minister Justin Trudeau a "loser" before taking aim at his successor, Mark Carney.
"Your current guy's good … he's a nice guy, but he's not nice when it comes to trade," he said.
"They're learning and they're suffering."

articles.title: Who are the candidates in Brazil's presidential election?
articles.summary: Voters in Sunday's election are choosing between two very different candidates, as Americas correspondent Ione Wells reports from Rio de Janeiro.

blocks.text: Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday to vote for their next president.
They are choosing between Brazil's current left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin.
As Americas correspondent Ione Wells reports from Rio de Janeiro, voters are choosing between two very different candidates.

articles.title: Who is B.C.'s new premier Lorne Doerkson?

image.caption: B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson celebrates on stage during provincial election night in Vancouver on Saturday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia

B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson spent his victory speech Saturday night introducing himself to British Columbians, and celebrating the "trailblazers" who came to the province searching for gold and a better life.
Doerkson becomes 1st premier from B.C.'s Interior since Bill Bennett left office in 1986
B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson struck political gold Saturday night.
The former small-town newspaper publisher delivered a stunning defeat to David Eby's NDP and led the B.C. Conservatives to a commanding majority government.
Early Sunday morning, Doerkson's Conservatives were leading in 64 ridings, reducing the NDP to just 27 seats and toppling several cabinet ministers.
It's a remarkable turnaround for a political party that was in disarray just five weeks ago, days before a snap election was called.
But where his political opponents may have seen weakness, Doerkson said British Columbians chose instead to seize an opportunity.

"For a very long time, a lot of British Columbians have felt like Victoria forgot about them, like the map maybe stopped at Hope," Doerkson told a throng of more than 1,000 supporters at the Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver.
"But tonight the whole map counts."
FULL SPEECH: Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson's victory speech
Rodeos to newspapers to politics
Born in New Westminster, Doerkson grew up in Surrey and the B.C. Interior, before settling in Williams Lake, where he raised a family.
He spent 20 years publishing community newspapers and volunteering with local business and community service groups before entering politics.
"That was a very good education for me," he told supporters. "You learn what’s really going on in a town: who’s hiring, who’s closing, who’s hoping."
Doerkson was first elected in Cariboo-Chilcotin as a B.C. Liberal in 2020, and later joined John Rustad's fledgling Conservative caucus.
His victory makes him the first premier from B.C.'s Interior since Bill Bennett left office in 1986.

items: Unexpected leader: Lorne Doerkson pitches himself to British Columbians

blocks.text: Doerkson was on his way home from South Africa last month when he learned his Conservative caucus colleagues wanted him to take over the party as interim leader.
Kerry-Lynne Findlay had just resigned after months of scandals that led to the departure or expulsion of more than a dozen MLAs.
Doerkson admitted he needed convincing.
"Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," he said in a pre-election interview with CBC News.
Lorne Doerkson speaks to supporters in the crowd during provincial election night Saturday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)
Promises to cut income taxes, red tape

Doerkson spent his victory speech Saturday night introducing himself to British Columbians at the same time as celebrating the "trailblazers" who came to the province searching for gold and a better life.
It's a spirit he told supporters that still animates the province, where people want to build something big, from resource communities through to the big metro areas.
"That is the trailblazing spirit of British Columbia and it never left, it just needs government that’s on its side," he said.
CBC News projects a B.C. Conservative majority government
Doerkson reiterated promises to cut red tape "like it’s never been cut before," speed up forestry and mining permits, and triple natural gas production by 2035.
"A province only works if all of it works," he said.
"A mill running in Quesnel keeps a trucker working in Surrey. A mine opening in the north keeps the port busy in Delta. It’s one economy and it runs through every town on our map."
Doerkson also pledged no new taxes and health care that is "fully and publicly funded."
Still, questions remain about how he'll pay for everything, including a promise to cut income taxes by $1,000 a year.
The province is already on track to see a $13.8-billion deficit in 2026-27.
The NDP spent their campaign warning that the Conservatives' platform could mean cuts to health care and education.
Speaking in Vancouver Saturday, Doerkson reiterated election promises, including to cut red tape 'like it’s never been cut before.' (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)
Overcoming divisions
As premier-designate, Doerkson now faces the challenge of not only governing but keeping together a coalition that includes social conservatives and more centrist, fiscal conservatives.
And though he has promised to repeal B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People’s Act, he appealed to First Nations communities as partners in the province’s development.
"This future is one we build together as partners with the certainty that all of us need," he said.
One source of division Doerkson won't need to deal with immediately will be the NDP.

With preliminary results showing New Democrats reduced to fewer than 30 seats, the Official Opposition's first priority will be choosing a new leader to replace David Eby who announced Saturday that he will step down.
With files from Matt Preprost, Simon Little and Katie DeRosa

articles.title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
articles.summary: Officials have so far managed to avoid a repeat of last weekend's rioting and looting as hundreds of thousands took part in demonstrations.

blocks.text: Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.

President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.

Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.

In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.

"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.
The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.

Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of Orléans which proceeded peacefully.
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.

In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.

Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.

Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

articles.title: Ukraine: Starlink satellite speeds restored to normal
articles.summary: The announcement comes after Starlink and Starshield restrictions had disrupted military operations in Ukraine and sparked tensions with the US.

image.caption: Ukrainian soldiers handle a Starlink terminalImage: Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were fully functional on Saturday, the Ukrainian government said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said speeds for Starlink and Starshield started returning to normal overnight.
Ukraine's ‌defense ministry confirmed on Saturday that the connection remained stable at over 400 kilometers per hour (kph).
"The main thing for today is ‌that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," Zelenskyy said on Telegram.
"This is crucial. This really matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered 'Shaheds,'" he added.
The announcement comes after over a week of Starlink and Starshield restrictions that disrupted military operations in Ukraine and sparked tensions with the US.
Ukrainian officials said that the capped speeds of 160 kph had hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
What caused Starlink's restrictions?
Starlink is operated by rocket company SpaceX, owned by billionaire Elon Musk, who is a close ally of US President Donald Trump.

US newspaper The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported earlier this week that US officials believed Musk acted unilaterally in capping the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network.
According to the WSJ report, officials signaled that Trump did not specifically order retribution against Kyiv.
But in response to the report, Musk said that "any limits to speed or usage" of Starshied were "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Both Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied that the Pentagon had directed any changes.
It remains unclear who is responsible for last week's Starlink slowdown.
Kyiv has come to question Washington's support over intelligence sharing, amid speculation that the White House may have ordered the restrictions on Starshield.

The Starlink slowdown came as the relationship between the US and Ukraine has become strained after President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

articles.title: Tens of thousands of Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff
articles.summary:
Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro

Tens of thousands of supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro and Tiago Rogero in Belo Horizonte

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.
Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.

On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.

Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”

blocks.caption: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves to supporters on Saturday. Photograph: Dhavid Normando/AP

blocks.text: “The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.

“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.
“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.

Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.

However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.

blocks.caption: People watch a televised debate between Flávio Bolsonaro and his election rival on Friday. Photograph: Adriano Machado/Reuters

blocks.text: Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”
“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo.

Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.
“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.

blocks.caption: Lula supporters on Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

blocks.text: Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.
Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.
Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.

“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.
Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.
“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.

“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.

Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”
“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.

blocks.caption: Some Lula supporters believe he can overturn the lead his rival secured in the first round of voting. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

blocks.text: Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.

Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.
“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.

“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US after Donald Trump’s January invasion, he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro supporters, some with the flags of the US, Israel and Brazil, also held last-minute rallies on Saturday. Photograph: Raquel Cunha/Reuters

blocks.text: Antonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”

Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.
Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.
“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing
articles.summary:
Government estimates at least 400,000 people took part, but trade unions say the number is double that

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful…

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.

But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.
Police also fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police.
The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that.

More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.
At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

blocks.caption: At the end of the Paris demonstration, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged and threw glass bottles and stones at police. Photograph: Thibault Camus/AP

blocks.text: At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”

One 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is currently blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.

At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue each weekend.
after newsletter promotion

Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”

Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them and we have to stand together.”

She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”

In Orléans, thousands of people shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress being held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, who is a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

The interior minister, Laurent Nunez, said 135 people had been arrested in France and weapons had been confiscated, including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana sword and airsoft weapons.

articles.title: German national facing trial for alleged attempt to join IS
articles.summary: A 21-year-old suspect is being held in pre-trial detention for allegedly trying to join the "Islamic State" terror group.

image.caption: The public prosecutor general (Generalbundesanwalt beim Bundesgerichtshof) is the federal prosecutor of Germany (File: 2019)Image: Christoph Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's prosecutor's office said that a German national has been placed in pre-trial detention for allegedly attempting to join the so-called "Islamic State" terror group, while abroad, German news agency dpa reported.
What is known about the case
The agency cited a spokeswoman for the Federal Prosecutor's Office as saying that an arrest warrant had been executed and that a 21-year-old was extradited to Germany.
The suspect is accused of travelling to Ethiopia from Berlin in January 2025, with the purpose of joining the IS terror group in Somalia.
Prosecutors allege that he never reached Somalia, but instead traveled to Pakistan to join IS, where he was reportedly arrested in February 2025.
The suspect stands accused of attempted membership in a terrorist organization abroad. He is also accused of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state.
Germany and the so-called "Islamic State"
Islamic extremists have carried out several attacks in Germany over the years. The deadliest was when a truck rammed a Berlin Christmas market in 2016, killing 12 people.
In July a German court sentenced a man and a woman to lengthy prison sentences for enslaving and abusing two Yazidi girls under the so-called "Islamic State" group in Iraq.
The Iraqi couple was convicted of war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. They were also convicted of sexually abusing children and aiding and abetting the listed offenses.
The couple, identified as Twana H.S. and Asia R.A., in line with German privacy laws, were most recently living in Germany and were arrested in the southern state of Bavaria in April in 2024.
